Every section is designed to build muscle memory through progressive difficulty: theory → troubleshooting → hands-on practice.

📝 Part 1: 200 Multiple Choice Questions

Purpose: Build foundational Helm knowledge across 5 categories. Every question has a detailed explanation with real-world context from anihpj/jobpost.

Categories covered: Core Concepts (Q1-Q30), Chart Structure & Templates (Q31-Q90), Release Management (Q91-Q130), Dependencies & Plugins (Q131-Q160), Repos, Security & CI/CD (Q161-Q200).

How to use: Answer 20-30 questions per study session. Read the explanation even for correct answers — they contain deeper insights. Target: 85%+ correct before moving to Part 2.

🔧 Part 2: 100 Troubleshooting Issues

Purpose: Learn systematic Helm diagnostic reasoning. Each issue follows the same pattern: Symptom → Terminal Output → 15 Causes (Most Likely / Less Likely / New Cluster) → Diagnostic Commands → Solution → Personal Advice.

Categories: Template Rendering (HT1-HT15), Release Management (HT16-HT30), Dependencies (HT31-HT45), Repos & Registry (HT46-HT60), CI/CD & GitOps (HT61-HT75), Hooks & Tests (HT76-HT85), Security & RBAC (HT86-HT100).

How to use: Read the symptom first — try to diagnose BEFORE reading the causes. This builds the diagnostic muscle memory critical for real-world Helm debugging.

🧪 Part 3: 100 Hands-On Lab Scenarios

Purpose: Practice real Helm tasks on your 6-cluster lab. Each scenario deploys anihpj/jobpost via Helm with an intentional bug — you find and fix it.

Structure per scenario: APP STORY → FILE STRUCTURE → Helm install/upgrade (with bug) → Observe symptoms → Debug commands → Full answer with before/after outputs → Fix commands → Cleanup.

How to use: Run each scenario on the specified cluster (ksw → 1-6). Time yourself — aim for 5-7 minutes per scenario. Target: Complete all 100 scenarios before going live with Helm in production.

🌳 Decision Trees + Appendices

Decision Trees (DT1-DT15): Quick diagnostic flowcharts for the 15 most common Helm issues. Start at the symptom, answer yes/no questions, arrive at the fix.

Appendices (A-M): Answer keys, top 50 Helm commands, chart structure reference, template function cheat sheet, CI/CD pipeline templates, learning roadmap, difficulty index, and the ⚡ Appendix M: 20 Helm Command Patterns — your last-30-minutes cram sheet.

How to use: Decision trees for quick reference during practice. Appendix M for exam prep. Cheat sheet (Appendix I) for daily Helm usage.

🏆 Skills You'll Master — Before vs After This Guide

❌ BEFORE — Common Beginner Pitfalls

  • ❌ "Why do I have 14 YAML files for one app?" — No packaging strategy
  • ❌ "I changed the image tag in 3 places but forgot the 4th" — Manual copy-paste errors
  • ❌ "How do I deploy the same app to dev/staging/prod?" — No environment management
  • ❌ "helm install worked but I can't remember what values I used" — No release tracking

  • ✅ Manage dev/staging/prod with values-{env}.yaml overrides
  • ✅ Track every deployment with helm history and helm get values
  • ✅ Rollback any failed upgrade in seconds with helm rollback
  • ✅ Use helm lint, helm template, and --dry-run to catch errors before deploy
  • ✅ Integrate Helm into GitHub Actions, ArgoCD, and GitLab CI/CD pipelines

🚨 Critical Helm Do's & Don'ts
  • ✅ DO: Use helm lint before every commit — catches syntax errors, missing values, and schema violations.
  • ✅ DO: Use helm install --dry-run --debug to see exactly what will be deployed before touching the cluster.
  • ✅ DO: Use --atomic for production deployments — auto-rollback on failure prevents broken states.
  • ✅ DO: Use helm history before every upgrade — know what revision you're on.
  • ❌ DON'T: Put plaintext secrets in values.yaml — use helm-secrets plugin or External Secrets Operator.
  • ❌ DON'T: Skip helm dependency update when Chart.lock is out of sync — you'll deploy wrong subchart versions.
  • ❌ DON'T: Use helm template and pipe to kubectl — you lose release tracking, history, and rollback.
  • ❌ DON'T: Forget --namespace — Helm installs to default unless you specify. Use --create-namespace for new namespaces.

📊 Helm Overview & Learning StrategySTRATEGY

What Is Helm & How To Master It

Helm is the package manager for Kubernetes — think apt/yum/brew but for Kubernetes applications. It packages all the YAML manifests for an application into a single Chart that can be installed with one command: helm install anihpj ./helm/anihpj.

5 Core Knowledge Domains: Chart Structure & Templates (30%), Release Management & Lifecycle (20%), Repos, Security & CI/CD/GitOps (20%), Helm Core Concepts & Architecture (15%), Dependencies, Hooks, Tests & Plugins (15%). Chart Templates are the heart of Helm — master Go templating and you master Helm.

Learning Strategy: Start with the Pre-Learning foundations (F.1-F.5) → Build theory with MCQs (Part 1) → Practice diagnostics with Issues (Part 2) → Hands-on muscle memory with Scenarios (Part 3). Use ksw to switch between your 6 clusters for different scenarios.

Your 6-cluster lab (below) is where you'll test every Helm chart you build. Use ksw to switch between clusters. Each scenario in Part 3 specifies which cluster to use. Always verify context before helm install!

📚 Pre-Learning: Helm FoundationsF.1–F.5

🟢 Novice-Friendly: Building Your Helm Mental Model

F.1 What Problem Does Helm Solve? — The "Wall of YAML" problem. Deploying anihpj/jobpost needs 14 raw YAML files with duplicated values (image tags, DB passwords, etc.). Helm packages everything into a single chart with templating — one helm install command deploys the entire application stack.

F.2 Helm Core Concepts — Chart = Package (.tgz file with templates + values), Repository = Registry (like Docker Hub for charts), Release = Running instance of a chart (named, versioned, trackable), Values = Configuration inputs that drive template rendering.

F.3 The anihpj/jobpost Application Stack — Web tier (Django + nginx), API tier (Django REST + gunicorn), Database tier (PostgreSQL 15 StatefulSet), Cache/Queue tier (Redis). Complete file tree with k8s/ (14 raw YAML files) and helm/anihpj/ (templated chart) side by side.

F.4 Helm vs kubectl vs Kustomize — Decision matrix: kubectl apply (1-2 simple files), Kustomize (environment overlays, no templating), Helm (complex templating, release lifecycle, chart distribution). Hybrid: Helm + Kustomize post-renderer pattern.

F.5 Your 6-Cluster Lab with Helm — How Helm connects to your clusters (uses ~/.kube/config), installing Helm (choco/apt/brew), first commands (helm repo add, helm install, helm list), safety practices (test on kind-cka-lab before kubeadm).

If you're new to Helm: Read through F.1–F.5 before diving into Part 1. These foundations will give you the mental models needed to understand the MCQs, troubleshooting issues, and lab scenarios. The entire guide builds the anihpj/jobpost Helm chart as its running example.

⛵ Category 1: Helm Core Concepts & Architecture (15%)Q1-Q30

🟢 Novice-Friendly: Understanding What Helm IS & Why It Exists

This category is about what Helm is and how it works. Think of Helm like a package manager for your operating system — apt-get install nginx on Ubuntu, brew install nginx on macOS. Helm does the same for Kubernetes: helm install anihpj ./chart deploys your entire application stack (PostgreSQL + Redis + Django API + Django Web + Ingress + NetworkPolicy) in one command. For anihpj/jobpost, instead of managing 14 separate YAML files, you manage one chart with values-driven templating.

Q1-Q30 30 Questions 🟢 Beginner

1.1 Why Helm? — The Problem & The SolutionQ1-Q6

Core Concepts Q1 of 200
What is Helm? Choose the BEST description of what Helm does in the Kubernetes ecosystem.
A) Helm is a Kubernetes distribution (like OpenShift or Rancher) that provides an alternative control plane with extra features
B) Helm is the package manager for Kubernetes — it helps you define, install, version, share, and upgrade Kubernetes applications by packaging all manifests, templates, and default configuration into a single portable unit called a Chart
C) Helm is a container runtime interface (CRI) implementation that replaces Docker and containerd for running pods
D) Helm is a monitoring and observability platform that collects metrics, logs, and traces from Kubernetes clusters
✅ Correct Answer: B

Helm is the package manager for Kubernetes. Just like apt-get (Debian/Ubuntu), yum (RHEL/CentOS), or brew (macOS) let you install, upgrade, and remove software on your operating system, Helm lets you do the same for Kubernetes applications. It packages all the YAML manifests, templates, and default configuration for an application into a single, versioned, shareable unit called a Chart.

The key innovation: Instead of managing 14 separate YAML files for anihpj/jobpost, you run ONE command — helm install anihpj ./helm/anihpj — and Helm deploys PostgreSQL + Redis + Django API + Django Web + Ingress + NetworkPolicy + HPA + RBAC, all configured correctly from your values.yaml.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Helm — The "Package Manager for Kubernetes" Mental Model
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                     PACKAGE MANAGER ANALOGY                      │
  │                                                                 │
  │     YOUR OPERATING SYSTEM               YOUR KUBERNETES CLUSTER   │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────┐      ┌─────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │  apt-get install nginx   │      │  helm install anihpj ./chart│  │
  │  │                          │      │                             │  │
  │  │  📦 Package: nginx.deb   │      │  📦 Chart: anihpj-1.0.tgz   │  │
  │  │  📚 Repo: apt repository │      │  📚 Repo: Helm repo / OCI   │  │
  │  │  🏠 Installed at: /usr   │      │  🏠 Release: "anihpj"       │  │
  │  │  ⚙️ Config: /etc/nginx   │      │  ⚙️ Config: values.yaml     │  │
  │  │  🔢 Version: nginx -v    │      │  🔢 Version: helm list      │  │
  │  │  🗑️ Remove: apt remove   │      │  🗑️ Remove: helm uninstall  │  │
  │  │  ⏪ Rollback: apt install │      │  ⏪ Rollback: helm rollback  │  │
  │  └──────────────────────────┘      └─────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                                                                 │
  │  THE "WALL OF YAML" PROBLEM — WHAT HELM SOLVES:                 │
  │                                                                 │
  │  WITHOUT HELM (14 separate files):                              │
  │  kubectl apply -f 00-namespace.yaml                             │
  │  kubectl apply -f 01-secrets.yaml                                │
  │  kubectl apply -f 02-configmap.yaml                              │
  │  kubectl apply -f 03-postgres-sts.yaml                           │
  │  ... (10 more files — each with hardcoded values)               │
  │  → 14 commands, values duplicated across files, easy to miss    │
  │                                                                 │
  │  WITH HELM (1 command):                                          │
  │  helm install anihpj ./helm/anihpj -n anihpj --create-namespace │
  │  → 1 command, values centralized in values.yaml, versioned      │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

🚀 Why Helm 3 is the standard: Helm 3 is client-only — unlike Helm 2 which required a server-side Tiller component (a security nightmare with cluster-admin privileges), Helm 3 uses your existing ~/.kube/config and standard Kubernetes RBAC. No extra cluster components. No god-mode service account. Just your helm binary talking directly to the API server with your permissions.

🔗 Connection to anihpj/jobpost: Throughout this guide, you'll build a Helm chart for the anihpj/jobpost Django application. You'll transform 14 raw Kubernetes YAML files into a single, configurable, reusable Chart — and learn every Helm concept along the way. By the end, helm install anihpj ./helm/anihpj -f values-prod.yaml will deploy your entire production job board to any cluster in one shot.

Core Concepts Q2 of 200
You are deploying anihpj/jobpost to Kubernetes. You have 14 separate YAML files (namespace, secrets, configmap, PostgreSQL StatefulSet, PostgreSQL Service, Redis Deployment, Redis Service, Django API Deployment, Django API Service, Django API HPA, Django Web Deployment, Django Web Service, Ingress, NetworkPolicy). What is the #1 problem with managing an application this way?
A) Kubernetes cannot handle more than 10 YAML files per application — you must use Helm for apps of this size
B) The YAML files are automatically deleted after 30 days unless managed by a package manager
C) This is the "Wall of YAML" problem — every environment (dev/staging/prod) needs slightly different values (image tags, replica counts, DB passwords, resource limits), forcing you to copy-paste-modify 14 files per environment. A single missed value causes outages. There is no versioning, no rollback, and no reuse across teams
D) Raw YAML files cannot be applied with kubectl — they must first be converted to JSON by a package manager like Helm
✅ Correct Answer: C

The "Wall of YAML" is the exact problem Helm was created to solve. When an application like anihpj/jobpost needs 14+ Kubernetes resources, managing them as raw YAML files leads to: (1) duplication — the same values appear in multiple files, (2) environment drift — dev/staging/prod diverge because someone forgot to update one file, (3) no versioning — you can't track what changed between deployments, and (4) no reuse — every team reinvents the same YAML patterns.

📝 Detailed Explanation
The "Wall of YAML" — 14 Files × 3 Environments = 42 Opportunities for Error
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              THE WALL OF YAML — anihpj/jobpost                  │
  │                                                                 │
  │  DEV ENV         STAGING ENV         PROD ENV                   │
  │  ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐        ┌──────────┐              │
  │  │ 14 files │    │ 14 files │        │ 14 files │              │
  │  │ replica:1│    │ replica:2│        │ replica:5│  ← Different! │
  │  │ cpu:250m │    │ cpu:500m │        │ cpu:2    │  ← Different! │
  │  │ db:1Gi   │    │ db:10Gi  │        │ db:100Gi │  ← Different! │
  │  │ image:dev│    │ image:rc │        │ image:v2 │  ← Different! │
  │  └──────────┘    └──────────┘        └──────────┘              │
  │                                                                 │
  │  ❌ PROBLEMS:                                                   │
  │  • 42 values to keep in sync across 3 × 14 files               │
  │  • "Did I update the DB password in staging AND prod?"         │
  │  • "Why does dev work but staging returns 500?"                │
  │  • "Who changed the replica count last week and why?"          │
  │  • New team member: "Which of these 14 files do I edit?"       │
  │                                                                 │
  │  ✅ HELM SOLUTION (1 chart, 3 value files):                     │
  │  helm/anihpj/                                                   │
  │  ├── templates/  (14 templates — written ONCE)                 │
  │  ├── values.yaml      (defaults)                                │
  │  ├── values-dev.yaml  (dev overrides)                           │
  │  └── values-prod.yaml (prod overrides)                          │
  │                                                                 │
  │  helm install anihpj ./helm/anihpj -f values-dev.yaml          │
  │  helm install anihpj ./helm/anihpj -f values-prod.yaml         │
  │  → Same templates, different values. No copy-paste errors.     │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

🔗 Connection to anihpj/jobpost: Your k8s/ directory has exactly this problem right now — 14 files with hardcoded values. In Part 3, you'll convert every one of those files into Helm templates, centralize all configurable values into values.yaml, and deploy to all 6 clusters with environment-specific overrides. One chart, infinite environments.

Core Concepts Q3 of 200
What is the core purpose of templating in Helm? Why not just use plain YAML files?
A) Templating applies the DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself) principle to Kubernetes manifests — you write the resource structure ONCE with {{ .Values.xxx }} placeholders, and Helm injects the correct values for each environment at install time. Template once, deploy anywhere
B) Templating makes YAML files load faster because the Kubernetes API server can parse Go templates more efficiently than raw YAML
C) Templating is required by Kubernetes — the API server rejects any YAML that wasn't generated by a template engine
D) Templating encrypts sensitive values like database passwords so they never appear in plaintext in any file
✅ Correct Answer: A

Templating is Helm's superpower. You write the structure of a Kubernetes resource (Deployment, Service, ConfigMap) once using Go template syntax, and Helm fills in the environment-specific values at install time. This is the DRY principle applied to infrastructure-as-code.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Template Once, Deploy Anywhere — The DRY Principle in Helm
  TEMPLATE (written once)                 VALUES (per environment)
  ┌────────────────────────────┐         ┌────────────────────────┐
  │ # django-api-deploy.yaml   │         │ # values-dev.yaml      │
  │ replicas: {{ .Values.api   │         │ api:                   │
  │   .replicaCount }}         │         │   replicaCount: 1      │
  │ image: {{ .Values.api      │         │   image:               │
  │   .image }}:{{ .Values.api │         │     tag: "dev-latest"  │
  │   .tag }}                  │         │   resources:           │
  │ resources:                 │         │     cpu: "250m"        │
  │   requests:                │         │     memory: "256Mi"    │
  │     cpu: {{ .Values.api    │         │                        │
  │       .resources.cpu }}    │         │ # values-prod.yaml     │
  │     memory: {{ .Values.api │         │ api:                   │
  │       .resources.memory }} │         │   replicaCount: 5      │
  └────────────────────────────┘         │   image:               │
                                         │     tag: "v2.5.1"      │
  SAME TEMPLATE +                        │   resources:           │
  DIFFERENT VALUES =                      │     cpu: "2000m"      │
  CORRECT DEPLOYMENT                      │     memory: "4Gi"     │
  FOR EVERY ENVIRONMENT                   └────────────────────────┘

Without templating, you'd need 3 separate copies of django-api-deploy.yaml — one for dev, one for staging, one for prod — with hardcoded values in each. Change the health check endpoint? Edit 3 files. Add a new environment variable? Edit 3 files. With Helm templating: edit the template ONCE, update values per environment. This is why Helm is indispensable at scale.

Core Concepts Q4 of 200
When should you use raw kubectl apply vs Helm for deploying to Kubernetes?
A) Always use Helm — kubectl apply is deprecated and will be removed in a future Kubernetes version
B) Use kubectl apply for 1-2 simple, static resources (a single Pod, a quick test Namespace). Use Helm when you need templating, environment-specific configuration, release versioning, rollback capability, or when distributing an application to other teams or the public
C) Use kubectl apply for production, Helm only for development — Helm's templating is too slow for production workloads
D) They are functionally identical — kubectl apply and helm install produce exactly the same result with no advantages either way
✅ Correct Answer: B

kubectl apply and Helm serve different purposes. kubectl apply is perfect for quick, one-off resources — a test pod, a simple namespace, a single ConfigMap. Helm shines when you need: templating (same structure, different values), release tracking (helm history, helm rollback), packaging (share charts via repositories), or lifecycle management (hooks for migrations, tests for validation).

📝 Detailed Explanation
kubectl apply vs Helm — Decision Framework
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  SCENARIO                              USE                      │
  ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  1-2 static YAML files, no variables   kubectl apply -f x.yaml  │
  │  Quick test pod or debug container     kubectl run test --rm -it │
  │  One-off namespace creation            kubectl create ns demo    │
  ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  3+ resources that share values        Helm (templating)         │
  │  Need dev/staging/prod variants        Helm (values files)       │
  │  Need release history & rollback       Helm (built-in)           │
  │  Distributing app to other teams       Helm (chart package)      │
  │  CI/CD pipeline deployment             Helm (--atomic, --wait)   │
  │  Database migration before app upgrade Helm (hooks)              │
  │  Smoke tests after deployment          Helm (helm test)          │
  ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  anihpj/jobpost = 14 resources → CLEARLY needs Helm            │
  │  One-off busybox debug pod → kubectl run is sufficient          │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

🔗 Connection to anihpj/jobpost: With 14 interconnected resources (PostgreSQL → Redis → Django API → Django Web → Ingress), shared configuration (DB host, Redis URL, secret keys), and the need to deploy to dev/staging/prod — anihpj/jobpost is a textbook case for Helm. You'll still use kubectl for debugging (kubectl logs, kubectl exec, kubectl describe), but deployment should be helm install.

Core Concepts Q5 of 200
What was the Tiller component in Helm 2, and why was it removed in Helm 3?
A) Tiller was a GUI dashboard for managing Helm charts visually — it was removed because Kubernetes Dashboard replaced its functionality
B) Tiller was a deprecated templating engine — it was removed because Go templates replaced it with better performance
C) Tiller was a separate database that stored chart metadata — it was removed because etcd can now store Helm release data natively
D) Tiller was the server-side component of Helm 2 that ran inside the cluster with cluster-admin privileges to process chart installations. It was removed in Helm 3 for security reasons — it was a single point of failure, had overly broad permissions, and made RBAC enforcement nearly impossible. Helm 3 is client-only, using your existing kubeconfig and RBAC
✅ Correct Answer: D

Tiller was the server-side component of Helm 2. It ran as a pod inside your cluster (typically in kube-system) and had cluster-admin permissions by default. When you ran helm install, your local Helm client sent the chart to Tiller, and Tiller created the resources. This architecture had critical flaws that led to its removal in Helm 3.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Helm 2 (with Tiller) vs Helm 3 (Client-Only) — Architecture Comparison
  HELM 2 (INSECURE)                       HELM 3 (SECURE)
  ┌────────────────────────┐             ┌────────────────────────┐
  │  $ helm install ...     │             │  $ helm install ...     │
  │       │                 │             │       │                 │
  │       ▼                 │             │       ▼                 │
  │  ┌─────────┐            │             │  ~/.kube/config         │
  │  │ TILLER  │  ⚠️        │             │  (YOUR permissions)     │
  │  │ (pod)   │ cluster-   │             │       │                 │
  │  │         │ admin      │             │       ▼                 │
  │  └────┬────┘            │             │  ┌─────────────┐        │
  │       │                 │             │  │ API SERVER  │        │
  │       ▼                 │             │  │ (validates   │        │
  │  ┌─────────────┐        │             │  │  YOUR RBAC) │        │
  │  │ API SERVER  │        │             │  └──────┬──────┘        │
  │  │ (sees Tiller│        │             │         │               │
  │  │  = always   │        │             │         ▼               │
  │  │  ALLOWED)   │        │             │  ┌──────────┐           │
  │  └─────────────┘        │             │  │ RELEASE  │           │
  │                         │             │  │ SECRETS  │           │
  │  ⚠️ PROBLEMS:           │             │  └──────────┘           │
  │  • Tiller = god-mode    │             │                         │
  │  • Anyone with Helm     │             │  ✅ ADVANTAGES:         │
  │    access = cluster-    │             │  • Your kubeconfig =    │
  │    admin effective      │             │    your permissions     │
  │  • No RBAC granularity  │             │  • RBAC works natively  │
  │  • Single point of      │             │  • No extra pod needed  │
  │    failure              │             │  • Release secrets      │
  │  • gRPC + TLS complex   │             │    stored directly      │
  └────────────────────────┘             └────────────────────────┘

🚀 Why this matters: Helm 3's client-only architecture means helm install uses YOUR Kubernetes credentials and YOUR RBAC permissions. If you can't create Deployments with kubectl, you can't create them with Helm. This aligns perfectly with Kubernetes' security model — no backdoors, no god-mode service accounts, no Tiller to patch and maintain.

Core Concepts Q6 of 200
Is Helm a CNCF project? What is its current status and why does this matter?
A) Yes — Helm is a CNCF Graduated project (the highest maturity level alongside Kubernetes, Prometheus, and Envoy). This means it has proven adoption, governance, and security practices at enterprise scale. It joined CNCF in 2015 and graduated in 2020
B) No — Helm is maintained solely by Microsoft and is not part of any open-source foundation
C) Helm is a CNCF Sandbox project — it's still experimental and not recommended for production use
D) Helm was a CNCF project but was archived in 2023 and replaced by Kustomize as the official Kubernetes package manager
✅ Correct Answer: A

Helm is a CNCF Graduated project — the highest maturity level in the Cloud Native Computing Foundation. Graduated projects have demonstrated widespread adoption, a healthy governance model, a committed maintainer base, and rigorous security processes. Helm graduated on April 30, 2020, joining Kubernetes, Prometheus, Envoy, CoreDNS, and others at the top tier.

  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │ Kubernetes · Prometheus · Envoy · Helm · CoreDNS        │    │
  │  │ containerd · Fluentd · etcd · Harbor · TiKV            │    │
  │  │ → Enterprise-proven, widely adopted, strong governance  │    │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │                                                                 │

  │                                                                 │

  │  2015 — Joined CNCF as an inaugural project                     │
  │  2018 — Moved to Incubating                                     │
