  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

🚀 Why CNCF Graduation matters for you: (1) Helm won't disappear — it has institutional backing and a large maintainer community, (2) It follows strict security and governance standards, (3) Major cloud providers (AWS, Azure, GCP) and platforms (GitLab, GitHub, ArgoCD) build first-class Helm integrations because it's a trusted standard, (4) Learning Helm is a career-safe investment — it's as fundamental to Kubernetes as kubectl itself.

🔗 Connection to anihpj/jobpost: Because Helm is CNCF Graduated, you can confidently build your anihpj/jobpost deployment strategy around it. The Helm chart you create today will be supported, maintained, and compatible with future Kubernetes versions for years to come.

1.2 Helm Architecture — Client-Only DesignQ7-Q12

Core Concepts Q7 of 200
What is the architecture of Helm 3? Does it have a server-side component like Helm 2's Tiller?
A) Helm 3 has a lightweight server-side agent called "Rudder" that handles release tracking — it's like Tiller but with restricted permissions
B) Helm 3 uses the Kubernetes API server's built-in package management subsystem — no separate binary is needed on the client side
C) Helm 3 is client-only — there is NO server-side component. The helm binary on your laptop talks directly to the Kubernetes API server using YOUR kubeconfig and YOUR RBAC permissions. Release data is stored as Secrets in the cluster
D) Helm 3 runs as a sidecar container in every pod that uses Helm charts, managing the lifecycle from within the cluster
✅ Correct Answer: C

Helm 3 is 100% client-side. The entire Helm system is a single binary — helm — that you run on your local machine or CI/CD runner. There is no pod, no service, no daemon running inside your cluster. This was the single biggest architectural change from Helm 2 to Helm 3, and it was driven entirely by security and simplicity concerns.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Helm 3 Architecture — Client-Only, No Tiller, No Server Component
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    HELM 3 ARCHITECTURE                           │
  │                                                                 │
  │  YOUR MACHINE                    KUBERNETES CLUSTER              │
  │  ┌──────────────────┐           ┌──────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │                  │           │                          │    │
  │  │  ┌────────────┐  │           │  ┌────────────────────┐  │    │
  │  │  │ helm binary │  │  HTTPS   │  │   API SERVER       │  │    │
  │  │  │ (v3.x)     │──┼──────────▶│  │   (validates RBAC) │  │    │
  │  │  └────────────┘  │           │  └────────┬───────────┘  │    │
  │  │       │          │           │           │              │    │
  │  │       ▼          │           │           ▼              │    │
  │  │  ┌────────────┐  │           │  ┌────────────────────┐  │    │
  │  │  │ ~/.kube/   │  │           │  │  RELEASE SECRETS   │  │    │
  │  │  │  config    │  │           │  │  (sh.helm.release) │  │    │
  │  │  └────────────┘  │           │  └────────────────────┘  │    │
  │  │       │          │           │                          │    │
  │  │       ▼          │           │  ┌────────────────────┐  │    │
  │  │  ┌────────────┐  │           │  │  YOUR RESOURCES    │  │    │
  │  │  │ ./chart/   │  │           │  │  (Deployments,     │  │    │
  │  │  │ templates/ │  │           │  │   Services, etc.)  │  │    │
  │  │  │ values.yaml│  │           │  └────────────────────┘  │    │
  │  │  └────────────┘  │           │                          │    │
  │  └──────────────────┘           └──────────────────────────┘    │
  │                                                                 │
  │  WHAT DOES NOT EXIST IN HELM 3:                                 │
  │  ❌ No Tiller pod                                                │
  │  ❌ No server-side process                                       │
  │  ❌ No gRPC tunnel                                                │
  │  ❌ No cluster-admin service account                             │
  │  ❌ No extra TLS certificates to manage                           │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

🔗 Connection to anihpj/jobpost: This client-only architecture means deploying anihpj/jobpost with Helm requires exactly zero cluster setup beyond what you already have. No Tiller to install. No extra RBAC to configure. Just helm install anihpj ./helm/anihpj and your existing kubeconfig handles authentication and authorization.

Core Concepts Q8 of 200
How does Helm authenticate to Kubernetes? What credentials does it use?
A) Helm has its own authentication system with username/password stored in ~/.helm/auth — separate from kubectl
B) Helm uses the exact same kubeconfig as kubectl (~/.kube/config by default). Whatever cluster, user, and namespace kubectl points to — Helm uses. If kubectl get pods works, helm list works. RBAC permissions are identical
C) Helm requires a separate ServiceAccount token mounted at /var/run/helm/token — it cannot reuse kubectl credentials
D) Helm uses cloud-specific IAM roles (AWS IAM, GCP Workload Identity) and does not support kubeconfig-based authentication
✅ Correct Answer: B

Helm inherits all of Kubernetes' authentication mechanisms by using the same kubeconfig file as kubectl. This means: (1) If you switch contexts with kubectl config use-context, Helm follows, (2) If you use OIDC, client certificates, or cloud IAM — Helm uses those too, (3) Your RBAC permissions are exactly the same — if you can't create Deployments with kubectl, Helm can't either.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Helm Authentication — Shared with kubectl
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  kubectl AND helm share the same identity:                      │
  │                                                                 │
  │  ~/.kube/config                                                 │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
  │  │ apiVersion: v1                                            │   │
  │  │ kind: Config                                              │   │
  │  │ current-context: kind-cka-lab  ← BOTH use this            │   │
  │  │ contexts:                                                 │   │
  │  │ - name: kubeadm                                          │   │
  │  │   context:                                                │   │
  │  │     cluster: kubeadm                                      │   │
  │  │     user: kubernetes-admin                                │   │
  │  │     namespace: default                                    │   │
  │  │ - name: kind-cka-lab                                      │   │
  │  │   context:                                                │   │
  │  │     cluster: kind-cka-lab                                 │   │
  │  │     user: kind-cka-lab                                    │   │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
  │                                                                 │
  │  RESULT:                                                        │
  │  $ kubectl get pods              ← Uses kind-cka-lab            │
  │  $ helm list -A                  ← Uses kind-cka-lab (SAME!)   │
  │                                                                 │
  │  $ kubectl config use-context kubeadm                            │
  │  $ kubectl get pods              ← Uses kubeadm                 │
  │  $ helm list -A                  ← Uses kubeadm (SAME!)         │
  │                                                                 │
  │  ⚠️ CRITICAL: Always verify context BEFORE running helm!        │
  │  $ kubectl config current-context                                │
  │  → Wrong context = deploying to the wrong cluster               │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

🔗 Connection to anihpj/jobpost: With your 6-cluster lab managed by ksw, Helm will always deploy to whichever cluster kubectl is pointing to. After ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab), helm install anihpj ./helm/anihpj deploys to kind-cka-lab. After ksw → 1 (kubeadm), the same command deploys to kubeadm. Context discipline is your #1 safety practice.

Core Concepts Q9 of 200
What exactly happens step-by-step when you run helm install anihpj ./helm/anihpj -n anihpj?
A) Helm sends the chart .tgz to the API server, which unpacks it, renders templates server-side, and applies the resulting YAML — all in one API call
B) Helm converts the chart directly to etcd key-value pairs and writes them to the cluster database, bypassing the API server for speed
C) Helm compiles the Go templates into a binary that runs as a Kubernetes Operator, which then manages the application lifecycle independently
D) Helm performs these steps in order: (1) Loads the chart from the local path, (2) Merges values from values.yaml + --set + -f flags, (3) Renders all templates using Go's template engine with the merged values, (4) Validates the rendered YAML against Kubernetes schemas, (5) Applies resources to the API server in dependency order (Namespaces first, then Secrets, etc.), (6) Records the release as a Secret in the namespace, (7) Executes any post-install hooks, (8) Prints NOTES.txt
✅ Correct Answer: D

The helm install command is not a "fire and forget" API call — it's a sophisticated multi-step pipeline that happens entirely on your local machine (steps 1-4) before anything touches the cluster (steps 5-7). Understanding this flow is critical for debugging Helm failures.

📝 Detailed Explanation
helm install — The Complete 8-Step Pipeline
  $ helm install anihpj ./helm/anihpj -n anihpj --create-namespace

  STEP 1: LOAD CHART (local)
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Helm reads Chart.yaml → validates apiVersion: v2, name, ver │
  │ Loads all files from templates/ directory into memory        │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                          │
                          ▼
  STEP 2: MERGE VALUES (local)
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ values.yaml (base) + values-prod.yaml (-f) + --set key=val  │
  │ → Final merged Values object (highest priority wins)        │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                          │
                          ▼
  STEP 3: RENDER TEMPLATES (local)
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Go template engine processes each file in templates/         │
  │ {{ .Values.api.replicaCount }} → 3                          │
  │ {{ .Release.Name }} → "anihpj"                              │
  │ → Generates raw Kubernetes YAML (Deployment, Service, etc.)  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                          │
                          ▼
  STEP 4: VALIDATE (local + server)
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Local: Check YAML syntax, required fields                   │
  │ Server: Kubernetes API server validates against resource     │
  │   schemas (e.g., Deployment must have spec.selector)        │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                          │
                          ▼
  STEP 5: APPLY RESOURCES (server)
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Sorted by Kind: Namespace → Secret → ConfigMap → PVC →      │
  │ Service → Deployment → StatefulSet → Ingress → HPA          │
  │ Each resource: POST/PUT to API server via kubectl libraries  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                          │
                          ▼
  STEP 6: RECORD RELEASE (server)
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Creates Secret: sh.helm.release.v1.anihpj.v1                 │
  │ Contains: chart metadata, merged values, rendered manifest   │
  │ Base64-encoded + gzipped                                      │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                          │
                          ▼
  STEP 7: EXECUTE HOOKS (server)
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Runs any resources with "helm.sh/hook": post-install         │
  │ e.g., database migration Job runs AFTER Deployment is ready  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                          │
                          ▼
  STEP 8: PRINT NOTES (local)
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Renders templates/NOTES.txt → displays to terminal           │
  │ "Thank you for installing anihpj!"                           │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ✅ Release "anihpj" has been installed. Happy Helming!

💡 Key insight: Steps 1-4 happen entirely on your machine. If rendering fails (bad template syntax), nothing is sent to the cluster. This is why --dry-run (which stops after Step 4) can catch errors without side effects. Steps 5-7 touch the cluster and require valid credentials.

Core Concepts Q10 of 200
Where does Helm store release information in the cluster? How can you find it?
A) Helm stores each release as a Kubernetes Secret named sh.helm.release.v1.<name>.v<revision> in the release namespace. The Secret contains the chart metadata, rendered manifest, and all configuration values. Find them with kubectl get secrets -l owner=helm
B) Helm stores releases in a dedicated SQLite database at /var/lib/helm/releases.db on the control plane node
C) Helm stores releases as ConfigMaps (not Secrets) because the data is not sensitive — only chart metadata is stored
D) Helm does not store any data in the cluster — all release information lives only in ~/.helm/releases/ on your local machine
✅ Correct Answer: A

Helm 3 stores every release as a Kubernetes Secret in the release namespace. This is the default (and recommended) storage backend. Each revision of a release (install, upgrade, rollback) creates a new Secret with an incrementing version number. These Secrets are the source of truth for Helm's release tracking.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Helm Release Secrets — What's Inside & How to Find Them
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  FIND RELEASE SECRETS:                                          │
  │                                                                 │
  │  $ kubectl get secrets -n anihpj -l owner=helm                  │
  │  NAME                               TYPE              DATA AGE │
  │  sh.helm.release.v1.anihpj.v1      helm.sh/release.v1   1   2d │
  │  sh.helm.release.v1.anihpj.v2      helm.sh/release.v1   1   1d │
  │  sh.helm.release.v1.anihpj.v3      helm.sh/release.v1   1   2h │
  │                                                                 │
  │  SECRET NAMING CONVENTION:                                      │
  │  sh.helm.release.v1.<RELEASE-NAME>.v<REVISION>                  │
  │                                                                 │
  │  WHAT'S INSIDE (base64 decoded + gunzipped):                    │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
  │  │ {                                                        │   │
  │  │   "name": "anihpj",                                      │   │
  │  │   "info": {                                              │   │
  │  │     "status": "deployed",                                │   │
  │  │     "first_deployed": "2026-06-13T10:00:00Z",           │   │
  │  │     "last_deployed": "2026-06-14T14:30:00Z"             │   │
  │  │   },                                                     │   │
  │  │   "chart": {        ← Chart.yaml metadata               │   │
  │  │     "name": "anihpj",                                    │   │
  │  │     "version": "1.0.0"                                   │   │
  │  │   },                                                     │   │
  │  │   "config": {       ← ALL values used (⚠️ = PLAINTEXT!) │   │
  │  │     "postgres": {"password": "secret123"},              │   │
  │  │     "django": {"secretKey": "abc..."}                   │   │
  │  │   },                                                     │   │
  │  │   "manifest": "---\napiVersion: ..." ← FULL YAML         │   │
  │  │ }                                                        │   │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
  │                                                                 │
  │  ⚠️  SECURITY: Anyone with Secret read access can see ALL your  │
  │     Helm values — including passwords, API keys, and TLS certs! │
  │     Use helm-secrets plugin, External Secrets Operator, or     │
  │     etcd encryption at rest to protect sensitive values.        │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Helm 3 also supports ConfigMaps and SQL backends as alternatives, but Secrets are the default and recommended backend. The --max-history flag limits how many revision Secrets are kept — preventing namespace clutter from hundreds of old revisions.

🔗 Connection to anihpj/jobpost: Every time you upgrade the anihpj chart, Helm creates a new Secret. helm rollback anihpj 5 reads revision 5's Secret, extracts the manifest, and re-applies it. This is why rollbacks are instant — the manifest was already saved at deploy time.

Core Concepts Q11 of 200
How does Helm track releases in the cluster? What labels identify Helm release Secrets?
A) Helm uses a custom CRD called HelmRelease that stores release metadata — Secrets are not involved
B) Each release revision is stored as a Kubernetes Secret labeled with owner=helm, name=<release>, and status=deployed. Find all releases with kubectl get secrets -l owner=helm -A
C) Helm stores releases in a dedicated ConfigMap named helm-releases in the kube-system namespace
D) Helm does not track releases in the cluster at all — release history is stored locally in ~/.helm/cache/
✅ Correct Answer: B

Helm 3 tracks every release revision using Kubernetes Secrets with well-known labels. This label-based approach means you (and tools like ArgoCD, Flux, and Lens) can discover all Helm-managed resources in a cluster instantly.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Helm Release Labels — How to Find Every Release in Your Cluster
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  FIND ALL HELM RELEASES ACROSS ALL NAMESPACES:                  │
  │                                                                 │
  │  $ kubectl get secrets -l owner=helm -A                         │
  │  NAMESPACE  NAME                            TYPE              │
  │  anihpj     sh.helm.release.v1.anihpj.v1   helm.sh/release.v1│
  │  anihpj     sh.helm.release.v1.anihpj.v2   helm.sh/release.v1│
  │  monitoring sh.helm.release.v1.prom.v1     helm.sh/release.v1│
  │  default    sh.helm.release.v1.nginx.v1    helm.sh/release.v1│
  │                                                                 │
  │  LABELS ON EACH RELEASE SECRET:                                 │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
  │  │ labels:                                                  │   │
  │  │   owner: helm                       ← IDENTIFIES Helm    │   │
  │  │   name: anihpj                      ← Release name       │   │
  │  │   status: deployed                  ← Current state      │   │
  │  │   version: "3"                      ← Revision number    │   │
  │  │   modifiedAt: "1718301600"          ← Unix timestamp     │   │
  │  │   chart: anihpj-1.0.0               ← Chart name+version │   │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
  │                                                                 │
  │  RELEASE STATUS VALUES:                                         │
  │  deployed · superseded · failed · uninstalling · pending-install│
  │  pending-upgrade · pending-rollback                             │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

💡 Why labels matter: Labels enable tools to query releases efficiently. kubectl get secrets -l owner=helm,status=deployed -A shows only actively running releases. kubectl get secrets -l owner=helm,status=failed -A finds broken deployments. This label convention is the foundation for Helm-aware dashboards and GitOps tools.

Core Concepts Q12 of 200
What does helm env display, and why is it useful for debugging?
A) helm env shows the environment variables of the Helm chart's containers — it's equivalent to kubectl exec <pod> -- env
B) helm env lists all Helm releases and their environment configurations for the current namespace
C) helm env displays all Helm client configuration — environment variables like HELM_NAMESPACE, HELM_KUBECONTEXT, HELM_CACHE_HOME, and paths to the Helm binary, cache, and config. It's the first command to run when Helm behaves unexpectedly
D) helm env sets environment variables for the current shell session to configure Helm — it does not display anything
✅ Correct Answer: C

helm env is the "system info" command for Helm. It shows exactly where Helm stores its data, which Kubernetes context it's connected to, and what environment variables are overriding default behavior. When Helm acts differently than expected, this is your first diagnostic command.

📝 Detailed Explanation
helm env — Your Helm Diagnostic Command
  $ helm env
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ HELM_BIN=/usr/local/bin/helm        ← Helm binary location      │
  │ HELM_CACHE_HOME=/home/user/.cache/helm ← Downloaded chart cache │
  │ HELM_CONFIG_HOME=/home/user/.config/helm ← Registry auth config │
  │ HELM_DATA_HOME=/home/user/.local/share/helm ← Plugins, starters │
  │ HELM_KUBECONTEXT=kind-cka-lab       ← CURRENT CLUSTER (CRITICAL!)│
  │ HELM_NAMESPACE=default              ← Default namespace          │
  │ HELM_REGISTRY_CONFIG=/home/user/.config/helm/registry/config.json│
  │                                                                 │
  │ ⚠️  CRITICAL DEBUGGING USES:                                    │
  │                                                                 │
  │  "Why is Helm deploying to the wrong cluster?"                  │
  │  → Check HELM_KUBECONTEXT — it may be set to a different ctx   │
  │                                                                 │
  │  "Why can't Helm find my plugin?"                               │
  │  → Check HELM_DATA_HOME — plugins are stored here               │
  │                                                                 │
  │  "Why is my chart cache corrupted?"                             │
  │  → Check HELM_CACHE_HOME — clear it with rm -rf                │
  │                                                                 │
  │  "Why is Helm deploying to 'default' namespace?"                │
  │  → Check HELM_NAMESPACE — overrides -n flag silently!          │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

🔗 Connection to anihpj/jobpost: Before deploying the anihpj chart, run helm env | grep KUBECONTEXT to confirm you're pointing at the right cluster. After using ksw to switch clusters, Helm follows kubectl's context — unless HELM_KUBECONTEXT is explicitly set, which overrides everything.

1.3 Charts, Repositories & RegistriesQ13-Q20

Core Concepts Q13 of 200
What IS a Helm chart? What files make up a chart?
A) A Helm chart is a single YAML file that defines all Kubernetes resources for an application — like a docker-compose.yml for Kubernetes
B) A Helm chart is a directory structure containing at minimum: Chart.yaml (metadata), values.yaml (default configuration), and a templates/ directory (Go-templated Kubernetes YAML). It's the deployable unit — package it into a .tgz file to share
C) A Helm chart is a compiled Go binary that runs inside the cluster as a controller, watching for configuration changes
D) A Helm chart is a JSON document stored in etcd that describes the desired state of an application
✅ Correct Answer: B

A Helm chart is a directory with a defined structure. The minimal chart contains Chart.yaml (name, version, description), a values.yaml (default configuration values), and a templates/ directory with Go-templated Kubernetes manifests. Package it with helm package ./chart to create a .tgz archive for distribution.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Anatomy of a Helm Chart — The Minimal & Complete Structure
  MINIMAL CHART                    COMPLETE CHART (anihpj)
  ┌──────────────────┐            ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │ anihpj/          │            │ anihpj/                      │
  │ ├── Chart.yaml   │            │ ├── Chart.yaml               │
  │ ├── values.yaml  │            │ ├── values.yaml              │
  │ └── templates/   │            │ ├── values-dev.yaml          │
  │     └── deploy.. │            │ ├── values-prod.yaml         │
  └──────────────────┘            │ ├── .helmignore              │
                                  │ ├── charts/     ← deps      │
  helm install anihpj ./anihpj    │ ├── templates/              │
  → Deploys with defaults         │ │   ├── _helpers.tpl        │
                                  │ │   ├── NOTES.txt           │
                                  │ │   ├── namespace.yaml      │
                                  │ │   ├── secrets.yaml        │
                                  │ │   ├── configmap.yaml      │
                                  │ │   ├── postgres-sts.yaml   │
                                  │ │   ├── ... (14 total)      │
                                  │ │   └── tests/              │
                                  │ └── schema/  ← JSON schema  │
                                  └──────────────────────────────┘

  REQUIRED: Chart.yaml + values.yaml + templates/
  OPTIONAL: charts/ + .helmignore + schema/ + values-*.yaml

🔗 Connection to anihpj/jobpost: Your helm/anihpj/ directory will follow exactly this structure. The 14 Kubernetes YAML files currently in k8s/ will become 14 Go templates in templates/, driven by a single values.yaml. This is the transformation you'll complete in Part 3.

Core Concepts Q14 of 200
What is the Chart.yaml file? Which fields are required vs optional?
A) Chart.yaml is the metadata file for a chart. Required fields: apiVersion (must be v2 for Helm 3), name (chart name), and version (SemVer). Optional: appVersion, description, type (application/library), dependencies, maintainers, icon
B) Chart.yaml is the primary template file that generates the Deployment manifest — it's functionally equivalent to a Kubernetes Deployment YAML
C) Chart.yaml is optional — Helm can deploy a chart from templates/ and values.yaml alone without any metadata file
D) Chart.yaml stores the rendered Kubernetes manifests after helm template runs — it's the output file, not the input
✅ Correct Answer: A

Chart.yaml is the identity card of your chart. Without it, Helm cannot identify, version, or manage your chart. The three required fields — apiVersion, name, version — are the absolute minimum for Helm to recognize a directory as a chart.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Chart.yaml — Required vs Optional Fields
  # Chart.yaml for anihpj/jobpost
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ apiVersion: v2              ← REQUIRED: Must be "v2" (Helm 3)  │
  │ name: anihpj                ← REQUIRED: Chart name (lowercase)  │
  │ version: 1.0.0              ← REQUIRED: SemVer chart version    │
  │                                                                 │
  │ appVersion: "2.5.1"         ← OPTIONAL: Version of the APP      │
  │ description: "Job posting application (Django + PG + Redis)"    │
  │ type: application           ← OPTIONAL: "application" or "library"│
  │ home: https://jobpost.com   ← OPTIONAL: Project URL              │
  │ icon: https://jobpost.com/logo.png                               │
  │ maintainers:                                                     │
  │   - name: DevOps Team                                            │
  │     email: devops@jobpost.com                                   │
  │ dependencies:               ← OPTIONAL: Sub-chart dependencies   │
  │   - name: postgresql                                            │
  │     version: 15.x.x                                             │
  │     repository: https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami              │
  │ keywords:                    ← OPTIONAL: Search/discovery tags   │
  │   - django                                                       │
  │   - job-board                                                   │
  │   - postgresql                                                  │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

💡 version vs appVersion: version is the CHART version (bump when you change templates). appVersion is the APPLICATION version (bump when you release new app code). They're independent — you can update the chart without changing the app, and vice versa.

Core Concepts Q15 of 200
What are the two chart types in Helm, and what is the difference between them?
A) Deployment charts (stateless) and StatefulSet charts (stateful) — the type determines which Kubernetes workload resource is created
B) Public charts (free) and Private charts (paid) — the type controls licensing and distribution rights
C) Application charts (type: application) deploy workloads and can be installed with helm install. Library charts (type: library) contain only reusable templates/helpers and CANNOT be installed — they're imported by other charts as dependencies
D) Stable charts (production-ready) and Incubator charts (experimental) — the type indicates maturity level
✅ Correct Answer: C

Helm charts come in two types defined in Chart.yaml: application (the default, installable, deploys resources) and library (template-only, not installable, provides reusable helpers). Library charts are Helm's answer to shared code — write a _helpers.tpl once, import it everywhere.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Application vs Library Charts
  APPLICATION CHART (type: application) — DEFAULT
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ anihpj/                                                         │
  │ ├── Chart.yaml    ← type: application (or omit — default)       │
  │ ├── values.yaml                                                 │
  │ └── templates/    ← Deployments, Services, etc.                 │
  │                                                                 │
  │ $ helm install anihpj ./anihpj   ← ✅ CAN be installed          │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  LIBRARY CHART (type: library) — REUSABLE HELPERS
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ anihpj-common/                                                  │
  │ ├── Chart.yaml    ← type: library                               │
  │ └── templates/                                                  │
  │     └── _helpers.tpl  ← Named templates: anihpj.labels,         │
  │                          anihpj.image, anihpj.fullname          │
  │                                                                 │
  │ $ helm install common ./anihpj-common  ← ❌ CANNOT be installed │
  │ Error: library charts are not installable                       │
  │                                                                 │
  │ USAGE: Import in another chart's Chart.yaml as a dependency     │
  │ Then use in templates: {{ include "anihpj-common.labels" . }}  │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Library charts solve the "copy-paste _helpers.tpl across 10 charts" problem. Define your organization's standard labels, image references, and naming conventions once in a library chart, and every application chart imports it.

Core Concepts Q16 of 200
What is a Helm repository? How does helm repo work?
A) A Helm repository is a Kubernetes namespace where charts are deployed — helm repo add creates a new namespace for Helm-managed resources
B) A Helm repository is an HTTP server that serves an index.yaml file listing available charts and their .tgz packages. helm repo add registers the URL, helm repo update fetches the latest index, and helm search repo queries it
C) A Helm repository is a Git repository containing chart source code — helm repo add clones the Git repo locally
D) A Helm repository is a Docker registry that stores container images alongside chart metadata
✅ Correct Answer: B

A Helm repository is simply an HTTP server with a specific structure: an index.yaml at the root that catalogs all available charts, and .tgz packages for each chart version. This is the same concept as an APT repository (Packages.gz + .deb files) or a YUM repository (repodata/ + .rpm files).

📝 Detailed Explanation
Helm Repository Structure — index.yaml + .tgz packages
  HELM REPOSITORY (HTTP SERVER)
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ https://charts.example.com/                                  │
  │ │                                                            │
  │ ├── index.yaml          ← THE CATALOG (downloaded by helm)  │
  │ │   ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │ │   │ apiVersion: v1                                    │    │
  │ │   │ entries:                                          │    │
  │ │   │   anihpj:                                         │    │
  │ │   │   - name: anihpj                                  │    │
  │ │   │     version: 1.0.0                                │    │
  │ │   │     description: "Job posting app"                │    │
  │ │   │     urls:                                         │    │
  │ │   │       - anihpj-1.0.0.tgz  ← Package location      │    │
  │ │   │     created: 2026-06-13T10:00:00Z                 │    │
  │ │   │     digest: sha256:abc123...                      │    │
  │ │   │   postgresql:                    ← Other charts   │    │
  │ │   │   - name: postgresql                              │    │
  │ │   │     version: 15.5.20                              │    │
  │ │   └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │ │                                                            │
  │ ├── anihpj-1.0.0.tgz    ← THE PACKAGE (chart as .tgz)      │
  │ └── postgresql-15.5.20.tgz                                  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  CLIENT SIDE:
  $ helm repo add jobpost https://charts.example.com
  $ helm repo update              ← Downloads index.yaml
  $ helm search repo anihpj       ← Searches local cached index
  $ helm install anihpj jobpost/anihpj ← Downloads .tgz + installs

🔗 Connection to anihpj/jobpost: Once you've built your anihpj chart, you can host it on a Helm repository (Chart Museum, Harbor, GitHub Pages, or an OCI registry) so your team can install it with helm repo add anihpj https://charts.yourcompany.com && helm install anihpj anihpj/anihpj.

Core Concepts Q17 of 200
What is an OCI registry for Helm charts, and how does it differ from a traditional Helm repository?
A) An OCI registry (like Docker Hub, ECR, Harbor) stores Helm charts as OCI artifacts alongside container images. Unlike traditional Helm repos (which use index.yaml + HTTP), OCI uses helm push/helm pull with oci:// protocol, supports content-addressable storage, and leverages existing container registry auth and security scanning
B) OCI registries are a legacy storage format — Helm 3 deprecated OCI support and only traditional HTTP repositories are recommended
C) OCI registries store charts as Docker images that run inside Kubernetes — the chart is executed as a container
D) OCI and traditional Helm repos are identical — there is no difference in how charts are stored or accessed
✅ Correct Answer: A

OCI (Open Container Initiative) registries are the modern way to distribute Helm charts. Instead of maintaining a separate HTTP server with index.yaml, you push charts to the same registry you use for container images — Docker Hub, Amazon ECR, Azure ACR, Google Artifact Registry, or Harbor. One registry for images AND charts.

📝 Detailed Explanation
OCI vs Traditional Helm Repository
  TRADITIONAL HELM REPO              OCI REGISTRY
  ┌──────────────────────────┐      ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │ HTTP server               │      │ Container registry        │
  │ index.yaml + .tgz files  │      │ (Docker Hub, ECR, etc.)  │
  │                          │      │                          │
  │ $ helm repo add ...      │      │ $ helm registry login    │
  │ $ helm repo update       │      │ $ helm push ./anihpj \   │
  │ $ helm install ...       │      │     oci://registry/ns    │
  │                          │      │ $ helm pull oci://...    │
  │ ❌ Separate infra needed │      │ $ helm install anihpj \ │
  │ ❌ Must manage HTTP      │      │     oci://registry/ns/\ │
  │    server + TLS          │      │     anihpj --version 1.0│
  │                          │      │                          │
  │                          │      │ ✅ Same auth as images   │
  │                          │      │ ✅ Built-in vulnerability│
  │                          │      │    scanning (ECR, etc.)  │
  │                          │      │ ✅ Content-addressable   │
  │                          │      │ ✅ No index.yaml needed  │
  └──────────────────────────┘      └──────────────────────────┘

OCI is the recommended distribution method for Helm 3.8+. Commands: helm registry login, helm push, helm pull, helm install oci://..., helm show all oci://....

Core Concepts Q18 of 200
What is chart versioning in Helm? What is the difference between version and appVersion?
A) version and appVersion must always be the same — Helm enforces this to prevent chart/application mismatches
B) version is automatically generated by Helm; appVersion is set manually in Chart.yaml
C) version is the chart version (SemVer) — bump when templates/values change. appVersion is the application version — bump when the container image changes. They are independent: you can release chart v1.1.0 with the same app v2.5.1 if only templates changed
D) version is the Kubernetes API version; appVersion is the minimum Kubernetes version required to run the chart
✅ Correct Answer: C

Helm charts follow Semantic Versioning (SemVer 2.0) for both version and appVersion, but they track different things. version is the chart's version (bump when you change templates, defaults, or dependencies). appVersion is informational — it tells users which version of your application is packaged inside.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Chart version vs appVersion — Independent Lifecycles
  RELEASE HISTORY FOR anihpj CHART:
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Chart v1.0.0 + App v2.5.0  ← Initial release                   │
  │ Chart v1.0.1 + App v2.5.0  ← Template bugfix (app unchanged)   │
  │ Chart v1.1.0 + App v2.5.0  ← New template feature              │
  │ Chart v1.1.0 + App v2.5.1  ← App patch (chart unchanged!)      │
  │ Chart v2.0.0 + App v3.0.0  ← BREAKING: chart + app major bump  │
  │                                                                 │
  │ Chart version bumps when:                                       │
  │ • Template logic changes (new if/else, new helper)              │
  │ • Default values change (new required values)                   │
  │ • Dependencies updated                                          │
  │                                                                 │
  │ appVersion bumps when:                                          │
  │ • New container image tag released                              │
  │ • Application code changes                                      │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

In helm list, both versions are displayed: anihpj anihpj 1 2026-06-13 deployed anihpj-1.0.0 2.5.1. This lets you see at a glance which chart version AND which app version is deployed.

Core Concepts Q19 of 200
How do you search for charts? What is the difference between helm search repo and helm search hub?
A) Both commands are identical — helm search hub is an alias for helm search repo
B) helm search repo searches your locally added repositories (cached index.yaml files). helm search hub searches the Artifact Hub — a public, community-maintained catalog of thousands of charts from hundreds of repositories worldwide
C) helm search repo searches Docker Hub; helm search hub searches GitHub for Helm charts
D) helm search repo searches the Kubernetes cluster for installed charts; helm search hub searches local files
✅ Correct Answer: B

helm search repo queries your local cache of added repositories — fast, offline-capable, limited to repos you've configured. helm search hub queries the Artifact Hub (artifacthub.io), a public catalog indexing 10,000+ charts from Bitnami, Prometheus, Grafana, ingress-nginx, and hundreds of other sources.

📝 Detailed Explanation
helm search repo vs helm search hub
  helm search repo nginx              helm search hub nginx
  ┌────────────────────────────┐      ┌────────────────────────────┐
  │ Searches: LOCAL cache       │      │ Searches: Artifact Hub API │
  │ Requires: helm repo add     │      │ Requires: Internet only    │
  │ Speed: Instant (cached)     │      │ Speed: API call (~1s)     │
  │ Scope: YOUR configured repos│      │ Scope: 10,000+ charts      │
  │                             │      │                             │
  │ $ helm search repo nginx    │      │ $ helm search hub nginx    │
  │ NAME                VERSION │      │ URL → artifacthub.io       │
  │ bitnami/nginx       18.x.x │      │ Shows ALL nginx charts     │
  │ bitnami/nginx-ingress 11.x │      │ from ALL repositories      │
  └────────────────────────────┘      └────────────────────────────┘

  WORKFLOW:
  1. helm search hub postgresql     ← Discover what exists
  2. helm repo add bitnami https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami
  3. helm search repo postgresql    ← Find exact version in repo
  4. helm install mydb bitnami/postgresql
Core Concepts Q20 of 200
Your team needs PostgreSQL for the anihpj/jobpost app. How do you find, add, and install a chart from a public repository?
A) Download the chart ZIP from GitHub, extract it, and run kubectl apply -f on all files
B) Copy the PostgreSQL Dockerfile, build an image, and deploy it as a Kubernetes Deployment manually
C) helm install postgresql — Helm automatically finds the most popular PostgreSQL chart online
D) helm repo add bitnami https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami → helm repo update → helm search repo postgresql → helm install anihpj-db bitnami/postgresql --set auth.password=secret123. The entire process takes under 60 seconds
✅ Correct Answer: D

This is the real power of Helm — deploying a production-grade PostgreSQL instance with persistent storage, replication, backups, and monitoring takes 4 commands and under a minute. Compare this to the hours it would take to write all those YAML files from scratch.

📝 Detailed Explanation
The Full Helm Install Workflow — Discovery to Deployment
  # STEP 1: Add the Bitnami repository (one-time)
  $ helm repo add bitnami https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami
  "bitnami" has been added to your repositories

  # STEP 2: Update local cache
  $ helm repo update
  Hang tight while we grab the latest from your chart repositories...
  ...Successfully got an update from the "bitnami" chart repository

  # STEP 3: Search for PostgreSQL
  $ helm search repo bitnami/postgresql
  NAME              CHART VERSION  APP VERSION  DESCRIPTION
  bitnami/postgresql   15.5.20      16.3.0      PostgreSQL (Postgres) is an open source...

  # STEP 4: Install with custom values
  $ helm install anihpj-db bitnami/postgresql \
      --set auth.database=jobpost \
      --set auth.username=anihpj \
      --set auth.password=secret123 \
      --set primary.persistence.size=10Gi

  # STEP 5: Verify
  $ helm list
  NAME       NAMESPACE  REVISION  STATUS    CHART                 APP VERSION
  anihpj-db  default    1         deployed  postgresql-15.5.20   16.3.0

🔗 Connection to anihpj/jobpost: In Part 2 and Part 3, you'll use this exact workflow to deploy PostgreSQL, Redis, and eventually the full anihpj/jobpost stack. The anihpj umbrella chart will even declare PostgreSQL and Redis as dependencies, so ONE helm install deploys the entire infrastructure.

1.4 Values & Configuration BasicsQ21-Q25

Core Concepts Q21 of 200
What is values.yaml and why is it the single most important file in a Helm chart?
A) values.yaml is the default configuration file for a chart. It declares every configurable parameter with sensible defaults. Templates reference values via {{ .Values.key }}. Users override defaults with --set or -f custom-values.yaml. It's the contract between chart developer and chart user
B) values.yaml is a compiled output file generated by helm template — it shows the final rendered values after all overrides are applied
C) values.yaml is a Kubernetes Secret that stores encrypted configuration — Helm decrypts it at install time
D) values.yaml is optional — charts work fine without it as long as templates have hardcoded defaults
✅ Correct Answer: A

values.yaml is the interface between the chart developer (who writes templates) and the chart user (who deploys the app). Well-designed values.yaml makes a chart self-documenting — users can read it and understand every configuration option without digging through templates.

📝 Detailed Explanation
values.yaml — The Contract Between Developer and User
  # values.yaml for anihpj/jobpost
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ # ── DEVELOPER WRITES THESE DEFAULTS ──                        │
  │                                                                 │
  │ replicaCount: 1              ← User can override to 3, 5, etc. │
  │                                                                 │
  │ image:                                                            │
  │   repository: anihpj-api      ← Default image name               │
  │   tag: "latest"               ← Default tag (user SHOULD override)│
  │   pullPolicy: IfNotPresent                                        │
  │                                                                   │
  │ postgres:                                                         │
  │   enabled: true               ← User can disable for external DB  │
  │   host: anihpj-db             ← Default service name              │
  │   port: 5432                                                      │
  │   database: jobpost                                               │
  │   auth:                                                           │
  │     username: anihpj          ← User MUST override password!      │
  │     password: "CHANGE_ME"     ← Placeholder — override required   │
  │                                                                   │
  │ resources:                                                        │
  │   requests:                   ← Sensible dev defaults             │
  │     cpu: 250m                                                     │
  │     memory: 256Mi                                                 │
  │   limits:                      ← User should tune for prod        │
  │     cpu: 1000m                                                    │
  │     memory: 512Mi                                                 │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

💡 Best practice: Every value in values.yaml should have a sensible default. If a value is REQUIRED with no safe default (like a database password), use {{ required "A valid .Values.postgres.auth.password is required!" .Values.postgres.auth.password }} in your template to fail with a clear error message.

Core Concepts Q22 of 200
How do you override values during helm install? What is the precedence order when multiple value sources are used?
A) --set overrides everything, -f files are ignored if --set is used, and values.yaml is only read if neither is specified
B) All value sources are merged equally — if the same key appears in multiple sources, Helm picks one randomly
C) values.yaml always takes precedence — --set and -f only fill in values that are missing from values.yaml
D) Value precedence (lowest→highest): values.yaml (chart defaults) → parent values.yaml (umbrella chart) → -f file (first specified) → -f file (later files override earlier) → --set (highest priority). Later sources OVERRIDE earlier ones for the same key
✅ Correct Answer: D

Helm merges values from multiple sources with a strict precedence order. --set always wins because it's the most explicit — "I am typing this right now, I know exactly what I want." Multiple -f files are merged left-to-right, with later files taking precedence.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Value Precedence — What Overrides What
  PRECEDENCE (lowest → highest):
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                 │
  │  ① values.yaml (chart defaults)        ← Lowest priority       │
  │       │                                                         │
  │       ▼                                                         │
  │  ② Parent chart's values.yaml          ← Umbrella chart values │
  │       │                                                         │
  │       ▼                                                         │
  │  ③ -f values-dev.yaml                  ← First file specified  │
  │       │                                                         │
  │       ▼                                                         │
  │  ④ -f values-override.yaml             ← Later file overrides  │
  │       │                                                         │
  │       ▼                                                         │
  │  ⑤ --set api.replicaCount=5            ← HIGHEST priority      │
  │                                                                 │
  │  EXAMPLE:                                                        │
  │  values.yaml:        replicaCount: 1    (chart default)         │
  │  -f values-dev.yaml: replicaCount: 2    (dev override)          │
  │  --set replicaCount=5                    (CLI override)          │
  │  → RESULT: replicaCount = 5  (--set wins)                       │
  │                                                                 │
  │  ⚠️  --set IS FLAT: --set postgres.auth.password=secret123     │
  │  ⚠️  -f FILES MERGE: -f base.yaml -f prod.yaml                 │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

🔗 Connection to anihpj/jobpost: For production: helm install anihpj ./helm/anihpj -f values-prod.yaml. In CI/CD: helm upgrade anihpj ./helm/anihpj -f values-prod.yaml --set image.tag=$CI_COMMIT_SHA. The --set for the image tag ensures the exact build is deployed, overriding whatever is in values-prod.yaml.

Core Concepts Q23 of 200
How do you preview all configurable values in a chart before installing it?
A) helm show values <chart> — displays the entire values.yaml from the chart so you can see every configurable parameter with its default value before installation
B) helm inspect config <chart> — opens an interactive configuration wizard in the terminal
C) You must download and extract the chart .tgz file to read values.yaml manually — there is no CLI command for this
D) helm values <chart> — prints only the values that have been overridden from defaults
✅ Correct Answer: A

helm show values is your window into a chart's configuration before you install it. For the Bitnami PostgreSQL chart, this shows 100+ configurable parameters — from auth.password to primary.persistence.size to replication.enabled. Always run this before installing an unfamiliar chart.

📝 Detailed Explanation
helm show — Inspecting Charts Before Installing
  # Preview ALL configurable values
  $ helm show values bitnami/postgresql
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ auth:                                                           │
  │   postgresPassword: ""          ← Set this for superuser        │
  │   username: "postgres"                                          │
  │   password: ""                  ← Set this for app user         │
  │   database: "postgres"                                          │
  │                                                                 │
  │ primary:                                                        │
  │   persistence:                                                  │
  │     enabled: true                                               │
  │     size: 8Gi                   ← Storage size                  │
  │     storageClass: ""            ← StorageClass name             │
  │   resources:                                                    │
  │     requests:                                                   │
  │       cpu: 250m                                                 │
  │       memory: 256Mi                                             │
  │                                                                 │
  │ replication:                                                    │
  │   enabled: false                ← Enable for HA                 │
  │   readReplicas: 1                                               │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  OTHER helm show COMMANDS:
  helm show chart <chart>    ← Chart.yaml contents
  helm show readme <chart>   ← README.md (usage guide)
  helm show all <chart>      ← Everything (chart + values + readme)

Works identically for local charts (helm show values ./helm/anihpj) and remote charts (helm show values bitnami/postgresql).

Core Concepts Q24 of 200
You need to configure the anihpj chart's PostgreSQL password for production. The chart expects postgres.auth.password. What is the correct nested value syntax for --set?
A) --set postgres.auth.password=secret123 — dotted notation maps directly to nested YAML keys
B) --set '{"postgres":{"auth":{"password":"secret123"}}}' — you must pass nested values as JSON
C) Both A and B are correct — --set postgres.auth.password=secret123 uses dotted notation and --set 'postgres.auth.password=secret123' (quoted) handles special characters. For complex structures, JSON syntax is more readable
D) --set postgres[0].auth[0].password=secret123 — nested values must use array-index notation
✅ Correct Answer: C

Helm's --set supports both dotted notation (simple) and JSON notation (complex). Dotted notation works for basic nested values. JSON notation is preferred for lists, maps with special characters, or deeply nested structures.

📝 Detailed Explanation
--set Syntax — Dotted vs JSON Notation
  DOTTED NOTATION (simple, most common):
  --set postgres.auth.password=secret123
  --set api.replicaCount=3
  --set resources.limits.cpu=2000m
  --set ingress.hosts[0].host=jobpost.com    ← Array index

  JSON NOTATION (complex, for lists/maps):
  --set 'resources.limits={cpu:2000m,memory:4Gi}'
  --set 'tolerations=[{key:dedicated,operator:Equal,value:db,effect:NoSchedule}]'
  --set 'ingress.hosts=[{host:jobpost.com,paths:[{path:/}]}]'

  MULTIPLE --set FLAGS (chain them):
  helm install anihpj ./helm/anihpj \
    --set api.replicaCount=3 \
    --set postgres.auth.password=secret123 \
    --set resources.limits.cpu=2000m \
    --set ingress.enabled=true

  ⚠️  TIP: For more than 3-4 --set flags, use -f values-override.yaml instead.
  It's more readable, version-controllable, and less error-prone.
Core Concepts Q25 of 200
What are nested values in Helm, and why is the YAML structure of values.yaml important?
A) Nested values are a legacy feature — Helm 3 recommends flat key=value pairs instead of nested YAML structures
B) Nested values organize related configuration under a common parent key (e.g., postgres.auth.password instead of postgresAuthPassword). This grouping makes values.yaml readable, maintainable, and self-documenting. Templates access nested values with dot notation: {{ .Values.postgres.auth.password }}
C) Nested values are encrypted values stored inside other encrypted values — they provide defense-in-depth for secrets management
D) Nested values are automatically inherited by subcharts — child charts read parent values without any configuration
✅ Correct Answer: B

YAML's nested structure is what makes values.yaml readable at scale. Instead of hundreds of flat keys like postgresAuthPassword, postgresAuthUsername, redisAuthPassword, apiReplicaCount, you group related settings: postgres.auth.password, redis.auth.password, api.replicaCount.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Flat vs Nested — Why Structure Matters
  ❌ FLAT (bad at scale):
  postgresHost: anihpj-db
  postgresPort: 5432
  postgresAuthUsername: anihpj
  postgresAuthPassword: secret123
  redisHost: anihpj-redis
  redisPort: 6379
  redisAuthPassword: redis123
  apiReplicaCount: 3
  → 20+ flat keys, nothing grouped, hard to find

  ✅ NESTED (organized):
  postgres:
    host: anihpj-db
    port: 5432
    auth:
      username: anihpj
      password: secret123
  redis:
    host: anihpj-redis
    port: 6379
    auth:
      password: redis123
  api:
    replicaCount: 3
  → Logical groups, easy to navigate, self-documenting

  TEMPLATE USAGE:
  {{ .Values.postgres.auth.password }}   ← Dot notation mirrors YAML nesting

💡 Best practice: Keep nesting to 3-4 levels maximum. Deeper nesting becomes hard to override with --set. If you find yourself going 5+ levels deep, consider flattening or splitting into separate top-level keys.

1.5 Helm Command Basics & First DeploymentQ26-Q30

Core Concepts Q26 of 200
You have a Helm chart at ./helm/anihpj. What is the exact command to install it as a release named "jobboard" in the "anihpj" namespace, creating the namespace if it doesn't exist?
A) helm deploy jobboard ./helm/anihpj --ns anihpj --make-ns
B) helm install jobboard ./helm/anihpj -n anihpj --create-namespace
C) helm apply jobboard -f ./helm/anihpj -n anihpj
D) kubectl helm install jobboard --chart=./helm/anihpj --namespace=anihpj
✅ Correct Answer: B

helm install <RELEASE-NAME> <CHART> -n <NAMESPACE> --create-namespace is the canonical install command. The release name ("jobboard") is what appears in helm list. The chart path (./helm/anihpj) can be a local directory, a packaged .tgz, or a repository reference like bitnami/nginx.

📝 Detailed Explanation
helm install — Anatomy of the Command
  helm install <RELEASE-NAME> <CHART> [flags]
                │                  │
                │                  └── Chart reference (directory, .tgz, or repo/chart)
                │
                └── Release name (must be unique within namespace)

  ESSENTIAL FLAGS:
  -n, --namespace      Target namespace
  --create-namespace   Auto-create namespace if missing
  -f, --values         Specify YAML file with override values
  --set                Override individual values from CLI
  --dry-run            Simulate install (render + validate, don't apply)
  --atomic             Auto-rollback on failure
  --wait               Wait for all resources to be ready
  --timeout            Max time to wait (default: 5m)
  --debug              Enable verbose output

  REAL EXAMPLE — anihpj/jobpost:
  helm install anihpj ./helm/anihpj \
    -n anihpj \
    --create-namespace \
    -f values-prod.yaml \
    --atomic \
    --wait \
    --timeout 10m

🔗 Connection to anihpj/jobpost: This exact command deploys your entire job board — PostgreSQL, Redis, Django API, Django Web, Ingress, NetworkPolicy — in one shot. The --atomic flag ensures that if ANY resource fails, Helm rolls back everything automatically.

Core Concepts Q27 of 200
How do you list all installed Helm releases across all namespaces?
A) kubectl get helmreleases --all-namespaces
B) helm list -A (or helm ls --all-namespaces) — shows release name, namespace, revision, status, chart version, and app version for every deployed release across the entire cluster
C) helm get all
D) kubectl get secrets -l owner=helm -A (this works but returns raw Secrets, not formatted release info)
✅ Correct Answer: B

helm list -A is the quickest way to see everything Helm is managing in your cluster. Shows: release name, namespace, revision number, last update time, status (deployed/failed/pending), chart name+version, and app version. Option D technically works but returns raw base64-encoded Secrets — not human-readable.

📝 Detailed Explanation
helm list — All Your Releases at a Glance
  $ helm list -A
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ NAME      NAMESPACE  REV  UPDATED                  STATUS    CHART              APP VERSION│
  │ anihpj    anihpj     3    2026-06-13 14:30:00     deployed  anihpj-1.0.0      2.5.1      │
  │ prom      monitoring 1    2026-06-10 09:00:00     deployed  prometheus-25.x   2.54.0     │
  │ nginx     default    2    2026-06-09 16:00:00     deployed  nginx-18.x        1.27.0     │
  │ failed-db staging    1    2026-06-08 11:00:00     failed    postgresql-15.x   16.3.0     │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  USEFUL helm list FLAGS:
  -A, --all-namespaces    List releases across all namespaces
  -a, --all               Include superseded/pending releases
  -n <ns>                 Filter to specific namespace
  --failed                Show only failed releases
  --deployed              Show only deployed releases
  --filter <regex>        Filter by release name (e.g., --filter anih)
  -q, --short             Release names only (useful for scripts)
  -o yaml|json            Machine-readable output

💡 Pro tip: helm list -A --failed after a deployment to quickly spot broken releases. helm list -n anihpj -o json | jq '.[].status' for scripting.

Core Concepts Q28 of 200
How do you get detailed status of a specific Helm release including its deployed resources, computed values, and notes?
A) kubectl describe helmrelease <name>
B) helm info <release>
C) helm status <release> — shows deployment status, all Kubernetes resources created, computed configuration values, and the rendered NOTES.txt. To get specific data: helm get manifest, helm get values, helm get notes
D) helm describe <release>
✅ Correct Answer: C

helm status is your go-to command for understanding a release's current state. It shows when the release was deployed, its status, the list of Kubernetes resources it manages, and any NOTES.txt output from the chart.

📝 Detailed Explanation
helm status + helm get — Full Release Inspection
  $ helm status anihpj -n anihpj
  NAME: anihpj
  LAST DEPLOYED: Thu Jun 13 14:30:00 2026

  STATUS: deployed
  REVISION: 3
  TEST SUITE: None
  NOTES:
  Thank you for installing anihpj/jobpost!
  Access the web UI at: http://jobpost.com

  RESOURCES:                          ← All K8s objects created
  ==> v1/Secret
  NAME                    TYPE                   DATA  AGE
  anihpj-db-secret        Opaque                 3     3d
  anihpj-api-secret       Opaque                 2     3d

  ==> v1/Service
  NAME                    TYPE        CLUSTER-IP     PORT(S)
  anihpj-db               ClusterIP   10.96.100.1    5432/TCP

  helm get manifest anihpj   ← Full rendered YAML of all resources
  helm get values anihpj     ← ALL values used (including defaults)
  helm get notes anihpj      ← NOTES.txt output
  helm get hooks anihpj      ← Hook resources that ran
Core Concepts Q29 of 200
How do you uninstall a Helm release? What happens to the Kubernetes resources and release history?
A) helm uninstall <release> -n <ns> — deletes all Kubernetes resources created by the release AND removes all release history Secrets. Add --keep-history to preserve revision Secrets for auditing
B) kubectl delete namespace <ns> — the only way to remove Helm-managed resources is to delete the entire namespace
C) helm delete <release> — removes the release record but leaves all Kubernetes resources running (they become orphaned)
D) helm remove <release> — uninstalls the chart but preserves PVCs and Secrets for data recovery
✅ Correct Answer: A

helm uninstall (aliases: helm del, helm delete, helm un) cleans up everything: all Kubernetes resources (Deployments, Services, etc.) AND all release history Secrets. This is a clean teardown.

📝 Detailed Explanation
helm uninstall — What Gets Deleted
  $ helm uninstall anihpj -n anihpj
  release "anihpj" uninstalled

  WHAT GETS DELETED:
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ ✅ All Kubernetes resources (Deployments, Services, etc.)       │
  │ ✅ All release Secrets (sh.helm.release.v1.anihpj.v*)          │
  │ ❌ PVCs — NOT deleted by default (protects your data!)          │
  │ ❌ Namespace — NOT deleted (may contain other releases)          │
  │ ❌ Custom Resources created by hooks                            │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  USEFUL FLAGS:
  --keep-history    Preserve release Secrets for auditing
  --dry-run         Simulate (see what would be deleted)
  --no-hooks        Skip pre-delete/post-delete hooks
  --timeout         Max time to wait (default: 5m)

  TO DELETE PVCs (if you really want to):
  kubectl delete pvc -n anihpj -l app.kubernetes.io/instance=anihpj

🔗 Connection to anihpj/jobpost: When testing scenarios in Part 3, you'll frequently helm uninstall anihpj -n anihpj and reinstall. PVCs survive uninstall by default, so your database data persists across reinstall cycles during development.

Core Concepts Q30 of 200
How do you retrieve data from a deployed Helm release? What can helm get show you?
A) helm get all <release> returns a single JSON blob — you cannot retrieve specific subsets of release data
B) helm get can only retrieve data from the latest revision — historical revisions are not accessible
C) helm get downloads the chart .tgz file from the repository for local inspection
D) helm get manifest (full YAML), helm get values (all config), helm get hooks (hook resources), helm get notes (NOTES.txt), helm get all (everything combined). Add --revision N to inspect any historical revision
✅ Correct Answer: D

helm get is the read-side of Helm's release management. Every piece of information stored during install/upgrade is retrievable. The --revision flag is particularly powerful — it lets you inspect exactly what was deployed at any point in time.

📝 Detailed Explanation
helm get — Retrieving Release Data
  helm get manifest anihpj -n anihpj
  → Full rendered YAML of all resources (what was actually applied)

  helm get values anihpj -n anihpj --all
  → ALL computed values (user overrides + chart defaults merged)

  helm get values anihpj -n anihpj --revision 2
  → Values as they were at revision 2 (useful for debugging!)

  helm get manifest anihpj --revision 1 | kubectl diff -f -
  → Compare current cluster state vs what revision 1 deployed

  helm get hooks anihpj -n anihpj
  → Show hook resources (migration Jobs, backup Jobs, etc.)

  helm get notes anihpj -n anihpj
  → Show NOTES.txt output (connection strings, URLs, instructions)

  helm get all anihpj -n anihpj
  → Everything above in one output

🔗 Connection to anihpj/jobpost: helm get values anihpj -n anihpj --all is your "what exactly is deployed and how is it configured?" command. helm get manifest anihpj --revision 5 | kubectl diff -f - shows if someone manually modified resources outside of Helm (drift detection).

2.1 Chart Structure Deep DiveQ31-Q36

Chart Structure Q31 of 200
What is the complete directory layout of a production Helm chart? Name every file and folder.
A) A complete chart contains: Chart.yaml (metadata), values.yaml (defaults), templates/ (Go-templated YAML + _helpers.tpl + NOTES.txt), optional charts/ (subchart deps), .helmignore (exclude files), values-*.yaml (env overrides), schema/ (JSON schema), and tests/ (helm test pods)
B) Helm charts only require Chart.yaml and one .yaml file in templates/ — everything else is auto-generated
C) The complete chart layout is: Dockerfile, docker-compose.yml, values.yaml, templates/
D) Charts have no fixed structure — you can organize files however you want as long as helm lint passes
✅ Correct Answer: A

A well-structured Helm chart follows a convention that Helm (and other tools like ArgoCD, IDEs, linters) expect. Every file has a defined purpose. Understanding this structure is the foundation for building production-ready charts.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Complete Helm Chart Directory Layout (anihpj/jobpost)
  helm/anihpj/                        ← Chart root (matches Chart.yaml name)
  │
  ├── Chart.yaml                      ← REQUIRED: name, version, apiVersion
  ├── values.yaml                     ← REQUIRED: default configuration
  ├── .helmignore                     ← OPTIONAL: files excluded from .tgz
  │
  ├── charts/                         ← OPTIONAL: subchart dependencies
  │   └── postgresql-15.5.20.tgz      ←   Downloaded by "helm dep update"
  │
  ├── templates/                      ← REQUIRED: Go-templated K8s manifests
  │   ├── _helpers.tpl                ←   Named reusable templates
  │   ├── NOTES.txt                   ←   Post-install message (REQUIRED for UX)
  │   ├── namespace.yaml              ←   K8s Namespace
  │   ├── secrets.yaml                ←   K8s Secrets
  │   ├── configmap.yaml              ←   K8s ConfigMaps
  │   ├── postgres-sts.yaml           ←   PostgreSQL StatefulSet
  │   ├── postgres-svc.yaml           ←   PostgreSQL Service
  │   ├── redis-deploy.yaml           ←   Redis Deployment
  │   ├── redis-svc.yaml              ←   Redis Service
  │   ├── django-api-deploy.yaml      ←   Django API Deployment
  │   ├── django-api-svc.yaml         ←   Django API Service
  │   ├── django-api-hpa.yaml         ←   HPA for API
  │   ├── django-web-deploy.yaml      ←   Django Web Deployment
  │   ├── django-web-svc.yaml         ←   Django Web Service
  │   ├── ingress.yaml                ←   Ingress (TLS + routing)
  │   ├── networkpolicy.yaml          ←   NetworkPolicy rules
  │   ├── rbac.yaml                   ←   RBAC (ServiceAccounts, Roles)
  │   └── tests/                      ←   OPTIONAL: helm test pods
  │       └── test-connection.yaml    ←     Test pod spec
  │
  ├── values-dev.yaml                 ← OPTIONAL: dev overrides
  ├── values-staging.yaml             ← OPTIONAL: staging overrides
  ├── values-prod.yaml                ← OPTIONAL: prod overrides
  │
  └── schema/                         ← OPTIONAL: JSON schema validation
      └── values.schema.json          ←   Validates structure & types

🔗 Connection to anihpj/jobpost: This is EXACTLY the directory you'll build in Part 3. Your current k8s/ directory (14 raw YAML files) maps 1:1 to templates/ (14 Go-templated YAML files). The transformation is: hardcoded values → {{ .Values.xxx }} placeholders.

Chart Structure Q32 of 200
What is Chart.yaml and which three fields are absolutely required for Helm to recognize a directory as a chart?
A) name, description, maintainers
B) apiVersion: v2, name, version — these three fields are the minimum. Without them, helm lint and helm install will reject the chart
C) apiVersion, appVersion, type
D) name, version, icon
✅ Correct Answer: B

apiVersion: v2 tells Helm this is a Helm 3 chart. name identifies the chart (must be lowercase, match directory name). version follows SemVer for release tracking. Missing any of these and Helm will refuse to process the chart.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Chart.yaml — The Minimum Viable Chart
  # ABSOLUTE MINIMUM Chart.yaml (Helm 3)
  apiVersion: v2
  name: anihpj
  version: 1.0.0

  # These 3 lines are ALL you need for a valid chart.
  # $ helm lint ./anihpj
  # ==> Linting ./anihpj
  # 1 chart(s) linted, 0 chart(s) failed  ✅

  # Without apiVersion:
  # Error: chart.yaml requires apiVersion

  # Without name:
  # Error: chart.yaml requires name

  # Without version:
  # Error: chart.yaml requires version
Chart Structure Q33 of 200
What is the .helmignore file and why should every chart have one?
A) .helmignore lists Kubernetes resources that Helm should NOT manage — it's like a Kubernetes exclusion list
B) .helmignore is a deprecated Helm 2 feature — Helm 3 automatically ignores unnecessary files
C) .helmignore works exactly like .gitignore — it prevents specified files from being included when you run helm package. Essential for keeping .git/, *.swp, README.md, and editor temp files out of your packaged .tgz chart
D) .helmignore is a security file that lists which Kubernetes namespaces the chart is allowed to deploy to
✅ Correct Answer: C

Every Helm chart should have a .helmignore file. Without it, helm package will include your entire Git history, editor backup files, local test values, and other junk in the .tgz — bloating the package and potentially leaking sensitive information.

📝 Detailed Explanation
.helmignore — Keep Your Chart Package Clean
  # .helmignore (recommended minimum)
  .git/
  .gitignore
  .gitmodules
  .idea/
  .vscode/
  *.swp
  *.bak
  *.tmp
  *.orig
  *~
  .DS_Store
  README.md
  LICENSE

  # Local test values (might contain real secrets!)
  values-local.yaml
  values-test.yaml

  # BEFORE .helmignore (bad):
  $ helm package ./anihpj
  → anihpj-1.0.0.tgz (45MB — includes .git/ with 500MB history!)

  # AFTER .helmignore (good):
  $ helm package ./anihpj
  → anihpj-1.0.0.tgz (12KB — just Chart.yaml + values.yaml + templates/)

B) NOTES.txt is a plain text changelog showing what changed between chart versions

What is Chart.lock and how does it relate to helm dependency update?

B) Chart.lock is automatically deleted after each install to prevent stale dependency data
C) Chart.lock stores the rendered Kubernetes manifests after the last helm template run

✅ Correct Answer: D
