3.2 Rollbacks & HistoryQ99-Q106

Release Mgmt Q99 of 200
How does helm rollback work? Does it delete the bad revision?
A) Rollback deletes the bad revision and restores the previous one permanently
B) helm rollback anihpj 3 reads revision 3's manifest and creates a NEW revision. The bad revision is NOT deleted — it's marked superseded. You can rollback a rollback. Every state transition is preserved
C) Rollback only goes back one revision at a time — multiple rollbacks needed
D) Rollback only works within 5 minutes of the upgrade
✅ Correct Answer: B

Helm rollback is non-destructive. Every revision is preserved. Rollback creates a NEW revision — if it doesn't fix the issue, rollback the rollback. Complete confidence to experiment.

📝 Detailed Explanation
helm rollback — Non-Destructive Revision Chain
  REVISION HISTORY:
  $ helm history anihpj
  ┌──────────┬──────────────┬──────────────────────┬──────────┐
  │ REVISION │ UPDATED      │ STATUS               │ CHART    │
  ├──────────┼──────────────┼──────────────────────┼──────────┤
  │ 1        │ Mon Jun 13   │ superseded           │ anihpj-1 │
  │ 2        │ Mon Jun 13   │ superseded           │ anihpj-1 │
  │ 3        │ Mon Jun 13   │ superseded ← BAD!    │ anihpj-1 │
  │ 4        │ Mon Jun 13   │ deployed             │ anihpj-1 │
  └──────────┴──────────────┴──────────────────────┴──────────┘

  ROLLBACK CREATES A NEW REVISION:
  $ helm rollback anihpj 2
  Rollback was a success! ✅

  ┌──────────┬──────────────┬──────────────────────┬──────────┐
  │ REVISION │ UPDATED      │ STATUS               │ CHART    │
  ├──────────┼──────────────┼──────────────────────┼──────────┤
  │ 1        │ Mon Jun 13   │ superseded           │ anihpj-1 │
  │ 2        │ Mon Jun 13   │ superseded           │ anihpj-1 │
  │ 3        │ Mon Jun 13   │ superseded (bad)     │ anihpj-1 │
  │ 4        │ Mon Jun 13   │ superseded           │ anihpj-1 │
  │ 5        │ Mon Jun 13   │ deployed  ← NEW!     │ anihpj-1 │
  └──────────┴──────────────┴──────────────────────┴──────────┘
  # Revision 3 is NOT deleted — just marked superseded.
  # Revision 5 is a NEW revision (copy of rev 2's manifest).

  KEY TAKEAWAYS:
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ • Rollback is NON-DESTRUCTIVE — nothing is ever deleted         │
  │ • Rollback CREATES a new revision (not a true "rewind")        │
  │ • You CAN rollback a rollback — full confidence to experiment   │
  │ • Every state transition is preserved in revision history       │
  │ • Use --max-history to limit stored revision Secrets            │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Release Mgmt Q100 of 200
What does --max-history control and why should you set it?
A) Limits how far back helm rollback can go
B) Sets the maximum releases allowed per namespace
C) Controls parallel upgrade concurrency
D) Limits stored revision Secrets (default: 256). Set to 10 for production — prevents namespace bloat from hundreds of revision Secrets accumulating over months of deployments. Old revisions auto-pruned
✅ Correct Answer: D

Without --max-history, daily deployments create 365 revision Secrets per year per release. Set --max-history 10 during install for automatic cleanup.

📝 Detailed Explanation
--max-history — Preventing Secret Bloat
  helm install anihpj ./chart --set maxHistory=10

  # Or in values.yaml:
  helm:
    maxHistory: 10

  After 100 deployments with maxHistory=10:
  $ kubectl get secrets -n anihpj -l owner=helm
  NAME                               AGE
  sh.helm.release.v1.anihpj.v91     2d   ← Oldest kept
  sh.helm.release.v1.anihpj.v92     1d
  ...                                  ← Only 10 kept!
  sh.helm.release.v1.anihpj.v100    1h   ← Latest

  # Revisions 1-90 automatically deleted!
Release Mgmt Q101 of 200
What actually happens during a helm rollback? Is the old revision "restored" or is a new revision created?
A) Helm deletes all revisions after the target and sets the target revision as "deployed" — rewriting history
B) Helm reads the manifest from the target revision's release Secret, applies it to the cluster, and creates a NEW revision with that manifest. Old revisions are preserved — nothing is deleted. Status of the bad revision changes to "superseded"
C) Helm reinstalls the chart from scratch using the values that were active at that revision
D) Helm copies the target revision's Secret to overwrite the latest revision's Secret in-place
✅ Correct Answer: B

A rollback is not a "rewind" — it's a forward operation that creates a brand new revision. Helm reads the stored manifest from the target revision's Secret, applies those exact resources to the cluster, and records the result as a new (higher-numbered) revision. The previous "bad" revision is marked "superseded" but remains available for future rollbacks or inspection.

📝 Detailed Explanation
helm rollback — The Forward Operation That Looks Backward
  REVISION CHAIN BEFORE ROLLBACK:
  ┌──────────┬──────────────┬──────────────┬─────────────────────────┐
  │ REVISION │ STATUS       │ MANIFEST     │ SECRET                  │
  ├──────────┼──────────────┼──────────────┼─────────────────────────┤
  │ 1        │ superseded   │ v1 manifests │ sh.helm...anihpj.v1     │
  │ 2        │ superseded   │ v2 manifests │ sh.helm...anihpj.v2     │
  │ 3        │ deployed     │ v3 manifests │ sh.helm...anihpj.v3 ← BAD!
  └──────────┴──────────────┴──────────────┴─────────────────────────┘
  # Users report 500 errors after rev 3 upgrade!

  $ helm rollback anihpj 2 -n anihpj

  WHAT HAPPENS INTERNALLY:
  STEP 1: Read Secret sh.helm.release.v1.anihpj.v2
  STEP 2: Extract base64-encoded manifest from .data.release
  STEP 3: Apply those manifests to the cluster
  STEP 4: Create NEW Secret sh.helm.release.v1.anihpj.v4
          (containing rev 2's manifest, but versioned as rev 4)

  REVISION CHAIN AFTER ROLLBACK:
  ┌──────────┬──────────────┬──────────────┬─────────────────────────┐
  │ REVISION │ STATUS       │ MANIFEST     │ SECRET                  │
  ├──────────┼──────────────┼──────────────┼─────────────────────────┤
  │ 1        │ superseded   │ v1 manifests │ sh.helm...anihpj.v1     │
  │ 2        │ superseded   │ v2 manifests │ sh.helm...anihpj.v2     │
  │ 3        │ superseded   │ v3 manifests │ sh.helm...anihpj.v3     │
  │ 4        │ deployed  ←──│ v2 manifests │ sh.helm...anihpj.v4 NEW!│
  └──────────┴──────────────┴──────────────┴─────────────────────────┘
  # Rev 3 NOT deleted — just marked superseded. Rev 4 is new!

  🔗 Connection to anihpj/jobpost: If an upgrade breaks the API
  (rev 3), rollback to rev 2 restores the working state. The
  broken rev 3 remains available for debugging — you can view
  its manifest with helm get manifest --revision 3.

This non-destructive design means you can rollback a rollback — if rev 4 doesn't fix the issue either, helm rollback anihpj 1 creates rev 5 using rev 1's manifest. Complete safety net for production deployments.

Release Mgmt Q102 of 200
You deploy anihpj/jobpost to production with daily helm upgrade. After 6 months, kubectl get secrets -n anihpj shows 180+ release secrets. What should you have set during helm install to prevent this?
A) --set secretRetention=30 — limits secrets to 30 days
B) --set revisionLimit=10 — limits the revision counter
C) --cleanup-on-upgrade — deletes old secrets on each upgrade
D) --set maxHistory=10 (or --max-history 10) during helm install. This limits stored revision Secrets — Helm auto-prunes the oldest revisions, keeping only the most recent N. Default is 256 (Helm 3)
✅ Correct Answer: D

Without --max-history, Helm stores every revision forever (up to the default of 256). With daily deployments, that's 365 revision Secrets per year per release — each containing the full rendered manifest and all values. Setting --max-history 10 keeps only the last 10 revisions and automatically deletes older Secrets.

📝 Detailed Explanation
maxHistory — Controlling Release Secret Accumulation
  WITHOUT maxHistory (default: 256):
  $ kubectl get secrets -n anihpj -l owner=helm | wc -l
  183  ← After 6 months of daily upgrades!

  Each Secret contains:
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ sh.helm.release.v1.anihpj.v147                                  │
  │   data:                                                         │
  │     release: (base64-encoded gzipped JSON — the FULL manifest!) │
  │   labels:                                                       │
  │     owner: helm                                                  │
  │     status: superseded                                           │
  │     version: "147"                                              │
  │   size: ~50KB (typical for anihpj chart)                        │
  │                                                                 │
  │ 183 secrets × 50KB = ~9MB — not huge, but clutters kubectl     │
  │ get secrets output and slows etcd queries                       │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  WITH maxHistory set to 10:
  $ helm install anihpj ./helm/anihpj --set maxHistory=10

  # Or in values.yaml:
  helm:
    maxHistory: 10

  After 100 upgrades:
  $ kubectl get secrets -n anihpj -l owner=helm
  NAME                               AGE
  sh.helm.release.v1.anihpj.v91     9d
  sh.helm.release.v1.anihpj.v92     8d
  ...                                ...
  sh.helm.release.v1.anihpj.v100    1h
  # Only 10 secrets! Revisions 1-90 auto-deleted!

  BEST PRACTICE: Set --max-history 10 in production CI/CD.
  Keep enough revisions for rollback safety, not infinite history.
Release Mgmt Q103 of 200
After upgrading anihpj 5 times and rolling back twice, helm history anihpj shows revision numbers 1 through 7. Why is revision 4 NOT the same as revision 2 even though you rolled back TO revision 2?
A) Helm revision numbers are random — they don't correspond to the actual sequence of operations
B) Revision 4 was deleted when you rolled back to revision 2 — the numbering just skips deleted revisions
C) Revision numbers are always incrementing and never reused. A rollback to rev 2 creates a NEW revision with the NEXT number in sequence (rev 4). Rev 4 contains rev 2's manifest but is its own distinct revision. This preserves a complete, immutable audit trail
D) Only the most recent 3 revisions are numbered — older ones get renumbered to maintain ordering
✅ Correct Answer: C

Helm revision numbers are monotonically increasing counters — they never go backward, never get reused, and never skip. A rollback creates a NEW revision at the NEXT number. This design gives you an immutable audit trail of every state change: install → upgrade → upgrade → rollback → upgrade. You can always trace what happened and when.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Revision Numbering — Monotonic, Immutable, Never Reused
  COMPLETE REVISION TIMELINE (anihpj/jobpost):
  ┌──────┬──────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ REV  │ OPERATION    │ WHAT HAPPENED                               │
  ├──────┼──────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ 1    │ helm install │ First deployment — anihpj v1.0.0            │
  │ 2    │ helm upgrade │ Updated postgres.image → 16-alpine          │
  │ 3    │ helm upgrade │ Updated api.replicaCount → 5 (BROKE API!)   │
  │ 4    │ helm rollback│ Rollback to rev 2 → NEW revision using      │
  │      │   to rev 2   │ rev 2's manifest. Rev 4 = rev 2's YAML.    │
  │ 5    │ helm upgrade │ Fixed the bug, deployed corrected config    │
  │ 6    │ helm upgrade │ Updated web.replicaCount → 3                │
  │ 7    │ helm rollback│ Rollback to rev 5 → NEW revision (rev 7)   │
  │      │   to rev 5   │ Rev 7 = rev 5's manifest.                  │
  └──────┴──────────────┴─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  KEY PROPERTIES:
  • Rev 4 and Rev 2 have the SAME manifest, DIFFERENT revision numbers
  • You can rollback to ANY past revision — not just the previous one
  • Rev 3 (broken) is preserved forever → debug what went wrong
  • The revision number tells you the ORDER of operations, not the STATE

  WHY MONOTONIC? — AUDIT TRAIL:
  helm history anihpj tells the COMPLETE story of your release.
  If revisions were reused, you'd lose the record of failed upgrades.
  With immutable numbering, you always know: "rev 3 was the bad one."
Release Mgmt Q104 of 200
How do you view the exact rendered Kubernetes manifests that were deployed at a specific revision (e.g., revision 3)?
A) helm get values anihpj --revision 3 — values tell you everything about the deployed state
B) helm get manifest anihpj --revision 3 — this prints the complete rendered YAML (Deployment, Service, ConfigMap, etc.) that was applied to the cluster at revision 3. Use it to compare what changed between revisions
C) kubectl get all -n anihpj -o yaml — this shows the current live state, which is always the same as any revision
D) You can't view past revision manifests — Helm only stores the latest one
✅ Correct Answer: B

helm get manifest anihpj --revision N is your time machine — it retrieves the exact YAML that Helm applied to the cluster at that revision. Every release Secret stores the full rendered manifest (gzipped, base64-encoded), so you can inspect any past revision's state even if it's been superseded many times over.

📝 Detailed Explanation
helm get manifest --revision — Time-Travel Debugging
  $ helm history anihpj -n anihpj
  ┌──────────┬──────────────┬──────────────────────┬──────────┐
  │ REVISION │ STATUS       │ DESCRIPTION          │ CHART    │
  ├──────────┼──────────────┼──────────────────────┼──────────┤
  │ 1        │ superseded   │ Initial install      │ anihpj-1 │
  │ 2        │ superseded   │ Upgraded PG to 16    │ anihpj-1 │
  │ 3        │ superseded   │ Scaled API to 5      │ anihpj-1 │
  │ 4        │ deployed     │ Rollback to rev 2    │ anihpj-1 │
  └──────────┴──────────────┴──────────────────────┴──────────┘

  # What did the BROKEN revision 3 look like?
  $ helm get manifest anihpj --revision 3 -n anihpj
  ---
  apiVersion: apps/v1
  kind: Deployment
  metadata:
    name: anihpj-api
    labels:
      app.kubernetes.io/name: anihpj
  spec:
    replicas: 5    ← Ah-ha! This is what broke the API!
    ...

  # Compare two revisions (manual diff):
  $ helm get manifest anihpj --revision 2 > rev2.yaml
  $ helm get manifest anihpj --revision 3 > rev3.yaml
  $ diff rev2.yaml rev3.yaml
  15c15
  <   replicas: 1
  ---
  >   replicas: 5   ← The breaking change identified!

  ALSO AVAILABLE:
  helm get values anihpj --revision 3    ← Values used at rev 3
  helm get hooks anihpj --revision 3     ← Hooks that ran at rev 3
  helm get notes anihpj --revision 3     ← NOTES.txt output at rev 3
  helm get all anihpj --revision 3       ← Everything combined

This is invaluable for debugging production incidents — compare what changed between "it worked" and "it broke" by diffing two revision manifests.

Release Mgmt Q105 of 200
What does helm get values anihpj --revision 3 show vs helm get values anihpj --revision 3 --all?
A) Without --all: shows only user-supplied values (from --set, -f files, CLI overrides). With --all: shows the COMPLETE computed values including all defaults from values.yaml — exactly what the template engine received. Use --all to see the full configuration that produced a revision
B) Both show the same output — --all is a deprecated flag kept for backward compatibility
C) --revision 3 --all shows values from ALL revisions combined, not just revision 3
D) Without --all shows the manifest; with --all shows the values. They're completely different commands
✅ Correct Answer: A

The --all flag is the difference between "what the user asked for" and "what Helm actually used." User-supplied values (from --set, -f) only show overrides. With --all, you see the complete merged values object — defaults + overrides — that was fed into the template engine.

📝 Detailed Explanation
helm get values — User Values vs Computed Values
  # What the user provided at install time:
  $ helm install anihpj ./helm/anihpj \
      --set api.replicaCount=3 \
      --set postgres.storage=50Gi

  $ helm get values anihpj --revision 1
  USER-SUPPLIED VALUES:
  api:
    replicaCount: 3
  postgres:
    storage: 50Gi
  # Only shows what was explicitly set. Missing all defaults!

  $ helm get values anihpj --revision 1 --all
  COMPUTED VALUES:
  api:
    replicaCount: 3          ← User override
    image:
      repository: anihpj-api
      tag: latest             ← From values.yaml default
      pullPolicy: IfNotPresent ← From values.yaml default
  postgres:
    image: postgres:15-alpine ← From values.yaml default
    storage: 50Gi             ← User override
    storageClass: standard    ← From values.yaml default
  redis:
    enabled: true             ← From values.yaml default
    image: redis:7-alpine     ← From values.yaml default
  ...

  USE CASES:
  --all → "What did the template engine ACTUALLY receive?"
         Debug why a template rendered a certain way.

  (no --all) → "What did the USER explicitly override?"
              Useful for documentation and auditing.
Release Mgmt Q106 of 200
How do you compare two revisions to see exactly what changed between them? Does Helm have a built-in diff command?
A) helm diff anihpj 2 3 — built into Helm 3.7+ as a native subcommand
B) helm compare anihpj --revision 2 --revision 3 — built-in comparison with color-coded output
C) Helm does NOT have a built-in diff. Use the helm-diff plugin (helm plugin install https://github.com/databus23/helm-diff), which adds helm diff. Or manually: helm get manifest --revision 2 | kubectl diff -f - to compare a revision against the live cluster. For revision-vs-revision: dump both manifests and use standard diff
D) Use helm get manifest --revision 2 --diff-with 3 — the --diff-with flag handles comparison
✅ Correct Answer: C

Helm intentionally keeps the core binary small and relies on plugins for extended functionality. The helm-diff plugin is the de facto standard for comparing revisions, previewing upgrades, and seeing what helm upgrade would change before applying it. It's the most popular Helm plugin with millions of downloads.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Comparing Revisions — helm-diff Plugin & Manual Methods
  METHOD 1 — helm-diff plugin (RECOMMENDED):
  $ helm plugin install https://github.com/databus23/helm-diff
  $ helm diff revision anihpj 2 3 -n anihpj
  anihpj-api, Deployment (apps) has changed:
    spec:
      replicas:
  -     - 1
  +     - 5     ← Clearly shows what changed!

  # Also: preview what an upgrade WOULD change:
  $ helm diff upgrade anihpj ./helm/anihpj -f values-prod.yaml

  METHOD 2 — Manual diff (no plugin needed):
  $ helm get manifest anihpj --revision 2 > /tmp/rev2.yaml
  $ helm get manifest anihpj --revision 3 > /tmp/rev3.yaml
  $ diff -u /tmp/rev2.yaml /tmp/rev3.yaml

  METHOD 3 — Compare revision to LIVE cluster:
  $ helm get manifest anihpj --revision 2 | kubectl diff -f -
  # Shows differences between rev 2's manifest and current state

  WHY NO BUILT-IN DIFF?
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Helm team philosophy: Keep the core lean. Plugins extend it.    │
  │ helm-diff is maintained by the community (databus23) and is     │
  │ the #1 most-installed Helm plugin. Install it once, use forever.│
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  🔗 Connection to anihpj/jobpost: Before every production upgrade,
  run helm diff upgrade to preview the exact changes. If replicas
  jump from 1→5 unexpectedly, catch it BEFORE applying.

3.3 Uninstalling & CleanupQ107-Q110

Release Mgmt Q107 of 200
What does helm uninstall anihpj actually do? What gets deleted and what survives?
A) Only the release record is deleted — all Kubernetes resources remain untouched
B) Everything is deleted: resources, namespace, release secrets, and the chart itself from the repository
C) The namespace is deleted (cascading delete of all resources) and the release record is removed
D) Helm deletes ALL resources it created (Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps, Secrets, Ingress, HPA, etc.), deletes the release record, and deletes ALL release history Secrets. The namespace is NOT deleted. PVCs may survive depending on their reclaimPolicy (Retain = survives, Delete = deleted)
✅ Correct Answer: D

helm uninstall performs a complete cleanup of the release: all Kubernetes resources created by the chart are deleted, all release history Secrets are removed, and the release record is gone from helm list. The namespace persists (unless it was created by --create-namespace and is now empty — but Helm doesn't auto-delete namespaces).

📝 Detailed Explanation
helm uninstall — What Gets Deleted vs What Survives
  BEFORE UNINSTALL:
  $ helm list -n anihpj
  NAME    NAMESPACE  REVISION  STATUS    CHART         APP VERSION
  anihpj  anihpj     4         deployed  anihpj-1.0.0  2.5

  $ kubectl get all -n anihpj
  NAME                              READY   STATUS    RESTARTS
  pod/anihpj-api-7d9f8c6b4-abcde   1/1     Running   0
  pod/anihpj-web-5c8b9d7f6-fghij   1/1     Running   0
  pod/anihpj-db-0                  1/1     Running   0
  pod/anihpj-redis-6e4a2c1d-kjlmn  1/1     Running   0
  ...

  $ helm uninstall anihpj -n anihpj
  release "anihpj" uninstalled

  AFTER UNINSTALL:
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ ✅ DELETED:                                                     │
  │   • All K8s resources: Deployments, StatefulSets, Services,     │
  │     ConfigMaps, Secrets, Ingress, HPA, NetworkPolicy, RBAC      │
  │   • ALL release history Secrets (sh.helm.release.v1.anihpj.*)  │
  │   • Release record (no longer shows in helm list)               │
  │                                                                 │
  │ ❌ SURVIVES:                                                    │
  │   • Namespace (anihpj) — NOT deleted by Helm                    │
  │   • PVCs with reclaimPolicy: Retain — data preserved!           │
  │   • Any resources created manually (not by the chart)           │
  │   • The chart files on disk (your ./helm/anihpj/ directory)    │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  🔗 CRITICAL FOR anihpj/jobpost:
  If PostgreSQL PVC has reclaimPolicy: Retain (default for many
  StorageClasses), your database data SURVIVES helm uninstall.
  You can reinstall the chart and bind to the same PVC to recover!
Release Mgmt Q108 of 200
What does helm uninstall anihpj --keep-history do differently from a standard uninstall?
A) Resources are deleted, but the release history Secrets are preserved. The release disappears from helm list but you can still access revision data with helm get manifest --revision N. Use for auditing, compliance, or potential recovery before the retention period expires
B) All Kubernetes resources are kept but marked for deletion — they're removed after 30 days
C) The release is paused instead of deleted — all pods are scaled to 0 but not removed
D) Only the release record is kept; all Kubernetes resources and secrets are deleted as usual
✅ Correct Answer: A

--keep-history is the audit-friendly uninstall. All Kubernetes resources are removed (your app stops running), but the revision Secrets are preserved. This means you can still run helm get manifest --revision 3 and inspect what was deployed — critical for compliance environments where you need to prove "what was running and when."

📝 Detailed Explanation
--keep-history — Delete the App, Keep the Record
  STANDARD UNINSTALL:
  $ helm uninstall anihpj -n anihpj
  → All resources GONE, all history GONE.
  → helm get manifest anihpj --revision 1 → ERROR: release not found

  UNINSTALL WITH --keep-history:
  $ helm uninstall anihpj -n anihpj --keep-history
  release "anihpj" uninstalled

  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ WHAT HAPPENS:                                                   │
  │ ✅ K8s resources DELETED (pods stop, app goes down)             │
  │ ✅ Release removed from helm list                               │
  │ ✅ History Secrets PRESERVED (sh.helm.release.v1.anihpj.v1-4)  │
  │ ✅ You CAN still run:                                           │
  │      helm get manifest anihpj --revision 3 -n anihpj            │
  │      helm get values anihpj --revision 1 -n anihpj --all        │
  │      helm history anihpj -n anihpj  (yes, still works!)         │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  WHEN TO USE --keep-history:
  • Compliance: SOC2, HIPAA, PCI require deployment audit trails
  • Incident post-mortems: "What config was running before the outage?"
  • Safe decommissioning: Delete the app, keep the evidence
  • Temporary shutdown: Uninstall but preserve the ability to review
    what was deployed (then manually delete Secrets later)

  WHEN NOT TO USE:
  • Regular CI/CD cleanup (clutters namespace with orphan secrets)
  • Development environments (use standard uninstall for cleanliness)
Release Mgmt Q109 of 200
After helm uninstall anihpj, you notice the PostgreSQL PVC still exists with data intact. Why did this happen and is it a bug?
A) This is a Helm bug — PVCs should always be deleted with the release
B) This is by design. PVCs are NOT deleted by helm uninstall by default — they're managed by the StorageClass reclaimPolicy. If reclaimPolicy is "Retain", the PV and data survive. If "Delete", the PV is deleted with the PVC. This protects against accidental data loss
C) PVCs are always deleted — you must have created it manually outside the chart
D) Helm uninstall has a 30-minute delay before deleting PVCs to allow recovery
✅ Correct Answer: B

This is a critical safety feature, not a bug. Helm intentionally does NOT manage PVC lifecycle — the StorageClass's reclaimPolicy controls what happens to the underlying PV and data. This prevents helm uninstall from accidentally destroying your database. For anihpj/jobpost, this means your job listings and user data survive even if you uninstall and reinstall the chart.

📝 Detailed Explanation
PVC Survival — By Design, Not a Bug
  THE PVC LIFECYCLE — WHO CONTROLS WHAT:
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Helm controls: Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps, etc.          │
  │                 → helm uninstall DELETES these                  │
  │                                                                 │
  │ StorageClass controls: PVC → PV binding and deletion            │
  │                 → reclaimPolicy determines PVC fate             │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  RECLAIM POLICIES:
  ┌──────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Retain       │ PV survives after PVC deletion. Admin must       │
  │              │ manually delete PV and cleanup storage.          │
  │              │ DATA IS SAFE — but orphaned PVs accumulate.      │
  ├──────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Delete       │ PV is automatically deleted when PVC is deleted. │
  │              │ DATA IS GONE — clean but dangerous.              │
  ├──────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Recycle      │ DEPRECATED. Basic scrub (rm -rf /) then reuse.   │
  └──────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  PRACTICAL EXAMPLE (anihpj/jobpost):
  $ helm uninstall anihpj -n anihpj
  # Pods, Services, Deployments all gone. App is DOWN.

  $ kubectl get pvc -n anihpj
  NAME              STATUS   VOLUME         CAPACITY   STORAGECLASS
  anihpj-db-pvc     Bound    pvc-abc123     10Gi       fast-ssd (Retain)

  # PVC still exists! Data is safe!

  $ helm install anihpj ./helm/anihpj -n anihpj
  # StatefulSet binds to the EXISTING PVC — data recovered!

  TO FORCE PVC DELETION (if you really want to):
  kubectl delete pvc anihpj-db-pvc -n anihpj
  # Then reclaimPolicy determines if PV/data survive.

  🔗 Connection to anihpj/jobpost:
  In production, use reclaimPolicy: Retain for PostgreSQL PVCs.
  This creates a safety net: even if someone accidentally runs
  helm uninstall, your database files survive on disk.
Release Mgmt Q110 of 200
After helm uninstall anihpj, you check kubectl get secrets -n anihpj -l owner=helm and see nothing. Is this expected?
A) Yes, this is expected. helm uninstall deletes ALL release history Secrets by default. The owner=helm label is removed along with the Secrets. Use --keep-history if you want to preserve them
B) No, this is a bug — helm uninstall should preserve release Secrets for 30 days
C) The Secrets are moved to a different namespace (kube-system) for archival

Standard helm uninstall performs a complete cleanup: every release Secret (the entire revision history) is deleted. After uninstall, helm list shows nothing, helm history returns "release not found," and the namespace contains no Helm-owned Secrets. This is the default behavior — use --keep-history to preserve the audit trail.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Release Secret Lifecycle — Creation to Deletion
  RELEASE SECRET LIFECYCLE:
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ CREATED: On every helm install, upgrade, or rollback            │
  │ NAMING:  sh.helm.release.v1.{RELEASE}.v{REVISION}               │
  │ LABELS:  owner=helm, status=deployed|superseded|..., version=N  │
  │ CONTENT: Base64-encoded, gzipped JSON (manifest + values + ...) │
  │ DELETED: On helm uninstall (all at once)                        │
  │          OR auto-pruned when exceeding --max-history            │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  BEFORE UNINSTALL:
  $ kubectl get secrets -n anihpj -l owner=helm
  NAME                                  TYPE     DATA   AGE
  sh.helm.release.v1.anihpj.v1          helm.sh  1      7d
  sh.helm.release.v1.anihpj.v2          helm.sh  1      6d
  sh.helm.release.v1.anihpj.v3          helm.sh  1      3d
  sh.helm.release.v1.anihpj.v4          helm.sh  1      1h

  $ helm uninstall anihpj -n anihpj
  release "anihpj" uninstalled

  AFTER UNINSTALL:
  $ kubectl get secrets -n anihpj -l owner=helm
  No resources found in anihpj namespace.  ← ALL GONE

  WITH --keep-history:
  $ helm uninstall anihpj -n anihpj --keep-history
  $ kubectl get secrets -n anihpj -l owner=helm
  NAME                                  TYPE     DATA   AGE
  sh.helm.release.v1.anihpj.v1          helm.sh  1      7d
  ...                                    ← SECRETS SURVIVE!
  # But helm list shows nothing — release is gone.

3.4 Helm Hooks — Controlling Execution OrderQ111-Q118

Release Mgmt Q111 of 200
What are Helm hooks and what problem do they solve?
A) Hooks are Bash scripts that run before/after helm CLI commands on your local machine
B) Hooks are Kubernetes resources (Jobs, Pods, ConfigMaps) annotated with helm.sh/hook that run at specific points in the release lifecycle (pre-install, post-upgrade, pre-delete, etc.). They solve the ordering problem: "run a DB migration BEFORE the new pods start" or "take a backup BEFORE deleting the database"
C) Hooks are webhook URLs that Helm calls to notify external systems of release events
D) Hooks are Helm plugins that intercept and modify template rendering
✅ Correct Answer: B

Helm hooks are the lifecycle callback system for releases. They're ordinary Kubernetes resources (typically Jobs) with a special helm.sh/hook annotation that tells Helm "don't apply this with everything else — run it at THIS specific point instead." This is how you automate database migrations, backups, certificate generation, and any other ordered task that must happen before or after resource deployment.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Helm Hooks — Lifecycle Callbacks for Your Release
  HOOK ANNOTATION SYNTAX:
  metadata:
    annotations:
      "helm.sh/hook": pre-install       ← Run BEFORE resources applied
      "helm.sh/hook": post-upgrade      ← Run AFTER upgrade completes
      "helm.sh/hook-weight": "-5"       ← Order among hooks (lower = first)
      "helm.sh/hook-delete-policy": hook-succeeded  ← Auto-cleanup

  ALL 9 HOOK TYPES:
  ┌──────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ INSTALL LIFECYCLE    │ UPGRADE LIFECYCLE                         │
  ├──────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ pre-install          │ pre-upgrade                               │
  │ post-install         │ post-upgrade                              │
  ├──────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ DELETE LIFECYCLE     │ ROLLBACK LIFECYCLE                        │
  ├──────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ pre-delete           │ pre-rollback                              │
  │ post-delete          │ post-rollback                             │
  ├──────────────────────┤                                           │
  │ TEST LIFECYCLE       │                                           │
  ├──────────────────────┤                                           │
  │ test                 │                                           │
  └──────────────────────┴───────────────────────────────────────────┘

  🔗 Connection to anihpj/jobpost:
  pre-upgrade hook → Run Django migrations BEFORE new API pods start
  pre-delete hook   → Backup PostgreSQL BEFORE database is deleted
  post-install hook → Create initial superuser AFTER everything is up

Without hooks, you'd need external scripts and manual timing. With hooks, the entire lifecycle is self-contained in the chart — one helm install runs migrations, creates users, and deploys your app in the correct order.

Release Mgmt Q112 of 200
Which hook would you use to run a database migration (e.g., python manage.py migrate) before new application pods start during an upgrade?
A) pre-upgrade — runs after templates are rendered but BEFORE any new resources are applied. Perfect for DB migrations: migrate first, then roll out new pods that depend on the new schema
B) post-install — runs after all resources are deployed; too late for migrations
C) pre-install — only runs on the first install, not during upgrades
D) pre-delete — runs before deleting the release, not during upgrades
✅ Correct Answer: A

pre-upgrade is the perfect hook for database migrations. It runs AFTER Helm renders the new templates but BEFORE it applies any resources to the cluster. The sequence is: (1) old pods still running, (2) migration Job runs against the DB, (3) migration completes, (4) new pods with updated code replace old pods. The application never experiences schema-code mismatch.

📝 Detailed Explanation
pre-upgrade Hook — Database Migration Before Pod Rollout
  TIMELINE OF helm upgrade WITH pre-upgrade HOOK:
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ TIME  │ EVENT                                                    │
  ├───────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ T+0s  │ helm upgrade anihpj ./helm/anihpj --set api.image=v2.5  │
  │       │ → Old pods (v2.4) still running and serving traffic      │
  │       │                                                          │
  │ T+1s  │ Helm renders new templates (v2.5 manifests)              │
  │       │                                                          │
  │ T+2s  │ pre-upgrade hook triggers:                               │
  │       │   Job "anihpj-db-migrate" created                        │
  │       │   → python manage.py migrate                             │
  │       │   → ALTER TABLE jobpost_job ADD COLUMN remote_allowed... │
  │       │   → Migration SUCCESS                                    │
  │       │                                                          │
  │ T+30s │ Hook Job completes. Helm waits for it (by default).      │
  │       │                                                          │
  │ T+31s │ Helm applies new resources:                              │
  │       │   → New Deployment (v2.5) rolls out                     │
  │       │   → New pods replace old pods (rolling update)           │
  │       │   → New code sees migrated schema → NO ERRORS!           │
  └───────┴──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  THE HOOK TEMPLATE (templates/db-migrate-job.yaml):
  apiVersion: batch/v1
  kind: Job
  metadata:
    name: {{ .Release.Name }}-db-migrate
    annotations:
      "helm.sh/hook": pre-upgrade,pre-install
      "helm.sh/hook-weight": "-5"
      "helm.sh/hook-delete-policy": hook-succeeded
  spec:
    template:
      spec:
        restartPolicy: Never
        containers:
          - name: migrate
            image: {{ .Values.api.image }}
            command: ["python", "manage.py", "migrate"]

Without this hook, new pods would start with code expecting the new schema while the DB still has the old schema — causing 500 errors until you manually run migrations.

Release Mgmt Q113 of 200
You have 3 hooks: a DB backup, a schema migration, and a data validation. They must run in that EXACT order. How do you control hook execution order?
A) Hooks run alphabetically by resource name — name them 01-backup, 02-migrate, 03-validate
B) Hooks always run in the order they appear in the templates/ directory
C) Use the helm.sh/hook-weight annotation with numeric values. Hooks execute in ascending weight order (lowest first). Set backup=0, migrate=5, validate=10. Hooks with the same weight run in parallel. Default weight is 0 if not specified
D) Hooks can't be ordered — they always run in parallel
✅ Correct Answer: C

Hook weights are Helm's mechanism for ordering hooks within the same lifecycle point. The annotation "helm.sh/hook-weight": "-5" (a string representation of a number) determines execution order. Lower weights run first. Negative weights are common for "must run before everything else" hooks. Hooks with the same weight value run concurrently.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Hook Weights — Ordering Hook Execution
  HOOK WEIGHT RULES:
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ • Weights are STRINGS (not integers): "0", "-5", "10"           │
  │ • Lower numbers execute FIRST                                   │
  │ • Same weight → PARALLEL execution                              │
  │ • Default weight (not specified) = "0"                          │
  │ • Negative weights → "run before the default-weight hooks"      │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  EXAMPLE — 3 pre-upgrade hooks for anihpj/jobpost:
  ┌────────────────────┬────────┬───────────────────────────────────┐
  │ HOOK               │ WEIGHT │ EXECUTION ORDER                   │
  ├────────────────────┼────────┼───────────────────────────────────┤
  │ db-backup          │ "-10"  │ 1st — Backup BEFORE any changes   │
  │ db-migrate         │ "0"    │ 2nd — Migrate schema              │
  │ data-validate      │ "5"    │ 3rd — Validate migrated data      │
  │ smoke-test         │ "5"    │ 3rd — (PARALLEL with validate!)   │
  └────────────────────┴────────┴───────────────────────────────────┘

  EXECUTION SEQUENCE:
  TIME ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────►
  ┌──────┐  ┌──────────────┐  ┌───────────────┐
  │BACKUP│  │   MIGRATE    │  │ VALIDATE      │
  │w=-10 │→│    w=0        │→│ w=5           │
  └──────┘  └──────────────┘  │               │
                              │ SMOKE-TEST    │ ← PARALLEL!
                              │ w=5           │
                              └───────────────┘

  TEMPLATE ANNOTATIONS:
  metadata:
    annotations:
      "helm.sh/hook": pre-upgrade
      "helm.sh/hook-weight": "-10"   ← Runs FIRST
      "helm.sh/hook-delete-policy": hook-succeeded
Release Mgmt Q114 of 200
Your DB migration hook Job completed successfully, but the Job pod still exists. How do you automatically clean up hook resources after they finish?
A) All hook resources are automatically deleted — no configuration needed
B) Use kubectl delete job after every helm install — Helm can't manage hook cleanup
C) Set ttlSecondsAfterFinished: 0 in the Job spec — Kubernetes auto-deletes it
D) Use the helm.sh/hook-delete-policy annotation. Options: hook-succeeded (delete after success), hook-failed (delete after failure), or before-hook-creation (delete previous instance before creating new one). Combine with commas: "hook-succeeded,before-hook-creation"
✅ Correct Answer: D

Hook delete policies control automatic cleanup of hook resources. Without them, completed Job pods accumulate forever. The most common policy is "hook-succeeded,before-hook-creation" — delete the Job after it succeeds, and also delete any previous instance before creating a new one (important for upgrades).

📝 Detailed Explanation
Hook Delete Policies — Automatic Cleanup
  DELETE POLICY OPTIONS:
  ┌─────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────┐
  │ hook-succeeded              │ Delete AFTER the hook succeeds     │
  │ hook-failed                 │ Delete AFTER the hook fails        │
  │ before-hook-creation        │ Delete previous instance BEFORE   │
  │                             │ creating a new one (useful for     │
  │                             │ upgrades — no name conflicts)     │
  └─────────────────────────────┴───────────────────────────────────┘

  COMMON COMBINATIONS:
  "helm.sh/hook-delete-policy": hook-succeeded
  # Clean up after success. If it fails, keep pod for debugging.

  "helm.sh/hook-delete-policy": hook-succeeded,hook-failed
  # Always clean up — no trace left. Use when logs are sufficient.

  "helm.sh/hook-delete-policy": before-hook-creation,hook-succeeded
  # Delete old instance before upgrade, then delete after success.

  WITHOUT DELETE POLICY:
  $ kubectl get jobs -n anihpj
  NAME                    COMPLETIONS   DURATION   AGE
  anihpj-db-migrate       1/1           15s        7d   ← ORPHAN!
  anihpj-db-migrate-2     1/1           18s        5d   ← ORPHAN!
  anihpj-db-migrate-3     1/1           12s        1d   ← ORPHAN!
  # 10 upgrades = 10 orphan Jobs. Clean them up!

  WITH "hook-succeeded,before-hook-creation":
  $ kubectl get jobs -n anihpj
  No resources found.  ← Automatically cleaned!
Release Mgmt Q115 of 200
You want a database backup Job to run before helm uninstall deletes the anihpj PostgreSQL StatefulSet. Which hook type and delete policy should you use?
A) post-delete hook with before-hook-creation — backups run after deletion but cleanup before recreation
B) pre-delete hook with "hook-succeeded" delete policy. The backup Job runs BEFORE any resources are deleted, backs up the database, and cleans itself up after success. If the backup fails, the Job stays for debugging and helm uninstall proceeds (hooks don't block deletion by default)
C) pre-upgrade hook — it's the only hook that can access the database
D) post-install hook — backups only need to run once during initial install
✅ Correct Answer: B

pre-delete is the safety net hook — it runs BEFORE Helm deletes any resources. This is your last chance to back up data, export logs, or notify external systems. Important: hooks do NOT block deletion by default — if the backup Job is still running, Helm proceeds with deletion anyway. To make deletion wait for the hook, add "helm.sh/hook-weight" and ensure the hook completes within a reasonable time.

📝 Detailed Explanation
pre-delete Hook — Backup Before Destruction
  TIMELINE OF helm uninstall WITH pre-delete HOOK:
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ TIME  │ EVENT                                                    │
  ├───────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ T+0s  │ helm uninstall anihpj -n anihpj                         │
  │       │ → anihpj-db-0 still running (data intact)                │
  │       │                                                          │
  │ T+1s  │ pre-delete hook triggers:                                │
  │       │   Job "anihpj-db-backup" created                         │
  │       │   → pg_dump anihpj > /backup/anihpj-2026-06-13.sql      │
  │       │   → Upload to S3: s3://anihpj-backups/                  │
  │       │   → Backup SUCCESS                                       │
  │       │                                                          │
  │ T+45s │ Backup Job completes. hook-succeeded → Job auto-deleted  │
  │       │                                                          │
  │ T+46s │ Helm proceeds with deletion:                             │
  │       │   → StatefulSet anihpj-db deleted                       │
  │       │   → Service anihpj-db deleted                           │
  │       │   → PVC anihpj-db-pvc deleted (or retained)             │
  │       │   → All other resources deleted                          │
  └───────┴──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  THE BACKUP HOOK TEMPLATE:
  apiVersion: batch/v1
  kind: Job
  metadata:
    name: {{ .Release.Name }}-db-backup
    annotations:
      "helm.sh/hook": pre-delete
      "helm.sh/hook-weight": "-10"       ← Run before other hooks
      "helm.sh/hook-delete-policy": hook-succeeded
  spec:
    template:
      spec:
        restartPolicy: Never
        containers:
          - name: backup
            image: postgres:15-alpine
            command: ["pg_dump", "-h", "anihpj-db", "-U", "anihpj",
                      "-d", "jobpost", "-f", "/backup/dump.sql"]
Release Mgmt Q116 of 200
Are hook resources managed as part of the Helm release? What happens when you upgrade a chart that has hooks?
A) Hook resources are NOT part of the release — they're managed separately. Helm tracks them via annotations but they don't appear in helm get manifest. On upgrade, old hooks are NOT updated — only hooks in the new chart version execute. Use "before-hook-creation" delete policy to clean up previous hook instances
B) Hooks are full release members — they appear in helm get manifest and are updated on every upgrade
C) Hooks are part of the release but only the latest hook resource is kept — old ones are automatically pruned
D) Hooks are Kubernetes-native and have no relationship to Helm releases
✅ Correct Answer: A

Hook resources exist in a parallel universe from the main release. They are NOT included in the release manifest, are NOT updated during upgrades, and are NOT deleted during rollback. Helm manages their lifecycle separately based on hook annotations and delete policies. This isolation prevents hooks from interfering with normal release operations.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Hooks vs Release Resources — Separate Lifecycles
  RELEASE RESOURCES (Managed by Helm):
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ • Created/Updated/Deleted by helm install/upgrade/uninstall     │
  │ • Appear in helm get manifest                                  │
  │ • Rollback reverts them to previous revision's state           │
  │ • Example: Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps, Secrets           │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  HOOK RESOURCES (Managed separately):
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ • Created at specific lifecycle points (pre-install, etc.)      │
  │ • Do NOT appear in helm get manifest                           │
  │ • NOT updated during upgrades (old hooks stay, new ones run)    │
  │ • NOT rolled back — hooks from the rollback-target revision    │
  │   may or may not run (depends on hook type)                     │
  │ • Cleaned up by hook-delete-policy, not by Helm commands        │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  PRACTICAL IMPLICATION:
  # Install with a hook:
  $ helm install anihpj ./helm/anihpj
  → Hook Job "anihpj-db-migrate" runs once, then deleted.

  # Upgrade (chart version 2, with updated hook):
  $ helm upgrade anihpj ./helm/anihpj-v2
  → OLD hook Job from v1 is NOT touched.
  → NEW hook Job (from v2) runs if it's a pre-upgrade/post-upgrade hook.

  # Without "before-hook-creation" — name collision!
  $ helm upgrade anihpj ./helm/anihpj
  Error: Job "anihpj-db-migrate" already exists!
  # Fix: Add "before-hook-creation" to delete-policy.
Release Mgmt Q117 of 200
A pre-upgrade hook Job is stuck in "Running" state. Will helm upgrade wait for it forever?
A) Yes — hooks are blocking and Helm waits indefinitely until the hook completes or fails
B) No — hooks are fire-and-forget. Helm doesn't wait for them at all
C) Helm waits for hooks by default but respects the --timeout flag. If the hook doesn't complete within the timeout (default: 5 minutes), Helm fails the operation. The hook Job continues running in the cluster — you must manually debug and delete it. Failed hooks do NOT roll back the release by default
D) Helm automatically kills stuck hooks after 60 seconds and proceeds with the upgrade
✅ Correct Answer: C

Helm does wait for hooks to complete, but with a timeout. If your migration Job takes 6 minutes but --timeout is 5 minutes (300s), Helm fails with "upgrade failed: timed out waiting for the condition." However, the hook Job keeps running in the cluster — Helm doesn't kill it. You need to check kubectl logs, understand why it's stuck, fix the issue, delete the Job, and retry the upgrade.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Hook Timeouts — What Happens When Hooks Stall
  HOOK BEHAVIOR WITH --timeout:
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ DEFAULT: Helm waits up to 5 minutes (300s) for hooks            │
  │                                                                 │
  │ helm upgrade anihpj ./helm/anihpj --timeout 10m                 │
  │ → Extends hook timeout to 10 minutes (600s)                     │
  │                                                                 │
  │ IF HOOK COMPLETES within timeout:                               │
  │   ✅ Helm proceeds with upgrade                                 │
  │                                                                 │
  │ IF HOOK TIMES OUT:                                              │
  │   ❌ Helm FAILS the upgrade                                     │
  │   ⚠️ Hook Job CONTINUES RUNNING in the cluster                  │
  │   ⚠️ Release is NOT automatically rolled back                   │
  │   ⚠️ Old pods are STILL RUNNING (upgrade didn't happen)         │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  DEBUGGING STUCK HOOKS:
  $ helm upgrade anihpj ./helm/anihpj --timeout 10m
  Error: UPGRADE FAILED: timed out waiting for the condition

  $ kubectl get jobs -n anihpj
  NAME                    STATUS    COMPLETIONS   DURATION
  anihpj-db-migrate       Running   0/1           10m     ← STUCK!

  $ kubectl logs job/anihpj-db-migrate -n anihpj
  django.db.utils.OperationalError: could not connect to server:
      Connection refused
  → Database not reachable! Fix the connection, delete the Job,
    and retry the upgrade.

  $ kubectl delete job anihpj-db-migrate -n anihpj
  $ helm upgrade anihpj ./helm/anihpj --timeout 10m
  ✅ Release "anihpj" has been upgraded.

  🔗 TIP: Use --atomic with hooks:
  helm upgrade --atomic --timeout 10m ...
  → If hook times out → Helm auto-rolls back to previous revision!

B) Check helm status anihpj (shows hook status), then kubectl get jobs/pods -n <ns> (find the hook resource), kubectl logs (see what went wrong), kubectl describe (check events/mounts/images). Fix the issue, delete the failed hook resource, and retry the Helm operation

Always check hook delete policies: if the hook has "hook-failed" delete policy, it auto-deletes on failure and you lose the logs!

📝 Detailed Explanation
Debugging Failed Hooks — Step-by-Step
  SYMPTOM:

  Error: INSTALLATION FAILED: 1 error occurred:
      hook pre-install anihpj/templates/db-migrate-job.yaml failed

  DEBUGGING WORKFLOW:
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ STEP 1: Check helm status for hook summary                      │
  │ $ helm status anihpj -n anihpj                                  │
  │ HOOKS:                                                          │
  │ ---                                                             │
  │ #  Name               Status                                     │
  │ 1  anihpj-db-migrate  failed  ← HERE'S THE PROBLEM              │
  │                                                                 │
  │ STEP 2: Find the hook resource                                  │
  │ $ kubectl get jobs -n anihpj                                    │
  │ NAME                    STATUS    COMPLETIONS   DURATION         │
  │ anihpj-db-migrate       Failed    0/1           30s              │
  │                                                                 │
  │ $ kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l job-name=anihpj-db-migrate     │
  │ NAME                          STATUS   RESTARTS                 │
  │ anihpj-db-migrate-abcde       Error    0                        │
  │                                                                 │
  │ STEP 3: Read the logs                                          │
  │ $ kubectl logs job/anihpj-db-migrate -n anihpj                  │
  │ django.core.exceptions.ImproperlyConfigured:                    │
  │   settings.DATABASES is improperly configured.                  │
  │   Please supply SECRET_KEY value.                               │
  │ → Ah-ha! Missing environment variable!                          │
  │                                                                 │
  │ STEP 4: Describe for events                                     │
  │ $ kubectl describe job/anihpj-db-migrate -n anihpj              │
  │ Events:                                                         │
  │   Warning  BackOff  Back-off restarting failed container        │
  │                                                                 │
  │ STEP 5: Fix, clean up, retry                                    │
  │ 1. Fix the template (add SECRET_KEY env var)                    │
  │ 2. $ kubectl delete job anihpj-db-migrate -n anihpj             │
  │ 3. $ helm uninstall anihpj -n anihpj  (clean slate)             │
  │ 4. $ helm install anihpj ./helm/anihpj -n anihpj                │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ⚠️ WARNING: If hook has "hook-failed" delete policy,
  the Job auto-deletes on failure — you WON'T see it in
  kubectl get jobs. Remove that policy for debugging!

What are Helm tests and how are they different from hooks?
A) Tests and hooks are the same thing — "test" is just an alias for "post-install" hooks
B) Tests are unit tests written in Go that validate template rendering logic
C) Tests are YAML lint checks that run before chart installation
D) Tests are Kubernetes Pods/Jobs annotated with "helm.sh/hook": test that validate a release is working correctly. Unlike hooks (which run automatically during lifecycle events), tests are invoked manually with helm test <release>. 📝 Detailed Explanation
Helm Tests vs Hooks — Different Purposes
  HOOKS (automatic)              vs    TESTS (manual)
  ┌──────────────────────────┐        ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │ Run at lifecycle points  │        │ Run on demand             │
  │ (pre-install, etc.)      │        │ (helm test )     │
  ├──────────────────────────┤        ├──────────────────────────┤
  │ DO things:                │        │ VERIFY things:            │
  │ • Migrate databases       │        │ • Can the API respond?    │
  │ • Backup data             │        │ • Is Redis connected?     │
  │ • Generate certs          │        │ • Can DB accept queries?  │
  ├──────────────────────────┤        ├──────────────────────────┤
  │ Block deployment until    │        │ Non-blocking — release    │
  │ complete (with timeout)   │        │ is already deployed       │
  ├──────────────────────────┤        ├──────────────────────────┤
  │ Annotated:                │        │ Annotated:                │
  │ helm.sh/hook: pre-upgrade│        │ helm.sh/hook: test        │
  └──────────────────────────┘        └──────────────────────────┘

  TYPICAL TEST FLOW (anihpj/jobpost):

What does a basic Helm test pod look like? How do you write a test-connection.yaml template?
A) A Pod annotated with "helm.sh/hook": test and "helm.sh/hook-delete-policy": hook-succeeded that runs a simple connectivity check (e.g., wget -qO- http://anihpj-api:8000/health/). If the command exits 0, the test passes. If non-zero, the test fails. The Pod is automatically deleted after completion
B) A Go test file in the chart's test/ directory that runs with helm test --unit
C) A shell script in templates/tests.sh that Helm executes locally
D) A ConfigMap with test assertions that Helm validates against the cluster state
✅ Correct Answer: A

A Helm test is just a Kubernetes Pod with specific annotations. There's no special test framework — the test "passes" if the container exits with code 0 and "fails" if it exits with a non-zero code. The wget or curl command inside the test pod validates that your application is actually reachable and responding.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Helm Test Template — Anatomy of a Test Pod
  templates/tests/test-api-connection.yaml:
  apiVersion: v1
  kind: Pod
  metadata:
    name: "{{ .Release.Name }}-api-test"
    annotations:
      "helm.sh/hook": test                    ← Makes it a test
      "helm.sh/hook-delete-policy": hook-succeeded  ← Auto-cleanup
  spec:
    restartPolicy: Never                      ← Don't retry on failure
    containers:
      - name: api-test
        image: busybox:1.36
        command:
          - wget
          - -qO-
          - "http://{{ .Release.Name }}-api:8000/api/health/"
        # If wget exits 0 → TEST PASSES ✅
        # If wget exits non-zero → TEST FAILS ❌

  templates/tests/test-db-connection.yaml:
  apiVersion: v1
  kind: Pod
  metadata:
    name: "{{ .Release.Name }}-db-test"
    annotations:
      "helm.sh/hook": test
      "helm.sh/hook-delete-policy": hook-succeeded
  spec:
    restartPolicy: Never
    containers:
      - name: db-test
        image: postgres:15-alpine
        env:
          - name: PGPASSWORD
            valueFrom:
              secretKeyRef:
                name: {{ .Release.Name }}-db-secret
                key: password
        command:
          - pg_isready
          - -h
          - "{{ .Release.Name }}-db"
          - -U
          - anihpj
        # pg_isready exits 0 if DB is accepting connections

  RUNNING TESTS:
  $ helm test anihpj -n anihpj --logs
  TEST: anihpj-api-test
  {"status":"ok","database":"connected","redis":"connected"} ✅
  TEST: anihpj-db-test
  anihpj-db:5432 - accepting connections ✅

Tests give you confidence that the deployment actually works — not just that Helm applied YAML without errors. Always include at least one test in production charts.

Release Mgmt Q121 of 200
How do you run Helm tests for a release and view their output?
A) Tests run automatically during helm install — no additional command needed
B) helm test <release> -n <ns> runs all test-annotated resources. Add --logs to stream test output in real-time. Add --timeout 5m to set a timeout. Test results appear in helm status permanently
C) helm verify <release> — uses chart provenance to validate deployment integrity
D) kubectl apply -f templates/tests/ — tests are just regular Kubernetes resources
✅ Correct Answer: B

helm test is your smoke test command. It finds all Pods with "helm.sh/hook": test annotation, creates them, waits for them to complete, and reports the results. Test results are permanently recorded in the release status — even weeks later, helm status anihpj shows the last test run and its outcome.

📝 Detailed Explanation
helm test — Running and Viewing Test Results
  BASIC TEST RUN:
  $ helm test anihpj -n anihpj
  NAME: anihpj
  Last Started:   2026-06-13 14:30:00
  Last Completed: 2026-06-13 14:30:15
  Phase:          Succeeded

  TEST WITH LOGS (real-time output):
  $ helm test anihpj -n anihpj --logs
  NAME: anihpj
  POD: anihpj-api-test
  {"status":"ok","database":"connected","redis":"connected"}

  $ helm test anihpj -n anihpj --timeout 2m
  # Fails if tests don't complete within 2 minutes

  TEST FAILURE:
  $ helm test anihpj -n anihpj
  NAME: anihpj
  Last Started:   2026-06-13 14:35:00
  Last Completed: 2026-06-13 14:35:08
  Phase:          Failed
  NOTES:
  ❌ API health check failed: Connection refused
  ❌ Database check passed

  # Test results persist in helm status:
  $ helm status anihpj -n anihpj
  ...
  TEST SUITE:     anihpj-api-test
  Last Started:   2026-06-13 14:35:00
  Last Completed: 2026-06-13 14:35:08
  Phase:          Failed           ← Still shows last result!

  CI/CD INTEGRATION:
  helm test anihpj -n anihpj --timeout 2m || exit 1
  # Fails pipeline if tests don't pass
Release Mgmt Q122 of 200
After running helm test, you see old test pods accumulating. How do you ensure tests are automatically cleaned up?
A) Run helm test --cleanup — this flag deletes all previous test pods before running new ones
B) Test pods are always auto-deleted — Helm has a built-in 1-hour TTL for test resources
C) Set "helm.sh/hook-delete-policy": hook-succeeded on test Pod annotations. After a successful test run, Helm automatically deletes the Pod. For failed tests, the Pod is kept for debugging. Combine with before-hook-creation to also delete before the next test run
D) Use kubectl delete pod -l helm.sh/hook=test -n <ns> — manual cleanup is the only option
✅ Correct Answer: C

Test cleanup uses the same hook delete policy mechanism as lifecycle hooks. Without a delete policy, test Pods accumulate forever. The recommended policy is "hook-succeeded" — keep failed test pods for debugging (view logs, check events) but clean up successful ones automatically.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Test Pod Cleanup — Delete Policies in Action
  WITHOUT delete policy (BAD):
  $ helm test anihpj -n anihpj --logs
  # Test passes, but pod stays...

  $ kubectl get pods -n anihpj
  NAME                      READY   STATUS      RESTARTS   AGE
  anihpj-api-test           0/1     Completed   0          5m
  anihpj-api-test-2         0/1     Completed   0          3m
  anihpj-api-test-3         0/1     Completed   0          1m
  # 3 test runs = 3 orphan pods!

  WITH "hook-succeeded" (GOOD):
  annotations:
    "helm.sh/hook": test
    "helm.sh/hook-delete-policy": hook-succeeded
  # After test passes → Pod auto-deleted!

  $ kubectl get pods -n anihpj
  No resources found. ← Clean!

  WITH "hook-succeeded,hook-failed" (AGGRESSIVE):
  annotations:
    "helm.sh/hook": test
    "helm.sh/hook-delete-policy": hook-succeeded,hook-failed
  # Always delete — no debugging info left. Use only when
  # you're confident in your logging/monitoring.

  BEST PRACTICE FOR CI/CD:
  annotations:
    "helm.sh/hook": test
    "helm.sh/hook-delete-policy": hook-succeeded
  # Pass → clean. Fail → keep for CI artifact collection.
  # CI pipeline can run: kubectl logs -l helm.sh/hook=test
  # before deleting the failed pods.

3.6 Dry-Run, Debugging & Troubleshooting ReleasesQ123-Q130

Release Mgmt Q123 of 200
What does helm install --dry-run actually do, and what does it NOT do?
A) --dry-run renders all templates, merges values, and sends the generated manifests to the Kubernetes API server for validation (server-side schema checking) but does NOT actually create any resources. It catches: template syntax errors, value type mismatches, missing required fields, and deprecated API versions. It does NOT catch: network issues, image pull failures, resource quota limits, or admission webhook rejections
B) --dry-run only validates Chart.yaml syntax — it doesn't render templates or contact the API server
C) --dry-run deploys everything to a temporary "dry-run" namespace that's automatically cleaned up
D) --dry-run is identical to helm template — they're aliases for the same operation
✅ Correct Answer: A

--dry-run is your pre-flight safety check. It does everything except actually create resources: renders templates, merges values, and submits the manifests to the API server for schema validation. The API server will tell you "this Ingress uses an API version that doesn't exist" or "this field is not valid for Deployment" — but no resources are created.

📝 Detailed Explanation
--dry-run — What It Checks vs What It Doesn't
  $ helm install anihpj ./helm/anihpj -n anihpj --dry-run

  WHAT --dry-run CATCHES:
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ ✅ Template syntax errors:                                       │
  │    Error: parse error at (anihpj/templates/deploy.yaml:42):     │
  │    unexpected {{ end }}                                          │
  │                                                                 │
  │ ✅ Missing values:                                               │
  │    Error: execution error: nil pointer evaluating               │
  │    .Values.postgres.image                                        │
  │                                                                 │
  │ ✅ API server validation:                                        │
  │    Error: Deployment.apps "anihpj-api" is invalid:              │
  │    spec.template.spec.containers[0].name: Required value        │
  │                                                                 │
  │ ✅ Deprecated API versions:                                      │
  │    WARNING: extensions/v1beta1 Ingress is deprecated,           │
  │    use networking.k8s.io/v1 instead                             │
  │                                                                 │
  │ ✅ JSON Schema validation:                                       │
  │    Error: values don't meet the specifications of the schema    │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  WHAT --dry-run DOES NOT CATCH:
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ ❌ Image pull errors (image doesn't exist or registry auth)      │
  │ ❌ Resource quota limits (namespace has 0 CPU left)              │
  │ ❌ Admission webhook rejections (OPA/Gatekeeper policies)        │
  │ ❌ Network connectivity (Service can't reach backend pods)       │
  │ ❌ Storage provisioning failures (CSI driver issues)             │
  │ ❌ Node resource availability (no node has enough memory)        │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ALWAYS run --dry-run before production deployments!
Release Mgmt Q124 of 200
What extra information does helm install --dry-run --debug provide over just --dry-run?
A) --debug enables interactive mode where you can step through template rendering line by line
B) --debug sends metrics to a debugging dashboard for performance analysis
C) --debug prints the COMPUTED VALUES (the full merged configuration after defaults + overrides) AND the rendered templates in addition to the dry-run manifest. This shows you exactly what values the template engine received and what it produced — invaluable for debugging "why is this field showing up wrong?"
D) --debug bypasses API server validation and only checks local template syntax

--debug is the X-ray vision for Helm. It prints the internal state: the computed values (what the template engine actually received after merging defaults, -f files, and --set overrides) and the fully rendered templates. This reveals bugs like "I set --set api.replicas=3 but the template still shows 1" — the debug output shows the merged values, revealing that a -f file overrode your --set.

--debug — Seeing Helm's Internal State

  OUTPUT INCLUDES:

  1. COMPUTED VALUES (merged config):
  COMPUTED VALUES:

      repository: anihpj-api
      tag: latest
      pullPolicy: IfNotPresent
    replicaCount: 1          ← From values.yaml default
    resources:
      limits:
        cpu: 500m
        memory: 512Mi
  postgres:
    image: postgres:15-alpine
    storage: 50Gi            ← From -f values-prod.yaml override!
  ...

  2. RENDERED TEMPLATES:

  kind: Deployment
  metadata:
    name: anihpj-api
    labels:
      app.kubernetes.io/name: anihpj
  spec:
    replicas: 1
    ...
  ---
  # Source: anihpj/templates/service.yaml
  ...

  DEBUG USE CASES:
  • "Why is replicaCount 1 when I set it to 5?"
    → Check COMPUTED VALUES: your -f file overrode --set

  • "Why is the image tag wrong?"
    → Check COMPUTED VALUES: the default from values.yaml won

  • "Template error on line 42 — what's the context?"
    → Check RENDERED TEMPLATES: see what was produced up to the error
Release Mgmt Q125 of 200
What is the key difference between helm template and helm install --dry-run?
A) They are identical — helm template is just a shorter alias for --dry-run
B) helm template renders templates locally without any cluster connection — it's a pure client-side operation that outputs YAML to stdout. helm install --dry-run connects to the cluster and submits manifests to the API server for server-side validation. Use helm template in CI/CD to generate YAML for GitOps; use --dry-run to validate against your actual cluster's API capabilities
C) helm template applies resources to the cluster; helm install --dry-run does not
D) helm template requires --dry-run to work; they must be used together
✅ Correct Answer: B

This is one of the most important distinctions in Helm operations. helm template is cluster-independent — it works without a kubeconfig, making it ideal for GitOps pipelines that generate YAML in CI and commit to a repo. helm install --dry-run requires cluster access because it sends manifests to the API server for validation — it catches issues that local rendering can't detect.

📝 Detailed Explanation
helm template vs --dry-run — Cluster vs Client-Only
  ┌──────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────┐
  │ helm template                │ helm install --dry-run           │
  ├──────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────┤
  │ CLIENT-SIDE ONLY             │ CLIENT + SERVER-SIDE             │
  │ No cluster connection needed │ Requires cluster connection      │
  │ Outputs YAML to stdout       │ Outputs validation results       │
  │ No API server validation     │ API server validates schemas     │
  │ No .Capabilities query       │ .Capabilities works (real API)   │
  │ lookup() returns nil         │ lookup() queries real cluster    │
  │ Works offline                │ Requires cluster connectivity    │
  │ Used for: GitOps, ArgoCD     │ Used for: Pre-deploy validation  │
  └──────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────┘

  helm template — GITOPS WORKFLOW:
  $ helm template anihpj ./helm/anihpj -f values-prod.yaml > manifests.yaml
  $ git add manifests.yaml && git commit -m "Generated manifests"
  $ git push
  → ArgoCD detects the change and applies manifests.yaml to the cluster.
  → No Helm or cluster access needed in CI!

  helm install --dry-run — PRE-DEPLOY VALIDATION:
  $ helm install anihpj ./helm/anihpj -n anihpj --dry-run
  Error: Ingress.networking.k8s.io "anihpj-web" is invalid:
    spec.rules[0].http.paths[0].pathType: Required value
  → Catches API-level validation errors BEFORE applying!

  WHEN TO USE EACH:
  ┌──────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ helm template        │ GitOps, ArgoCD, Flux, CI YAML generation  │
  │ --dry-run            │ Pre-deployment safety check, CI validation│
  │ Both                 │ CI: template → validate → dry-run → deploy│
  └──────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────┘
Release Mgmt Q126 of 200
You used helm template to generate YAML and applied it with kubectl apply. Later, helm list doesn't show the release. Why?
A) helm template doesn't generate valid Kubernetes YAML — kubectl apply silently ignores it
B) kubectl apply creates resources but doesn't create Helm release tracking metadata
C) The release only appears in helm list after the next helm upgrade
D) helm template | kubectl apply bypasses Helm's release tracking entirely. No release Secret is created, so helm list, helm status, helm rollback, and helm uninstall have no knowledge of these resources. This is a valid pattern (GitOps) but you lose Helm's lifecycle management
✅ Correct Answer: D

This is the fundamental tradeoff of the helm template + kubectl pattern. You get Helm's templating power without Helm's release management. No release Secrets are created, so Helm has no record of what was deployed. This is intentional — it's how ArgoCD and Flux use Helm: they want the templating but manage the lifecycle themselves through GitOps reconciliation.

📝 Detailed Explanation
helm template | kubectl apply — Tradeoffs
  TWO PATHS TO DEPLOY:

  PATH 1: helm install (FULL LIFECYCLE MANAGEMENT)
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ helm install → Release Secret created → helm list shows release │
  │ ✅ helm rollback works                                           │
  │ ✅ helm history works                                            │
  │ ✅ helm uninstall works                                          │
  │ ✅ helm get manifest/values works                                │
  │ ❌ Requires Helm at deploy time                                  │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  PATH 2: helm template | kubectl apply (GITOPS PATTERN)
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ helm template → YAML to stdout → kubectl apply → Resources      │
  │ ❌ No Release Secret → helm list shows NOTHING                   │
  │ ❌ helm rollback doesn't work → use kubectl or Git revert       │
  │ ❌ helm history doesn't work → use git log                      │
  │ ❌ helm uninstall doesn't work → use kubectl delete             │
  │ ✅ Works without Helm at deploy time (CI generates, Git stores) │
  │ ✅ ArgoCD/Flux native pattern                                    │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  WHY YOU'D CHOOSE PATH 2 (GitOps):
  • Git is the source of truth, not Helm's release Secrets
  • CI pipeline generates manifests once, stores in Git
  • ArgoCD deploys from Git — no Helm in the deploy pipeline
  • Rollback = git revert, not helm rollback
  • Audit trail = git log, not helm history

  🔗 Connection to anihpj/jobpost:
  For GitOps: helm template anihpj ./helm/anihpj -f values-prod.yaml
  For direct management: helm install anihpj ./helm/anihpj -n anihpj

How do you see the exact deployed manifest of a running release?
A) helm get manifest anihpj -n <ns> — prints the complete rendered YAML that was applied to the cluster. This is the definitive "what is deployed" command. Unlike kubectl get -o yaml (which shows live state including defaulted fields and status), helm get manifest shows exactly what Helm applied
B) kubectl get all -n <ns> -o yaml — the only way to see deployed resources
C) helm template ./chart — re-renders the chart with current values to guess what was deployed
D) helm get all anihpj shows values only, not manifests
✅ Correct Answer: A

helm get manifest shows the source of truth — the exact YAML that Helm sent to the API server at install/upgrade time. This is different from kubectl get -o yaml, which shows the current live state including defaulted fields, status, and any manual changes made via kubectl. Comparing helm get manifest against kubectl get -o yaml reveals configuration drift.

📝 Detailed Explanation
helm get manifest vs kubectl get -o yaml
  helm get manifest → WHAT HELM APPLIED:
  apiVersion: apps/v1
  kind: Deployment
  metadata:
    name: anihpj-api
    labels:
      app.kubernetes.io/name: anihpj
  spec:
    replicas: 3                      ← What Helm set
    selector:
      matchLabels:
        app.kubernetes.io/name: anihpj
    template:
      metadata:
        labels:
          app.kubernetes.io/name: anihpj
      spec:
        containers:
          - name: api
            image: anihpj-api:latest

  kubectl get deploy anihpj-api -o yaml → LIVE STATE:
  apiVersion: apps/v1
  kind: Deployment
  metadata:
    name: anihpj-api
    labels:
      app.kubernetes.io/name: anihpj
    resourceVersion: "12345678"       ← Added by API server
    uid: abc-def-123                  ← Added by API server
  spec:
    replicas: 3
    revisionHistoryLimit: 10         ← Defaulted by API server
    strategy:                         ← Defaulted by API server
      rollingUpdate:
        maxSurge: 25%
        maxUnavailable: 25%
      type: RollingUpdate
    ...
  status:                             ← Entire status section
    availableReplicas: 3              ← Added by API server
    conditions: [...]                 ← Added by API server

  DRIFT DETECTION:
  If someone runs: kubectl scale deploy anihpj-api --replicas=5
  → kubectl get shows replicas: 5
  → helm get manifest still shows replicas: 3
  → DRIFT DETECTED! The live state diverged from Helm.

--all reveals the complete picture. User overrides alone don't tell you what Helm actually used — defaults from values.yaml fill in the gaps. When debugging "why did this template render that way?", --all shows the full values object that was passed to the template engine.

📝 Detailed Explanation
helm get values — User Overrides vs Complete Values
  INSTALL COMMAND:
  $ helm install anihpj ./helm/anihpj -n anihpj \
      --set api.replicaCount=5 \
      --set postgres.storage=100Gi

  WITHOUT --all (only what user explicitly set):

  USER-SUPPLIED VALUES:
  api:
    replicaCount: 5
  postgres:
    storage: 100Gi
  # Missing: image tags, resource limits, redis config, etc.

  WITH --all (the COMPLETE story):
  $ helm get values anihpj -n anihpj --all
  COMPUTED VALUES:
  api:
    replicaCount: 5                    ← User override
    image:
      repository: anihpj-api
      tag: latest                      ← From values.yaml
      pullPolicy: IfNotPresent         ← From values.yaml
    resources:

        cpu: 500m                      ← From values.yaml

  postgres:
    image: postgres:15-alpine          ← From values.yaml
    storage: 100Gi                     ← User override
    storageClass: standard             ← From values.yaml
  redis:
    enabled: true                      ← From values.yaml
    image: redis:7-alpine              ← From values.yaml
  ingress:
    enabled: true                      ← From values.yaml
    host: anihpj.example.com           ← From values.yaml

  Use --all for: debugging template output, auditing, compliance
  Use (no --all) for: documenting what the user customized
