Today, a junior engineer is asked to "update the image to v2.5." They run helm upgrade anihpj ./s21-chart -n anihpj --set image.tag=v2.5 — but forget --reuse-values. Helm resets ALL values to chart defaults! The password becomes "changeme", replicas drop to 1, CPU limits halve. Production goes down silently — everything looks "deployed" but the app can't connect to the database.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE (S21):

├── Chart.yaml
├── values.yaml              ← database.password: "changeme" (DEFAULT)
└── templates/

cat << 'EOF' > ./s21-chart/templates/deployment.yaml

echo ""
echo "============================================"

echo ""
echo "=== BUG CONFIRMED: Custom values LOST! ==="

echo ""
echo "database.password is now 'changeme' (the DEFAULT) — NOT 'prod-secret-xyz'!"
echo "replicaCount is now 1 (the DEFAULT) — NOT 3!"
echo ""
echo "Production database connection BROKEN — Django can't authenticate!"
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. helm upgrade anihpj ./s21-chart -n anihpj --set image.tag=2.5-alpine --wait → Succeeds! But values are gone!
✗2. helm get values anihpj -n anihpj --all | grep password → shows "changeme" — the DEFAULT, not "prod-secret-xyz"!
✗3. kubectl get deploy anihpj-api -n anihpj -o jsonpath='{.spec.replicas}' → 1 — back to default, not 3!
✗4. Django can't connect to database — password changed silently! Production is DOWN!
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check current values: helm get values anihpj -n anihpj --all
→ Database password is "changeme" — the chart DEFAULT, not the custom value!
2Check upgrade command: The upgrade only passed --set image.tag=2.5-alpine
→ No --reuse-values flag and no -f values-prod.yaml — previous custom values were DISCARDED!
3Understand Helm's value precedence during upgrade: Without --reuse-values, Helm uses ONLY values.yaml defaults + new --set values
→ Previous custom values from the initial install are NOT preserved!
4Root cause: helm upgrade WITHOUT --reuse-values resets ALL values to chart defaults. Only new values passed via --set or -f are applied. All custom values from the initial install are DISCARDED. This is the #1 cause of "it worked yesterday but broke after the upgrade" in Helm-managed production systems.
5Fix: Always use helm upgrade ... --reuse-values OR always pass a -f values-prod.yaml file with ALL required values. For CI/CD: store the production values file in Git
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
helm upgrade succeeds → But app is broken
②
Check values → Back to defaults!
③
Upgrade command missing --reuse-values
④
Helm resets to defaults on upgrade
⑤
Always use --reuse-values or -f values.yaml!

Tenet: helm upgrade by default uses the chart's values.yaml as the base, then applies new --set/-f values on top. Previous release values are DISCARDED unless you use --reuse-values. This is by design — Helm treats each upgrade as a fresh calculation. The safest production pattern: (1) Always store production values in a separate file (values-prod.yaml), (2) Always pass -f values-prod.yaml during upgrades, (3) Or use --reuse-values to preserve the previous configuration. NEVER rely on "the values are still there from last time."

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ helm get values anihpj -n anihpj --all | grep password password: changeme ❌ Back to chart DEFAULT — custom values LOST!
$ kubectl get deploy anihpj-api -n anihpj -o jsonpath='{.spec.replicas}' 1 ❌ Back to default — was 3!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ helm rollback anihpj -n anihpj --wait Rollback was a success! Happy Helming! ✅
$ helm get values anihpj -n anihpj --all | grep password password: prod-secret-xyz ✅ Custom values RESTORED!
🔧
BASH — Restore custom values

helm rollback anihpj -n anihpj --wait

# Correct upgrade WITH --reuse-values
helm upgrade anihpj ./s21-chart -n anihpj --set image.tag=2.5-alpine --reuse-values --wait

# Verify custom values survived
helm get values anihpj -n anihpj --all | grep password
echo "✅ Custom values preserved with --reuse-values!"
🧹
BASH
helm uninstall anihpj -n anihpj 2>/dev/null
kubectl delete namespace anihpj 2>/dev/null
rm -rf ~/helm-lab/s21-chart

🧪 SCENARIO S22 — Category 2: Release Lifecycle Atomic Debug

helm rollback Fails — First Install Without --atomic Has No Revision 1

The Problem: anihpj/jobpost was installed WITHOUT --atomic. The first install failed (wrong image tag), and Helm reports "STATUS: failed" with no revision to roll back to. Running helm rollback anihpj 1 fails with "release: not found" because --atomic is needed on the FIRST install to create a rollback-able revision. Your job: understand why rollback fails on first install, fix the deployment with --atomic, and learn the critical first-install pattern.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm)
1

📋 First Install WITHOUT --atomic — Then Attempt Rollback

📖 APP STORY: The anihpj team deploys for the first time using helm install anihpj ./s22-chart -n anihpj WITHOUT --atomic. The image tag is wrong, pods fail. The engineer tries helm rollback anihpj 1 but gets "Error: release: not found"! Without --atomic on the first install, a failed install doesn't create a rollback-able revision. The deployment is in a broken state with NO way to roll back — the team must uninstall and start over.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE (S22): 
s22-chart/
├── Chart.yaml
├── values.yaml              ← image.tag: "does-not-exist"
└── templates/
    └── deployment.yaml
BASH — Install without --atomic, then fail rollback

cd ~/helm-lab

cat << 'EOF' > ./s22-chart/Chart.yaml
apiVersion: v2
name: anihpj-atomic
description: anihpj/jobpost — atomic install demo
type: application
version: 1.0.0
EOF

cat << 'EOF' > ./s22-chart/values.yaml
replicaCount: 1
image:
  repository: nginx
  tag: "does-not-exist"
EOF

cat << 'EOF' > ./s22-chart/templates/deployment.yaml

  name: {{ .Release.Name }}-api
spec:
  replicas: {{ .Values.replicaCount }}
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: {{ .Release.Name }}
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: {{ .Release.Name }}
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: "{{ .Values.image.repository }}:{{ .Values.image.tag }}"
EOF

echo "=== FIRST INSTALL WITHOUT --atomic ==="
helm install anihpj ./s22-chart -n anihpj --create-namespace --wait --timeout 1m 2>&1 || true
echo ""
echo "=== Attempting rollback — THIS WILL FAIL ==="
helm rollback anihpj 1 -n anihpj 2>&1 || true
echo ""
echo "=== BUG CONFIRMED: No revision to rollback to! ==="
helm history anihpj -n anihpj
echo ""
echo "Revision 1 status: FAILED — rollback impossible without --atomic on first install!"
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Install fails (non-existent image) — pods in ImagePullBackOff
✗2. helm rollback anihpj 1 -n anihpj → "Error: release: not found"
✗3. helm history anihpj -n anihpj → shows revision 1 as "failed" — can't rollback!
✗4. The release is stuck — must uninstall and start over!
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check release status: helm list -n anihpj
→ STATUS: failed — no successful revision to roll back to
2Without --atomic: A failed first install creates revision 1 in "failed" state — rollback requires a previously deployed revision
→ Revision 1 was never successfully deployed, so there's nothing to roll back to!
3Root cause: helm install without --atomic creates a revision even on failure, but that revision is marked "failed" and can't be rolled back to. --atomic on the first install ensures revision 1 is either fully deployed OR fully rolled back (release removed). Without it, you get a zombie release with no recovery path.
4Fix: Always use --atomic on first install. If already in failed state: uninstall and reinstall with --atomic
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
First install fails → Try rollback
②
rollback fails → "release not found"
③
No --atomic on first install → No rollback revision
④
Uninstall + reinstall with --atomic
⑤
Now upgrade failures auto-rollback!

Tenet: --atomic is critical on the FIRST install. It ensures revision 1 is either fully deployed or the release is cleaned up. Without it, a failed first install creates an unrecoverable zombie release. Pattern: helm install <name> <chart> --atomic --wait --timeout 5m. On subsequent upgrades, --atomic will roll back to revision 1 if the upgrade fails.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ helm rollback anihpj 1 -n anihpj Error: release: not found
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ helm uninstall anihpj -n anihpj release "anihpj" uninstalled
🔧

# Reinstall WITH --atomic (use existing image tag)
helm install anihpj ./s22-chart -n anihpj --create-namespace \
  --set image.tag=1.25-alpine --atomic --wait --timeout 5m
echo "✅ First install with --atomic — revision 1 is healthy!"
🧹

kubectl delete namespace anihpj 2>/dev/null

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. kubectl get secrets -n anihpj | grep "sh.helm" | wc -l → 11+ revision Secrets!
✗2. helm history anihpj -n anihpj → shows ALL 11 revisions — growing unbounded!
✗3. Each Secret stores the ENTIRE release configuration (~5KB) — 11 revisions = 55KB wasted
✗4. At 5 deploys/day for 6 months = 900+ Secrets bloating etcd and slowing kubectl!
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check revision count: helm history anihpj -n anihpj | wc -l
→ 12 lines (header + 11 revisions) — growing every deploy!
2Check max history setting: helm get values anihpj -n anihpj --all | grep maxHistory
→ No maxHistory set — default is 256 revisions!
3Root cause: Helm stores each revision as a Secret (sh.helm.release.v1.<name>.v<rev>). Without --max-history, Helm defaults to keeping up to 256 revisions. For CI/CD with frequent deploys, this fills the namespace with revision Secrets and bloats etcd.
4Fix: Set --max-history 10 (or appropriate number) during install
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
helm history shows 11+ revisions
②
No --max-history set on install
③
Each revision = 1 Secret in etcd
④
Set --max-history 10 to auto-prune
⑤
Cleanup old Secrets → etcd shrinks!

Tenet: --max-history controls how many revision Secrets Helm retains. Default is 256. For CI/CD with frequent deploys, set it to 10-25. For production, 10 is usually sufficient for rollback purposes. Old revisions are automatically pruned — the oldest revision is deleted when a new one exceeds the limit. You can also clean up manually: kubectl delete secret -n <ns> -l owner=helm,name=<release> --field-selector metadata.name!=sh.helm.release.v1.<name>.v<latest>

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)

📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ helm install anihpj ./s23-chart -n anihpj --set maxHistory=5 ✅ Max 5 revisions kept — auto-prunes old ones!

🧪 SCENARIO S24 — Category 2: Release Lifecycle Uninstall Debug

helm uninstall Leaves PVC Behind — Database Data Survives Unexpectedly

The Problem: The anihpj team runs helm uninstall anihpj -n anihpj to tear down the staging environment. The StatefulSet and its Pods are deleted, but the PersistentVolumeClaim survives! When they reinstall, the new StatefulSet creates a NEW PVC — the old data is still in the old PVC but inaccessible. The database appears "empty" after reinstall. Your job: find the orphaned PVC, recover the data, and understand PVC lifecycle management.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm)
1

📋 Deploy StatefulSet, Uninstall, Discover Orphaned PVC

📖 APP STORY: The staging environment for anihpj/jobpost runs a PostgreSQL StatefulSet. The QA team finishes testing and runs helm uninstall anihpj. Everything appears deleted. Next week, the team reinstalls for a new test cycle — but the database is empty! Investigation reveals the old PVC with reclaimPolicy: Retain survived the uninstall. The new StatefulSet created a different PVC, and the old data is "trapped" in the orphaned PVC. 6 months of test data is inaccessible but NOT lost — it's sitting in an orphaned volume.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE (S24): 
s24-chart/
├── Chart.yaml
├── values.yaml
└── templates/
    ├── storageclass.yaml       ← reclaimPolicy: Retain
    ├── pv.yaml
    └── postgres-sts.yaml       ← StatefulSet with volumeClaimTemplates
BASH — Deploy, uninstall, discover orphaned PVC
# SCENARIO S24: Uninstall Leaves PVC
mkdir -p ~/helm-lab/s24-chart/templates
cd ~/helm-lab

cat << 'EOF' > ./s24-chart/Chart.yaml
apiVersion: v2
name: anihpj-pvc
description: PVC lifecycle demo
type: application
version: 1.0.0
EOF

cat << 'EOF' > ./s24-chart/values.yaml
storage:
  className: "local-path"
  size: 1Gi
EOF

cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: StorageClass
metadata:
  name: local-path
  annotations:
    storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class: "true"
provisioner: kubernetes.io/no-provisioner
volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer
reclaimPolicy: Retain
EOF

sudo mkdir -p /mnt/data/s24-postgres
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolume
metadata:
  name: s24-pv
spec:
  capacity:
    storage: 1Gi
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce
  persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy: Retain
  storageClassName: local-path
  hostPath:
    path: /mnt/data/s24-postgres
EOF

cat << 'EOF' > ./s24-chart/templates/postgres-sts.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: {{ .Release.Name }}-postgres
spec:
  serviceName: {{ .Release.Name }}-postgres
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: {{ .Release.Name }}-postgres
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: {{ .Release.Name }}-postgres
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: postgres
          image: postgres:15-alpine
          env:
            - name: POSTGRES_DB
              value: jobpost
            - name: POSTGRES_PASSWORD
              value: secret123
          volumeMounts:
            - name: data
              mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data
  volumeClaimTemplates:
    - metadata:
        name: data
      spec:
        accessModes:
          - ReadWriteOnce
        resources:
          requests:
            storage: {{ .Values.storage.size }}
        storageClassName: {{ .Values.storage.className }}
EOF

echo "=== Deploy StatefulSet ==="
helm install anihpj ./s24-chart -n anihpj --create-namespace --wait
kubectl get pvc -n anihpj
echo ""
echo "=== Uninstalling — PVC will SURVIVE! ==="
helm uninstall anihpj -n anihpj
echo ""
echo "=== BUG CONFIRMED: PVC survives helm uninstall! ==="
kubectl get pvc -n anihpj
echo ""
echo "StatefulSet and Pod are GONE, but PVC is STILL BOUND!"
echo "Reinstalling would create a NEW PVC — old data ORPHANED!"
echo "Namespace can't be deleted while PVC and PV exist!"
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. helm uninstall anihpj -n anihpj → StatefulSet and Pod deleted!
✗2. kubectl get pvc -n anihpj → PVC STILL EXISTS! Not deleted!
✗3. The namespace can't be deleted because the PVC is still bound to the PV!
✗4. Reinstalling creates a NEW PVC — old data is orphaned and inaccessible!
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check PVC after uninstall: kubectl get pvc -n anihpj
→ PVC still exists with STATUS: Bound — reclaimPolicy: Retain!
2Root cause: Helm uninstall deletes Kubernetes resources but PVCs created by StatefulSet volumeClaimTemplates are NOT managed by Helm's lifecycle. The PVC's reclaimPolicy (Retain) keeps the PV and data even after the PVC is manually deleted. For data safety, this is correct — but it surprises teams who expect `helm uninstall` to clean everything.
3Fix: Manually delete orphaned PVCs before reinstalling, or use reclaimPolicy: Delete for dev environments
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
helm uninstall deletes StatefulSet
②
PVC survives — reclaimPolicy: Retain
③
Reinstall creates NEW PVC → old data orphaned
④
Manually delete orphaned PVC + PV
⑤
Use reclaimPolicy: Delete for dev!

Tenet: PVCs created by StatefulSet volumeClaimTemplates are NOT automatically deleted when the StatefulSet or Helm release is removed. This is by design — Kubernetes protects your data. You must manually delete PVCs: kubectl delete pvc -n <ns> -l app=<statefulset>. The PV's reclaimPolicy determines what happens to the underlying storage: Retain (keep), Delete (auto-delete), Recycle (deprecated). For production: Retain. For dev/staging: Delete.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)

$ kubectl get pvc -n anihpj NAME STATUS VOLUME CAPACITY data-anihpj-postgres-0 Bound s24-pv 1Gi ← SURVIVED!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl delete pvc data-anihpj-postgres-0 -n anihpj persistentvolumeclaim "data-anihpj-postgres-0" deleted ✅
$ kubectl get pvc -n anihpj No resources found in anihpj namespace. ✅ All clean!
🔧
BASH
# Manually delete orphaned PVC
kubectl delete pvc data-anihpj-postgres-0 -n anihpj

# Delete the PV too (if no longer needed)
kubectl delete pv s24-pv

# Now namespace can be deleted cleanly
kubectl delete namespace anihpj
echo "✅ All storage resources cleaned up!"
🧹
BASH
helm uninstall anihpj -n anihpj 2>/dev/null
kubectl delete pvc -n anihpj --all 2>/dev/null
kubectl delete pv s24-pv 2>/dev/null
kubectl delete sc local-path 2>/dev/null

🧪 SCENARIO S25 — Category 2: Release Lifecycle Timeout Debug

helm install Fails — --wait --timeout Too Short for Slow-Starting Pod

The Problem: The anihpj chart deploys PostgreSQL which takes 60-90 seconds to initialize on first start (data directory creation, WAL setup). The CI/CD pipeline uses --wait --timeout 30s. The deployment FAILS every time because PostgreSQL hasn't finished initializing within 30 seconds — but if you wait another 60 seconds, the pod becomes Ready on its own. Your job: understand the mismatch between timeout and startup time, set appropriate timeouts, and verify the pod actually works.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm)
1

📋 Deploy with Intentionally Short Timeout

📖 APP STORY: The anihpj CI/CD pipeline has a default timeout of 30 seconds for all Helm operations. The PostgreSQL StatefulSet in the anihpj chart needs ~90 seconds for first-time initialization (creating data directory, configuring WAL, setting up users). Every deployment fails with "timed out waiting for the condition" — but the team doesn't realize the pod eventually becomes ready 60 seconds later. They've been debugging a "failed deployment" for days when the deployment actually works — it just needs more time.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE (S25): 
s25-chart/
├── Chart.yaml
├── values.yaml
└── templates/
    ├── deployment.yaml        ← Uses init container to simulate slow start
    └── service.yaml
BASH — Deploy with short timeout
# SCENARIO S25: Timeout Too Short
mkdir -p ~/helm-lab/s25-chart/templates
cd ~/helm-lab

cat << 'EOF' > ./s25-chart/Chart.yaml
apiVersion: v2
name: anihpj-timeout
description: Timeout demo
type: application
version: 1.0.0
EOF

cat << 'EOF' > ./s25-chart/values.yaml
replicaCount: 1
image:
  repository: nginx
  tag: alpine
startupDelay: 45
EOF

cat << 'EOF' > ./s25-chart/templates/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: {{ .Release.Name }}-api
spec:
  replicas: {{ .Values.replicaCount }}
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: {{ .Release.Name }}
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: {{ .Release.Name }}
    spec:
      initContainers:
        - name: startup-delay
          image: busybox:1.36
          command: ["sh", "-c", "echo 'Simulating PostgreSQL initialization...'; sleep {{ .Values.startupDelay }}; echo 'Ready!'"]
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: "{{ .Values.image.repository }}:{{ .Values.image.tag }}"
          ports:
            - containerPort: 80
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /
              port: 80
            initialDelaySeconds: 0
            periodSeconds: 5
EOF

cat << 'EOF' > ./s25-chart/templates/service.yaml

kind: Service
metadata:
  name: {{ .Release.Name }}-api
spec:
  selector:
    app: {{ .Release.Name }}
  ports:
    - port: 80
EOF

echo "=== Installing with --timeout 15s (TOO SHORT!) ==="
helm install anihpj ./s25-chart -n anihpj --create-namespace --wait --timeout 15s 2>&1 || true
echo ""
echo "=== Pod is STILL starting — check status ==="
kubectl get pods -n anihpj
echo ""
echo "=== BUG CONFIRMED: helm install failed — but pod IS starting! ==="
echo "The init container needs ${startupDelay}s but --timeout was only 15s!"
echo "Wait a bit and check again — pod will be Running."
echo "CI/CD falsely reports failure for a working deployment!"
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Install with --timeout 15s → "Error: timed out waiting for the condition"
✗2. kubectl get pods -n anihpj → Pod is STILL INITIALIZING (init container running)!
✗3. Wait 45 seconds and check again → pod is Running! The deployment WORKED, just needed more time!
✗4. CI/CD pipeline falsely reports failure — team wastes hours debugging a working deployment!
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check pod status: kubectl get pods -n anihpj
→ Pod shows Init:0/1 — init container is STILL running (simulating PostgreSQL startup)
2Root cause: --timeout 15s is shorter than the pod's actual startup time (~45s init container + container start). Helm's --wait flag monitors pod readiness and gives up after --timeout seconds. The pod itself is fine — it's just slow to start. The timeout must account for: image pull time + init container execution + container startup + readiness probe success.
3Fix: Set --timeout to at least 5m for database workloads, 10m for production
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
helm install with --timeout 15s fails
②
Pod init container still running (45s)
③
Timeout shorter than startup time
④
Pod eventually becomes Ready on its own
⑤
Set --timeout 5m for slow-starting workloads!

Tenet: --timeout must be LONGER than your slowest pod's startup time. For databases (PostgreSQL, MySQL): allow 5-10 minutes for first-time initialization. For applications: 2-3 minutes for image pull + startup. For production: always use --timeout 10m. The timeout doesn't slow down successful deploys — it only affects how long Helm waits before giving up. Better to wait 10 minutes for a real failure than to falsely report failure after 30 seconds.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ helm install anihpj ./s25-chart -n anihpj --wait --timeout 15s Error: timed out waiting for the condition
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ helm install anihpj ./s25-chart -n anihpj --wait --timeout 5m ✅ Deployment successful — pod started within 45 seconds!
🔧
BASH
helm uninstall anihpj -n anihpj 2>/dev/null
helm install anihpj ./s25-chart -n anihpj --create-namespace --wait --timeout 5m
echo "✅ Deployment succeeded with appropriate timeout!"
🧹
BASH
helm uninstall anihpj -n anihpj 2>/dev/null
kubectl delete namespace anihpj 2>/dev/null
rm -rf ~/helm-lab/s25-chart

📋 First Install Works, Second Install Fails

📖 APP STORY: The anihpj CI/CD pipeline script does helm install anihpj ./chart -n anihpj on every git push. The first deployment succeeds perfectly. The developer pushes a bug fix 30 minutes later — the pipeline tries helm install AGAIN and crashes with "cannot re-use a name that is still in use." The pipeline is NOT idempotent. Every second deployment fails because `helm install` checks if the release name already exists.

s26-chart/
├── Chart.yaml
└── templates/
    └── deployment.yaml

cat << 'EOF' > ./s26-chart/Chart.yaml

cat << 'EOF' > ./s26-chart/templates/deployment.yaml

  name: {{ .Release.Name }}-api
spec:
  replicas: 1

    matchLabels:
      app: {{ .Release.Name }}

echo ""
echo "=== Second install (FAILS — name already in use!) ==="

echo ""
echo "=== BUG CONFIRMED: Release name collision! ==="
echo "helm install is NOT idempotent — CI/CD will break on EVERY second deploy!"

✗1. helm install anihpj ./s26-chart -n anihpj → "Error: cannot re-use a name that is still in use"
✗2. CI/CD pipeline breaks on second commit — not idempotent!

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Root cause: helm install is NOT idempotent — it fails if the release already exists. For CI/CD, use helm upgrade --install which installs if the release doesn't exist, or upgrades if it does.
2Fix: Replace helm install with helm upgrade --install
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
First helm install succeeds
②
Second helm install fails — name exists
③
helm install is NOT idempotent
④
Use helm upgrade --install
⑤
CI/CD now works every time!

Tenet: helm upgrade --install <name> <chart> is the IDEMPOTENT CI/CD command. It installs if the release doesn't exist, upgrades if it does. Always use this in pipelines — never helm install alone.

📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Find the stuck hook: kubectl get jobs -n anihpj -l helm.sh/hook
→ Hook Job is Running — infinite loop in the container!
2Root cause: A post-install hook Job is stuck in an infinite loop. Helm waits for ALL hooks to complete before marking the release as "deployed." Without a timeout on the Job spec and a Helm --timeout, the release is stuck indefinitely.
3Fix: Delete the stuck hook Job, then the release transitions to "deployed." Always set activeDeadlineSeconds on hook Jobs.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
helm list shows pending-install
②
Find stuck hook Job
③
Hook in infinite loop — never completes
④
Delete stuck hook Job
⑤
Release transitions to deployed!

Tenet: Hooks can block the ENTIRE release lifecycle. Always: (1) Set activeDeadlineSeconds on hook Job specs, (2) Set --timeout on helm install/upgrade, (3) Use helm.sh/hook-delete-policy: hook-failed to clean up failed hooks. If a hook is stuck: kubectl delete job <hook-name> -n <ns> — the release will transition to its final state.

helm upgrade --install Pulls Latest Chart — Version Not Pinned

The Problem: The anihpj team maintains a Helm chart in a local repository. Chart v1.0.0 is stable (uses nginx:alpine). A developer publishes v2.0.0 that changes the image to nginx:does-not-exist (breaking change). 🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab)
1

📋 Install from Repo Without --version

📖 APP STORY: The anihpj team maintains an internal Helm chart repo for their Django app. Chart v1.0.0 deploys nginx:alpine — it's been stable for months. A new team member creates v2.0.0 that changes the image to nginx:does-not-exist by mistake and pushes it to the repo. The CI/CD pipeline script uses helm upgrade --install anihpj local/anihpj-version WITHOUT --version. On the next deploy, Helm pulls v2.0.0 (LATEST) — and the deployment FAILS with ImagePullBackOff. Production goes down because nobody pinned the chart version — the pipeline silently switched from v1.0.0 to v2.0.0.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE (S30): 
s30-repo/
├── anihpj-version-1.0.0.tgz   ← Stable: nginx:alpine
├── anihpj-version-2.0.0.tgz   ← BROKEN: nginx:does-not-exist
└── index.yaml                   ← Lists both versions (v2.0.0 is latest)
BASH — Create local repo, v1.0.0 (stable) + v2.0.0 (broken), install latest

# SCENARIO S30: Chart Version Not Pinned — Local Repo Demo
# ============================================

mkdir -p ~/helm-lab/s30-repo/s30-v2/templates
cd ~/helm-lab

# ——— VERSION 1.0.0: STABLE (nginx:alpine) ———
cat << 'EOF' > ./s30-repo/s30-v1/Chart.yaml
apiVersion: v2
name: anihpj-version
description: anihpj/jobpost — STABLE v1.0.0
type: application
version: 1.0.0
appVersion: "1.0"
EOF

cat << 'EOF' > ./s30-repo/s30-v1/values.yaml
image:
  repository: nginx
  tag: alpine
EOF

cat << 'EOF' > ./s30-repo/s30-v1/templates/deployment.yaml

kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: {{ .Release.Name }}-api
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: {{ .Release.Name }}
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: {{ .Release.Name }}
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: "{{ .Values.image.repository }}:{{ .Values.image.tag }}"
EOF

# ——— VERSION 2.0.0: BROKEN (nginx:does-not-exist) ———
cat << 'EOF' > ./s30-repo/s30-v2/Chart.yaml

name: anihpj-version
description: anihpj/jobpost — BROKEN v2.0.0 with bad image

  repository: nginx

EOF

cat << 'EOF' > ./s30-repo/s30-v2/templates/deployment.yaml

  name: {{ .Release.Name }}-api
spec:
  replicas: 1

    matchLabels:
      app: {{ .Release.Name }}
  template:

helm package ./s30-repo/s30-v2 -d ./s30-repo/

# Generate Helm repo index

echo ""
echo "=== Repo index (v2.0.0 is LATEST) ==="
cat ./s30-repo/index.yaml
echo ""

# Add local repo and update
helm repo add local-s30 "file://$(pwd)/s30-repo" 2>/dev/null || true
helm repo update 2>/dev/null

echo ""
echo "=== Search available versions ==="
helm search repo local-s30/anihpj-version --versions
echo ""

# INSTALL WITHOUT --version — pulls LATEST (v2.0.0 → BROKEN!)
echo "============================================"
echo "INSTALLING WITHOUT --version → Pulls v2.0.0 (LATEST)!"
echo "============================================"
helm install anihpj local-s30/anihpj-version -n anihpj --create-namespace --wait --timeout 30s 2>&1 || true
echo ""

echo "=== BUG CONFIRMED: v2.0.0 deployed because --version was not pinned! ==="
echo "=== The repo's LATEST version (v2.0.0) has a non-existent image! ==="
kubectl get pods -n anihpj
kubectl describe pod -n anihpj -l app=anihpj 2>/dev/null | grep -A2 "Failed\|ImagePullBackOff\|ErrImagePull" || true
echo ""
echo "⚠️  v1.0.0 (stable, nginx:alpine) was SKIPPED because --version was not pinned!"
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. helm search repo local-s30/anihpj-version --versions → Shows v2.0.0 as LATEST, v1.0.0 as older!
✗2. Install without --version → Pulls v2.0.0 (the LATEST from the repo)!
✗3. kubectl get pods -n anihpj → Pod in ImagePullBackOff or ErrImagePull — nginx:does-not-exist can't be pulled!
✗4. The CI/CD pipeline silently switched from v1.0.0 (stable) to v2.0.0 (broken) because --version was not pinned!
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check what was installed: helm list -n anihpj
→ CHART: anihpj-version-2.0.0 — NOT the stable v1.0.0!
2Check repo index: cat ./s30-repo/index.yaml
→ v2.0.0 has the highest version — Helm pulls the LATEST by default!
3Root cause: Without --version, helm install/upgrade from a repository ALWAYS uses the LATEST chart version. When a new version is published (even with breaking changes), all unpinned installs immediately switch to it. This breaks CI/CD reproducibility — the same command produces different results over time as new chart versions are released.
4Fix: Always use --version 1.0.0 to pin the exact chart version. For production, pin to specific versions in your CI/CD scripts, never rely on "latest."
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
helm install from repo without --version
②
Helm pulls LATEST (v2.0.0) from repo index
③
v2.0.0 has breaking change → Pod fails
④
CI/CD silently switched versions!
⑤
Pin --version 1.0.0 → Reproducible!

Tenet: For repo-based installs, ALWAYS pin --version. For local directories, the directory IS the pinned version. For OCI registries, pin the digest. NEVER use "latest" chart version in production. Reproducibility is critical: helm install anihpj local-s30/anihpj-version --version 1.0.0 will ALWAYS deploy the same chart, regardless of how many new versions are published to the repo.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ helm search repo local-s30/anihpj-version --versions NAME CHART VERSION APP VERSION local-s30/anihpj-version 2.0.0 2.0 ← LATEST (pulled by default!) local-s30/anihpj-version 1.0.0 1.0
$ helm install anihpj local-s30/anihpj-version -n anihpj --wait Error: timed out waiting for the condition ← v2.0.0 deployed, image doesn't exist!
$ kubectl get pods -n anihpj NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS anihpj-api-0 0/1 ImagePullBackOff 0 ← nginx:does-not-exist!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ helm install anihpj local-s30/anihpj-version --version 1.0.0 -n anihpj --wait NAME: anihpj STATUS: deployed ✅ v1.0.0 — nginx:alpine works!
🔧
BASH — Uninstall broken release, install with --version pinned
# Uninstall the broken v2.0.0 release
helm uninstall anihpj -n anihpj 2>/dev/null

# CORRECT: Pin --version for reproducible deploys
helm install anihpj local-s30/anihpj-version --version 1.0.0 \
  -n anihpj --create-namespace --wait --timeout 2m

# Verify correct version deployed
helm list -n anihpj
echo "✅ anihpj-version-1.0.0 deployed — nginx:alpine running!"
echo "This deployment will ALWAYS use v1.0.0, regardless of new repo versions!"

📋 Deploy Chart with Hardcoded Namespace in Hook

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗2. kubectl get jobs -n anihpj-staging → No migration Job — it was created in anihpj-prod!

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check hook Job namespace: grep -n "namespace:" ./s31-chart/templates/hook-pre-upgrade.yaml
→ namespace: anihpj-prod — HARDCODED! Not using .Release.Namespace!
2Root cause: The hook Job template was copy-pasted from a production-specific setup. The namespace field was hardcoded to "anihpj-prod" instead of using {{ .Release.Namespace }}. Every deployment — regardless of the actual target namespace — runs the hook in "anihpj-prod". This is catastrophic in multi-namespace environments because hooks interact with external systems (databases, APIs) from the wrong context.
3Fix: Replace the hardcoded namespace with {{ .Release.Namespace }} so the hook always runs in the same namespace as the release
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Deploy to staging → Hook runs in production namespace
②
Check hook template → namespace: hardcoded!
③
Copy-paste from production → namespace not parameterized
④
Replace with {{ .Release.Namespace }}
⑤
Hook always runs in correct namespace!

Tenet: Never hardcode namespaces in ANY template — always use {{ .Release.Namespace }}. Hook Jobs, Services, ConfigMaps, and any cross-namespace resource must use the release namespace to prevent staging operations from affecting production. Copy-paste is the #1 cause of hardcoded namespaces — always review templates after copying from another environment.

📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix

🔧

  ./s31-chart/templates/hook-pre-upgrade.yaml

# Verify the fix
grep "namespace:" ./s31-chart/templates/hook-pre-upgrade.yaml

# Re-deploy to staging — hook now runs in the correct namespace

echo "✅ Hook now runs in anihpj-staging — production data is SAFE!"

kubectl delete namespace anihpj-prod 2>/dev/null

The migration failure evidence was auto-deleted before anyone could see it. The team spends hours trying to reproduce the error because the original logs were destroyed.

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

1Check hook annotations: grep "hook-delete-policy" ./s32-chart/templates/hook-pre-upgrade.yaml

①
Hook Job fails → Deleted instantly

kubectl get jobs → empty — evidence gone!

hook-failed policy destroyed logs
④
Use hook-succeeded during development
⑤
Failed Jobs preserved for debugging!

Tenet: hook-failed delete policy DESTROYS debugging evidence. Use hook-succeeded during development — it keeps failed Jobs so you can inspect logs. Only add hook-failed in production AFTER the hook is stable and tested. Alternative: use before-hook-creation to clean up before creating a new hook Job.

🧪 SCENARIO S33 — Category 2: Release Lifecycle Hook Debug

Hook Weight Conflict — Two Hooks with Same Weight Run in Parallel, Causing Race Condition

The Problem: The anihpj chart has two pre-upgrade hooks: a database backup (weight: "0") and a database migration (weight: "0"). Because they have the SAME weight, Helm runs them IN PARALLEL. The migration tries to alter tables while the backup is reading them — causing a DEADLOCK. The migration fails with "could not acquire lock," and the upgrade is blocked. Your job: understand hook weight ordering, fix the weight values so backup runs BEFORE migration, and prevent the race condition.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab)
1

📋 Deploy Chart with Two Hooks at Same Weight

📖 APP STORY: The anihpj team added a database backup hook before every upgrade. The existing migration hook runs at weight "0". The new backup hook was also assigned weight "0" by the developer who didn't understand hook weights. When an upgrade runs, both hooks fire simultaneously — the backup reads tables while the migration drops columns. PostgreSQL throws "could not acquire lock," the migration fails, and the upgrade is blocked. Two hooks fighting over the same database with no ordering — a classic race condition caused by equal weights.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE (S33): 
s33-chart/
├── Chart.yaml
├── values.yaml
└── templates/
    ├── deployment.yaml
    ├── hook-pre-upgrade-backup.yaml    ← weight: "0"
    └── hook-pre-upgrade-migration.yaml ← weight: "0" — SAME weight!
BASH — Create chart with two hooks at same weight
# SCENARIO S33: Hook Weight Conflict — Race Condition
mkdir -p ~/helm-lab/s33-chart/templates
cd ~/helm-lab

cat << 'EOF' > ./s33-chart/Chart.yaml
apiVersion: v2
name: anihpj-hook-weight
version: 1.0.0
EOF

cat << 'EOF' > ./s33-chart/templates/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: {{ .Release.Name }}-api
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: {{ .Release.Name }}
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: {{ .Release.Name }}
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: nginx:alpine
EOF

# BACKUP hook — weight: "0"
cat << 'EOF' > ./s33-chart/templates/hook-pre-upgrade-backup.yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: {{ .Release.Name }}-db-backup
  annotations:
    "helm.sh/hook": pre-upgrade
    "helm.sh/hook-weight": "0"        # ❌ BUG: Same weight as migration!
    "helm.sh/hook-delete-policy": hook-succeeded
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
        - name: backup
          image: busybox:1.36
          command: ["sh", "-c"]
          args:
            - |
              echo "=== DB BACKUP STARTING (weight: 0) ==="
              sleep 8
              echo "Backup reading tables..."
              sleep 3
              echo "=== BACKUP COMPLETE ==="
EOF

# MIGRATION hook — weight: "0" (SAME as backup!)
cat << 'EOF' > ./s33-chart/templates/hook-pre-upgrade-migration.yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: {{ .Release.Name }}-db-migration
  annotations:
    "helm.sh/hook": pre-upgrade
    "helm.sh/hook-weight": "0"        # ❌ BUG: Same weight as backup!
    "helm.sh/hook-delete-policy": hook-succeeded
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
        - name: migration
          image: busybox:1.36
          command: ["sh", "-c"]
          args:
            - |
              echo "=== DB MIGRATION STARTING (weight: 0) ==="
              echo "ERROR: Cannot acquire lock — backup is reading tables!"
              echo "Migration and backup are running IN PARALLEL due to same weight!"
              exit 1
EOF

echo "=== Installing chart (both hooks will run SIMULTANEOUSLY) ==="
helm install anihpj ./s33-chart -n anihpj --create-namespace --wait --timeout 30s 2>&1 || true
echo ""
echo "=== Check hook Jobs ==="
kubectl get jobs -n anihpj
echo ""
echo "=== BUG CONFIRMED: Both hooks ran at the SAME TIME (weight: 0)! ==="
echo "Backup reads tables while migration alters them — DEADLOCK!"
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Both hook Jobs start at the SAME time — visible in kubectl get jobs -n anihpj
✗2. Migration fails because backup is holding a table lock!
✗3. Same helm.sh/hook-weight: "0" on both hooks — no ordering!
✗4. Upgrade is BLOCKED — migration can't complete while backup runs!
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check hook weights: grep -A1 "hook-weight" ./s33-chart/templates/*.yaml
→ Both hooks have weight: "0" — they run in PARALLEL!
2Root cause: Helm executes hooks with the SAME weight concurrently. Lower weight = earlier execution. Weight "-10" runs before "0", which runs before "10". Same weight means NO ordering guarantee — hooks compete for resources.
3Fix: Set backup weight to "-10" (runs first), migration weight to "0" (runs after backup completes)
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Two hooks with weight: "0" → Run in parallel
②
Backup reads tables, migration alters them
③
Deadlock — migration can't acquire lock!
④
Set backup weight: "-10", migration: "0"
⑤
Backup completes → then migration runs safely!

Tenet: Same weight = PARALLEL execution. Lower weight = earlier execution. Higher weight = later execution. Always assign different weights to hooks that depend on each other. Backup should run BEFORE migration (lower weight). Migration should run AFTER backup (higher weight). This creates a deterministic, ordered workflow.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get jobs -n anihpj NAME COMPLETIONS DURATION AGE anihpj-db-backup 0/1 3s 3s ← Running! anihpj-db-migration 0/1 3s 3s ← Running SIMULTANEOUSLY!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get jobs -n anihpj -w anihpj-db-backup 1/1 10s 15s ← Completed FIRST anihpj-db-migration 1/1 5s 5s ← Started AFTER backup!
🔧
BASH
# Fix: Backup weight -10 (runs first), Migration weight 0 (runs after)
sed -i 's|"helm.sh/hook-weight": "0"|"helm.sh/hook-weight": "-10"|' \
  ./s33-chart/templates/hook-pre-upgrade-backup.yaml

# Re-deploy with correct weights
helm uninstall anihpj -n anihpj 2>/dev/null
helm install anihpj ./s33-chart -n anihpj --create-namespace --wait --timeout 30s
echo "✅ Backup runs FIRST (weight -10), then Migration (weight 0) — no deadlock!"
🧹
BASH
helm uninstall anihpj -n anihpj 2>/dev/null
kubectl delete namespace anihpj 2>/dev/null
rm -rf ~/helm-lab/s33-chart

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗2. Each helm test run creates a NEW pod — old ones NEVER deleted!

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check test pod annotations: grep -A3 "annotations:" ./s34-chart/templates/tests/test-api.yaml
→ Only has "helm.sh/hook": test — NO delete-policy!
2Root cause: Test pods are NOT auto-cleaned without hook-delete-policy. Each `helm test` creates a new pod, and the old ones remain as "Completed" pods forever. This is different from hook Jobs which have a default TTL — test pods have NO cleanup mechanism unless you add the annotation.

①
helm test runs → New pod created
②
Test completes → Pod stays as "Completed"
③

④
Add hook-delete-policy: hook-succeeded
⑤
Test pods auto-cleaned after completion!

Tenet: Test pods are NOT auto-cleaned by default. Always add "helm.sh/hook-delete-policy": hook-succeeded to test pod annotations. Without it, every helm test run leaves a Completed pod that accumulates forever. For CI/CD pipelines running tests on every deploy, this can create hundreds of orphaned pods per month.

🧪 SCENARIO S36 — Category 2: Release Lifecycle Rollback Debug

helm rollback --revision Skips Revisions — Wrong Understanding of Revision Numbers

The Problem: The anihpj team uses helm rollback anihpj 3 thinking "revision 3 = 3rd deployment." But rollbacks CREATE new revisions! After rollback to rev 3, Helm creates revision 4. The user's mental model (rev 3 = 3rd deploy) is wrong — revision numbers are ORDERING, not IDENTITY. Your job: understand how rollback creates new revision numbers, use helm history to see what each revision actually contains, and learn the truth about revision numbering.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm)
1

📋 Deploy, Upgrade Twice, Rollback — See Revision Numbers Jump

📖 APP STORY: The anihpj team deploys v1 (rev 1), upgrades to v2 (rev 2), upgrades to v3 (rev 3). Something breaks in v3. The on-call engineer runs helm rollback anihpj 2 expecting "go back to v2 config." Helm creates revision 4 with v2's config. Later, another engineer runs helm rollback anihpj 3 expecting "go to v3" — but revision 3 was v3 (broken)! Now revision 5 is created, and the team is confused about which revision contains which config. Revision numbers are just sequence counters — they don't identify which deployment is which.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE (S36): 
s36-chart/
├── Chart.yaml
└── templates/
    └── deployment.yaml
BASH — Deploy, upgrade, rollback to see revision numbering
# SCENARIO S36: Rollback Creates New Revisions
mkdir -p ~/helm-lab/s36-chart/templates
cd ~/helm-lab

cat << 'EOF' > ./s36-chart/Chart.yaml
apiVersion: v2
name: anihpj-rev
version: 1.0.0
EOF

cat << 'EOF' > ./s36-chart/templates/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: {{ .Release.Name }}-api
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: {{ .Release.Name }}
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: {{ .Release.Name }}
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: nginx:alpine
EOF

# Deploy v1: image=nginx:alpine
helm install anihpj ./s36-chart -n anihpj --create-namespace --wait
echo "=== Deployed v1 (revision 1) ==="
helm history anihpj -n anihpj

# Upgrade to v2: add label
helm upgrade anihpj ./s36-chart -n anihpj --set image.tag=1.25-alpine --wait
echo "=== Upgraded to v2 (revision 2) ==="
helm history anihpj -n anihpj

# Upgrade to v3: change label again
helm upgrade anihpj ./s36-chart -n anihpj --set image.tag=1.27-alpine --wait
echo "=== Upgraded to v3 (revision 3) ==="
helm history anihpj -n anihpj

# NOW: Rollback to revision 2
echo "=== Rolling back to revision 2 ==="
helm rollback anihpj 2 -n anihpj --wait
echo ""
echo "=== BUG CONFIRMED: Rollback CREATED revision 4! ==="
helm history anihpj -n anihpj
echo ""
echo "Revision 4 = v2's config (rollback target)"
echo "But rev 3 still exists! rev numbers are ORDER, not IDENTITY!"
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. helm history anihpj -n anihpj → Shows 4 revisions after 3 deploys + 1 rollback!
✗2. Revision 4 was created by the rollback — it's a NEW revision, not a "jump back"!
✗3. Revision numbers are MONOTONIC — rollback doesn't "go to" rev 2, it CREATES rev 4 with rev 2's config!
✗4. Team confuses "revision 3" (v3 broken) with "3rd deployment" — they're the same but after rollback it's confusing!
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Count revisions: helm history anihpj -n anihpj | wc -l
→ 5 lines (header + 4 revisions) — rollback INCREASED the count, not decreased it!
2Root cause: Rollback doesn't "go back" to a previous revision — it CREATES a NEW revision using the old revision's configuration. This preserves full history. Revision numbers are monotonically increasing sequence counters, not stable identifiers of deployments.
3Fix: Use helm history to see the DESCRIPTION column (shows "Upgrade complete" or "Rollback to X") to understand what each revision represents
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
3 deploys = revisions 1, 2, 3
②
Rollback to rev 2 → Creates rev 4!
③
Rev 4 has rev 2's config — NEW number
④
Revisions are sequence, not identity
⑤
Use helm history to see what each revision IS!

Tenet: Revision numbers are ORDERING, not IDENTITY. Rollback creates new revisions — it doesn't "jump back." Use helm history to see the DESCRIPTION column which tells you what each revision represents ("Upgrade complete" vs "Rollback to 2"). Never assume revision 3 = "the 3rd thing we deployed" — after rollbacks, the mapping is no longer 1:1.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)

📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix (understanding)
$ helm get values anihpj -n anihpj --revision 2 && helm get values anihpj -n anihpj --revision 4 Revision 2: image.tag=1.25-alpine ← Original v2 Revision 4: image.tag=1.25-alpine ← Rollback target (same config, NEW number!)
🔧

echo "Revision numbers are just sequence counters — use helm get values --revision N to inspect"

📋 Create Chart with Unreachable Dependency Repository

helm dependency update ./s37-chart 2>&1 || true
echo ""
echo "=== BUG CONFIRMED: Dependency repository unreachable! ==="
echo "CI/CD runners can't access internal corp network!"
echo "Chart works on dev laptop (VPN) but fails in CI/CD!"

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. helm dependency update ./s37-chart → FAILS with "Failed to fetch" error!
✗2. The repository URL points to internal network — unreachable from CI/CD!
✗3. Developer says "works on my machine" — but they're on office VPN!
✗4. CI/CD pipeline is BLOCKED — can't resolve chart dependencies!

1Check dependency repo: grep "repository:" ./s37-chart/Chart.yaml

2Root cause: Dependency repositories must be accessible from CI/CD runners, not just developer machines. Internal repos behind VPNs or firewalls block automated pipelines. The solution is to mirror dependencies to a public/accessible registry or use OCI-based chart distribution.

Tenet: Dependency repositories must be accessible from EVERY environment that runs helm dependency update — CI/CD runners, staging clusters, production clusters. Never use internal-only repository URLs unless you've verified network access from all deployment targets. For internal charts, use OCI registries (e.g., oci://registry.corp.com/charts/postgresql) which can be mirrored and accessed with proper credentials.

🧪 SCENARIO S38 — Category 2: Release Lifecycle Package Debug

helm package Includes .git Directory — Chart Bloated with Git History

The Problem: The anihpj team runs helm package ./anihpj and pushes to their OCI registry. The push TIMES OUT because the .tgz is 52MB! Investigation reveals that .helmignore is missing a .git entry — 50MB of Git history was packaged into the chart. OCI registries reject oversized layers, and artifact storage costs skyrocket. Your job: find why the chart is bloated, fix .helmignore, and learn to keep packages lean.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 6 (minikube) — Package operations only
1

📋 Create Chart, Initialize Git, Package Without .git in .helmignore

📖 APP STORY: The anihpj chart lives in a Git monorepo with 2 years of commit history. The team created a .helmignore but copy-pasted it from .gitignore — which does NOT exclude .git (because .gitignore assumes Git already manages that). When they run helm package, the .git/ directory (50MB) gets bundled into the chart. The OCI push times out after 5 minutes. The chart artifact is 52MB instead of 2KB — all because .helmignore doesn't exclude .git.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE (S38): 
s38-chart/
├── .git/                  ← 50MB of Git history
├── .helmignore            ← Missing ".git" entry!
├── Chart.yaml
└── templates/
    └── deployment.yaml
BASH — Create chart with .git directory, package without .helmignore fix
# SCENARIO S38: .git Directory Packaged into Chart
mkdir -p ~/helm-lab/s38-chart/templates
cd ~/helm-lab/s38-chart

cat << 'EOF' > ./Chart.yaml
apiVersion: v2
name: anihpj-bloat
version: 1.0.0
EOF

cat << 'EOF' > ./templates/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: {{ .Release.Name }}-api
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: {{ .Release.Name }}
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: {{ .Release.Name }}
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: nginx:alpine
EOF

# Create .helmignore WITHOUT .git entry (copy-pasted from .gitignore)
cat << 'EOF' > ./.helmignore
# Patterns to ignore when packaging charts
*.swp
*.bak
*.tmp
.DS_Store
# ❌ BUG: .git is NOT in .helmignore!
EOF

# Initialize a real git repo with some fake history
git init
git config user.email "dev@anihpj.com"
git config user.name "Dev"

# Create some large-ish files to simulate git history
for i in $(seq 1 5); do
  dd if=/dev/urandom of=./dummy-$i.bin bs=1M count=1 2>/dev/null
  git add dummy-$i.bin 2>/dev/null
  git commit -m "Commit $i" 2>/dev/null
  rm dummy-$i.bin
done

cd ~/helm-lab

echo "=== Packaging chart — .git directory will be included! ==="
helm package ./s38-chart -d /tmp
echo ""
echo "=== BUG CONFIRMED: Chart .tgz is BLOATED with .git history! ==="
ls -lh /tmp/anihpj-bloat-1.0.0.tgz
echo ""
echo ".git directory (Git history) was packaged into the chart!"
echo "OCI push will TIMEOUT or be REJECTED due to oversized layer!"
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. ls -lh /tmp/anihpj-bloat-1.0.0.tgz → Chart is several MB instead of ~2KB!
✗2. tar tzf /tmp/anihpj-bloat-1.0.0.tgz | grep ".git" → .git directory IS in the archive!
✗3. .helmignore does NOT contain .git — Git history packaged!
✗4. OCI push fails or times out — artifact storage costs explode!
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check chart contents: tar tzf /tmp/anihpj-bloat-1.0.0.tgz | grep "\.git"
→ .git/objects, .git/refs, .git/logs — ALL present!
2Check .helmignore: cat ./s38-chart/.helmignore
→ No ".git" entry! Only editor backup patterns!
3Root cause: .helmignore controls what helm package includes/excludes — it's the chart's .dockerignore. Without ".git" in .helmignore, the entire Git history (objects, refs, logs) gets packaged into the chart .tgz. This bloats the artifact from kilobytes to megabytes (or gigabytes for large repos).
4Fix: Add .git and .gitignore to .helmignore
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
helm package creates bloated .tgz
②
tar tzf shows .git inside archive
③
.helmignore missing ".git" entry
④
Add .git to .helmignore
⑤
Chart package is lean — 2KB!

Tenet: .helmignore is your chart's .dockerignore — it controls what gets packaged. Always include .git, .gitignore, *.swp, *~, .DS_Store, and editor backup files. The default helm create template includes these, but manually created charts often miss them. A bloated chart means slower pushes, rejected OCI layers, and wasted storage.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ ls -lh /tmp/anihpj-bloat-1.0.0.tgz -rw-r--r-- 1 user user 5.2M Jan 6 10:00 anihpj-bloat-1.0.0.tgz ← BLOATED!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ ls -lh /tmp/anihpj-bloat-1.0.0.tgz -rw-r--r-- 1 user user 1.2K Jan 6 10:05 anihpj-bloat-1.0.0.tgz ← LEAN!
🔧
BASH
# Fix: Add .git and other patterns to .helmignore
cat >> ./s38-chart/.helmignore << 'EOF'
.git
.gitignore
.gitmodules
*.bak
*~
EOF

# Re-package — chart is now lean!
helm package ./s38-chart -d /tmp
ls -lh /tmp/anihpj-bloat-1.0.0.tgz
echo "✅ Chart is now LEAN — .git excluded from package!"
🧹
BASH
rm -rf ~/helm-lab/s38-chart /tmp/anihpj-bloat-1.0.0.tgz

🧪 SCENARIO S39 — Category 2: Release Lifecycle API Debug

helm install --dry-run Succeeds but helm install Fails — Server-side API Validation

The Problem: The anihpj chart uses an Ingress resource with apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1beta1 — a deprecated API version. The developer runs helm install --dry-run against an older cluster and it PASSES. But when deployed to a new Kubernetes cluster, it FAILS because the API version was removed. --dry-run only validates TEMPLATE rendering — not whether the Kubernetes API server accepts the resources. Your job: understand the limits of --dry-run, detect deprecated API usage, and use --dry-run=server for real validation.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab)
1

📋 Create Chart with Deprecated API, See --dry-run Pass But Install Fail

📖 APP STORY: The anihpj team tests all changes with helm install --dry-run in CI/CD. A developer adds an Ingress using networking.k8s.io/v1beta1 — which works on their old dev cluster. The CI/CD dry-run PASSES. But when deployed to production (newer K8s), the install FAILS with "no matches for kind Ingress in version networking.k8s.io/v1beta1." The team trusted --dry-run as a deployment gate, but it only checks template syntax — not API server compatibility.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE (S39): 
s39-chart/
├── Chart.yaml
└── templates/
    ├── deployment.yaml
    └── ingress.yaml              ← Uses deprecated apiVersion!
BASH — Create chart with deprecated API version
# SCENARIO S39: --dry-run Passes But Install Fails
mkdir -p ~/helm-lab/s39-chart/templates
cd ~/helm-lab

cat << 'EOF' > ./s39-chart/Chart.yaml
apiVersion: v2
name: anihpj-dryrun
version: 1.0.0
EOF

cat << 'EOF' > ./s39-chart/templates/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: {{ .Release.Name }}-api
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: {{ .Release.Name }}
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: {{ .Release.Name }}
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: nginx:alpine
EOF

# Ingress uses DEPRECATED apiVersion!
cat << 'EOF' > ./s39-chart/templates/ingress.yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1beta1  # ❌ BUG: Deprecated API version!
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: {{ .Release.Name }}-ingress
spec:
  rules:
    - host: anihpj.com
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /
            backend:
              serviceName: {{ .Release.Name }}-api
              servicePort: 80
EOF

echo "=== STEP 1: --dry-run (client-side only) ==="
echo "This WILL PASS because it only checks template rendering..."
helm install test ./s39-chart --dry-run 2>&1 | head -5
echo "...dry-run PASSED!"

echo ""
echo "=== STEP 2: --dry-run=server (server-side validation) ==="
echo "This WILL FAIL because the API server rejects v1beta1!"
helm install test ./s39-chart --dry-run=server -n anihpj --create-namespace 2>&1 || true
echo ""
echo "=== BUG CONFIRMED: --dry-run passed, --dry-run=server FAILED! ==="
echo "Client-side dry-run only checks template syntax!"
echo "Server-side validation catches deprecated API versions!"
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. helm install test ./s39-chart --dry-run → PASSES! No error!
✗2. helm install test ./s39-chart --dry-run=server → FAILS! API version rejected!
✗3. --dry-run (client) only validates template rendering — not API compatibility!
✗4. Team trusted --dry-run as deployment gate — production install fails!
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check Ingress API version: grep "apiVersion" ./s39-chart/templates/ingress.yaml
→ networking.k8s.io/v1beta1 — DEPRECATED and removed in newer K8s!
2Root cause: helm install --dry-run (without =server) only validates that templates render correctly — it does NOT send resources to the Kubernetes API server. Deprecated API versions, invalid fields, and RBAC issues are invisible to client-side dry-run. Use --dry-run=server to validate against the actual cluster.
3Fix: Always use --dry-run=server in CI/CD, or use kubectl apply --dry-run=server for individual resources
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
--dry-run passes → Template renders OK
②
--dry-run=server fails → API rejects v1beta1
③
Client-side = template only, Server-side = full validation
④
Always use --dry-run=server in CI/CD
⑤
Catches API version + field validation!

Tenet: --dry-run (client) only validates template rendering. --dry-run=server sends resources to the API server for full validation (API versions, field validation, admission webhooks). Always use --dry-run=server in CI/CD to catch deprecated API usage before production deployment. For Helm 3.10+, --dry-run=server is available and recommended.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ helm install test ./s39-chart --dry-run=server Error: unable to build kubernetes objects from release manifest: resource mapping not found for name: "test-ingress" namespace: "anihpj" from "": no matches for kind "Ingress" in version "networking.k8s.io/v1beta1"
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ helm install test ./s39-chart --dry-run=server NAME: test STATUS: deployed (dry-run) ✅
🔧
BASH
# Fix: Update Ingress to current API version
sed -i 's|networking.k8s.io/v1beta1|networking.k8s.io/v1|' ./s39-chart/templates/ingress.yaml

# Also fix the Ingress spec format for v1 (pathType required)
cat > ./s39-chart/templates/ingress.yaml << 'EOF'
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: {{ .Release.Name }}-ingress
spec:
  rules:
    - host: anihpj.com
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: {{ .Release.Name }}-api
                port:
                  number: 80
EOF

# Verify with server-side dry-run
helm install test ./s39-chart --dry-run=server -n anihpj --create-namespace
echo "✅ Server-side validation PASSES with v1 API!"

BASH
rm -rf ~/helm-lab/s39-chart

values.yaml Contains Plaintext AWS Credentials — Security Audit Failure

The Problem: The anihpj team committed values-prod.yaml to Git with plaintext AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY. The security scanner flagged the repo — credentials have been exposed in Git history for 3 weeks. Anyone with repo access can read production AWS keys. Your job: detect the plaintext credentials, understand why values.yaml should NEVER contain secrets, and learn to use helm-secrets with SOPS for secure secret management.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Production security scenario
1

📋 Create Chart with Plaintext Credentials in values.yaml

📖 APP STORY: The anihpj team needed to connect to AWS S3 for job post attachments. A developer added AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY directly into values-prod.yaml and committed it. Three weeks later, a security audit discovered the credentials. The AWS keys had full S3 and RDS access. Git history shows exactly who committed them and when. The team must now rotate all credentials AND scrub Git history — a multi-day incident caused by putting secrets in values.yaml.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE (S40): 
s40-chart/
├── Chart.yaml
├── values-prod.yaml       ← Contains AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID + AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY!
└── templates/
    └── deployment.yaml
BASH — Create chart with plaintext credentials
# SCENARIO S40: Plaintext AWS Credentials in values.yaml
mkdir -p ~/helm-lab/s40-chart/templates
cd ~/helm-lab

cat << 'EOF' > ./s40-chart/Chart.yaml
apiVersion: v2
name: anihpj-secrets
version: 1.0.0
EOF

cat << 'EOF' > ./s40-chart/templates/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: {{ .Release.Name }}-api
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: {{ .Release.Name }}
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: {{ .Release.Name }}
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: nginx:alpine
          env:
            - name: AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID
              value: {{ .Values.aws.accessKeyId | quote }}
            - name: AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY
              value: {{ .Values.aws.secretAccessKey | quote }}
            - name: AWS_REGION
              value: {{ .Values.aws.region | quote }}
EOF

# values-prod.yaml — PLAINTEXT CREDENTIALS!
cat << 'EOF' > ./s40-chart/values-prod.yaml
# ❌ BUG: Plaintext AWS credentials in values file!
# This file will be committed to Git — exposing production keys!
aws:
  region: us-east-1
  accessKeyId: AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE       # ❌ REAL-LOOKING ACCESS KEY!
  secretAccessKey: wJalrXUtnFEMI/K7MDENG/bPxRfiCYEXAMPLEKEY  # ❌ SECRET KEY EXPOSED!
  s3Bucket: anihpj-jobpost-uploads
EOF

echo "=== Security scan of values-prod.yaml ==="
echo "Scanning for AWS credential patterns..."
grep -n "AKIA\|wJalr\|SECRET_ACCESS\|ACCESS_KEY" ./s40-chart/values-prod.yaml
echo ""
echo "=== BUG CONFIRMED: Plaintext AWS credentials found! ==="
echo "AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY are in plaintext!"
echo "If committed to Git, these are exposed FOREVER in Git history!"
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. grep "AKIA\|SECRET_ACCESS" ./s40-chart/values-prod.yaml → Credentials FOUND in plaintext!
✗2. Access key ID pattern AKIA* is an AWS IAM key — real credential!
✗3. If this file was committed, credentials are in Git history FOREVER!
✗4. Anyone with repository access can read production AWS keys!
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Scan for credential patterns: grep -E "AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}|wJalr|SECRET" ./s40-chart/values-prod.yaml
→ Matches found! AWS access key and secret key in plaintext!
2Root cause: values.yaml files are committed to Git — they are part of the chart source code. NEVER put plaintext secrets in values.yaml or values-prod.yaml. Use helm-secrets plugin with SOPS + AWS KMS/GCP KMS/Age for encryption, or use External Secrets Operator to inject secrets at runtime from a vault.
3Fix: Use helm-secrets plugin to encrypt values files, or move secrets to Kubernetes Secrets with External Secrets Operator
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Security scan → Plaintext AWS keys found
②
values-prod.yaml committed to Git
③
Credentials exposed in Git history FOREVER
④
Use helm-secrets + SOPS for encryption
⑤
Rotate compromised credentials immediately!

Tenet: values.yaml is committed to Git — NEVER put plaintext secrets in it. Use helm-secrets plugin with SOPS (supports AWS KMS, GCP KMS, Azure Key Vault, PGP, Age). Encrypt the values file: sops -e values-prod.yaml > values-prod.yaml.enc. Install with: helm secrets install. Alternative: use External Secrets Operator to sync secrets from AWS Secrets Manager / HashiCorp Vault into Kubernetes Secrets at runtime.
